The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".

The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment.

Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.

Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".

He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.

Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.

The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.

Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery".

The Pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – the first US citizen to do so.

The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery.

A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after a man climbed into a tiger enclosure and was fatally attacked by the animal.

An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. Police said the man sadly died at the scene.

A park spokesperson said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" remain with the man's family and confirmed the Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.

The spokesperson says many people had contacted them about the tiger and he was safe and well.

Staff who were at the scene who were "deeply affected by events" would receive specialist support, they added.

South Yorkshire Police said the man's family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said in a statement.

It added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage."

Earlier on Saturday, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".

Ella Ford, 24, from Moreton, Wirral, had visited the park with her boyfriend and filmed the tiger moments before the attack.

She described seeing a man by the tiger enclosure "pacing around with his headphones in".

A few minutes later, she saw the same man had "climbed up onto the barriers".

A woman was close by talking to him, she said, before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there".

Ford said she then witnessed the tiger grab hold of the man, who she reported as "shouting for help".

She estimates around 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park.

She described members of the public as being "confused, like what on earth's going on?"

"I just know some man was obviously trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything," she said.

Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, had been enjoying a family day out when park staff told them the site was being evacuated.

She said she had heard what sounded like "gunshots" and an air ambulance had circled above.

Pelham added: "There was a big, black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure."

She praised park staff for their handling of the incident, saying it had been "very, very well organised".

Foreign Secretary and MP for Doncaster North Ed Miliband said he was "deeply saddened" to hear of the incident and sent his "thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died."

He added he was "very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded."

Lee Pitcher, MP for Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme, expressed his gratitude to emergency services for their response.

In a statement shared to social media, he said he was "deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident that has taken place at Yorkshire Wildlife Park today".

Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with its Land of the Tigers area opening in 2011.

The purpose-built two-acre reserve is home to Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with around 500 left in the wild.

Photos of the enclosure on the park's website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.

Speaking outside Drumcree Church on Saturday, Lockhart said her constituents are angry.

"They're angry at the secretary of state for his intervention, but the most palpable anger is at Michelle O'Neill, this self-proclaimed 'first minister for all' for breaking the law flagrantly on the Garvaghy Road, and thumbing her nose at unionism and at the Orange Order and at this community."

Police had repeatedly warned those taking part in the unnotified protest that they could be liable for arrest.

O'Neill has defended her involvement, saying she was standing with the local community in opposition to an Orange Order parade through the area.

She previously dismissed a call from the DUP to resign over her role in protests telling the assembly she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them".

The DUP (Democratic Unionist Party) share power with Sinn Féin in the Northern Ireland Executive, but Lockhart says it can no longer be business as usual.

"You can not continue to engage with someone who is so blatant in her disregard and disdain for a large section of this community," she said.

"People want to see consequences, and we have said very clearly, profound consequence, and therefore we should use whatever is in our armoury to ensure that Michelle O'Neill, the person who really is supposed to be that first minister for all, as she claims, is dealt with in the appropriate way," she added.

The DUP could remove O'Neill from the first minister's position if the deputy first minister quits.

That role is held by Emma Little-Pengelly, but that seems unlikely.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that Lockhart "is right that the options are there", but stopped short of suggesting his party may collapse the executive.

Speaking on BBC News NI's Sunday Politics programme, he echoed Lockhart's words that "it will not be business as usual", but added: "does collapsing Stormont bring the Orangemen home"?

Robinson also called on the chief constable to "be very open" in telling the public "what was the threat that he perceived" when he asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission's determination.

He said he "certainly wouldn't" want Sir Chris to govern Northern Ireland if the executive did collapse.

TUV leader Jim Allister said he was "disappointed" by the DUP's "limp response".

He said Robinson promised "profound consequences, and then when he's asked what they are, it emerges that the Emperor of the DUP has no clothes".

Allister accused the DUP of "doing nothing", which he said showed "there are no political consequences" for Sinn Féin.

Sinn Féin assembly member John O'Dowd rejected claims that the move to ban the parade went in favour of his party, saying "the decision went in the way of the residents" who he said have "faced an awful four weeks" since the application to walk was lodged.

O'Dowd, who is also finance minister in the executive, was one of a number of Sinn Féin politicians who joined a protest with residents on the Garvaghy Road.

On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.

Speaking on BBC News NI's Sunday Politics programme, O'Dowd said: "I own my decision", adding that he thinks it was "the right thing to do".

"I got into politics to stand against the intimidation of communities such as the Garvaghy Road, who went through hell and high water over many, many years.

"I stood with the people of the Garvaghy Road. I will continue to stand with the people of Garvaghy Road because it was the right thing to do."

He added that he believes the community responded in "a peaceful, democratic way" to the decision to approve a march on 27 September.

"I would appeal, not only to Gavin, but maybe hopelessly to Carla and others, to calm their language and to show responsible leadership and calm leadership at this stage," he added.

"I don't think that continued demonisation or an attempt to criminalise the community of the Garvaghy Road is an appropriate way forward.

"What we need in Portadown is reconciliation."

The Parades Commission ruled that the march on Sunday 27 September could go ahead with restrictions in place.

That parade did not happen and, after a series of legal challenges and talks between residents and Orangemen, the secretary of state banned the procession on Friday.

Sir Chris Bryant said his decision to ban the Drumcree parade "was in the best interests of peace".

The secretary of state said he received advice from the PSNI chief constable that allowing the procession to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest.

On Saturday, a High Court judge said a legal appeal by Orangemen following the secretary of state's decision was not an emergency case and adjourned the hearing until Monday.

Lockhart said the 35 Orangemen from Portadown District Lodge had "stood lawfully" for the last two weeks on Drumcree hill.

"I've been on this hill from I was 10 years of age, it means something to me. It means a lot to my constituents here in Upper Bann," she said.

So does the Upper Bann MP still have confidence in her own party?

"I have confidence that I will ensure that my constituents' voices are heard within the party, and I will ensure that I continue to represent the views here in Portadown," she said.

AI is creating a 'human premium' for art made by people. But will it hold?

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 23:18:16 GMT

A few weeks back, in a former bank building that's now a music venue in Falmouth, Cornwall, I was DJ-ing at a night I run called Rave Machine. It was a noisy, high-energy, sweaty affair, just as a night's dancing should be.

All of the elements - the crowd, performers, staff, music, the journey home - connected to create something special, a one-off. It was also completely human.

Something, in theory, well out of reach of what technology could possibly offer.

In the DJ world, though, technology has already changed the equation. In the 1990s, a DJ had to not only pick the tracks, but also thread them together armed only with vinyl records, a pair of turntables and a mixer. Now, much more assistance is on offer, including software that will sync beats on different tracks should you ask it to (I don't). Apple Music and Spotify have an AI tune-mixing option too.

If you were out dancing, would it matter to you if a DJ was, well, not really DJing? If you loved the music being played, would you care if technology was doing the work?

It's a question that generative AI - the type of AI that creates content - is asking of us all. One of the thrills of that night in Falmouth was seeing our special guest, Andy Cato from Groove Armada, artfully weaving an array of tracks. How would I feel if a DJ was just pressing play? (And that does happen).

I mention all of this because that experience in Falmouth connects to a far broader question: whether we actually care if a piece of art has been created by a human, be that a painting, song, book, poem, or any other type of art.

The music platform Deezer says 44% of tracks uploaded to it are AI-generated. Its research also found that 97% of listeners couldn't tell what was AI-generated and what wasn't. But here's a third statistic: more than half of those surveyed said they did care if it was made by AI. They want humans to be involved.

Daniel Susskind, an economics professor at King's College London, says many of us place huge value on the human role in making art. It's what makes the creative process different from more functional, practical tasks, he thinks.

"I was once in a room of accountants, and one of them stood up and said, 'My clients come to me for the personal touch, the human process'," he remembers. "And I said, 'That isn't why they come to you, they come because they want their taxes done properly'."

But it's different with art, he says. "If I walk into the Sistine Chapel and look at the ceiling, I think not only is that extraordinarily beautiful, but isn't it amazing that a human hand, flesh and blood like my own, came up with that. A mind like mine dreamt that up," he says.

As Susskind describes it, what we value isn't just the destination, it's the knowledge that a human - one of us - got us there. We can wonder at that achievement.

Of course, it could be argued that computers and AI software were themselves created by humans. If Susskind feels awe walking into the Sistine Chapel, others might experience awe of a different type using a chatbot like ChatGPT.

Susskind points to another example, this time a chess match in 1997, when a world champion, Garry Kasparov, lost for the first time to a computer, Deep Blue. At the time, there were fears the computer's success would mean our interest in chess would wane. In fact, chess is more popular than ever, played by millions.

"It wasn't simply the moves on the board that people care about. It's the fact that it's a human being sitting behind them, moving those pieces along that matters," Susskind argues.

And some think that the advent of AI has actually placed extra value on things created by people. You might call that a human premium.

Kyle Chayka, a journalist at The New Yorker focused on technology, says AI writing is now widely considered to be "generic, obsequious and banal". As a result, he says, "I think readers are coming to value very obviously personal writing, and maybe even writing that's messier, less structurally sound or composed or perfected, than they maybe once would've desired."

Chayka goes on: "I think illustration and graphic design is going in the same direction, where the average is too easily accessible, and so designers are leaning into being weirder and more eye-catching and more unusual, trying to find things that AI can't generate so easily."

In response to the surge in AI-created content, academics are racing to develop a universally recognised symbol to denote something that is "human made" (similar to the "Fairtrade" label that emerged in the 1980s). Labels like "AI-free" are already appearing on covers of some books, films, and albums.

For C Thi Nguyen, a philosophy professor at the University of Utah, it's a question of our underlying values.

He says you can often work out your values by following what he calls a "why chain". If you like something or want to do something, ask "why?". If the answer is to make money or be successful, keep asking 'why?' When the process ends, that will be what you really value, he explains.

The question, he says, is whether human involvement and shared human experience will keep its place at the end of the "why chain".

Author John Lanchester is optimistic. He thinks the value of what only humans can do will prevail. In fact, he sympathises with the idea of a 'human premium'.

"If you commodify one kind of thing, the things you can't commodify start to seem more important," he tells me.

All of that might sound heartening for people hoping that humans will remain central to the creation of culture.

But I'm not so sure. The amount of AI-generated content is increasing so quickly that we may soon struggle to distinguish what has or hasn't involved AI.

You may well have seen coverage of the AI 'actor' Tilly Norwood, made last year by a company that bills itself as the world's "first AI talent studio". The Screen Actors Guild in the US was not impressed. "It has no life experience to draw from, no emotion, and, from what we've seen, audiences aren't interested in watching computer-generated content untethered from the human experience," they wrote.

I'm not saying AI will replace actors - of course not. But what feels untethered and strange now, may not, in some situations, feel so strange in time.

It's also worth remembering that long before Large Language Models went mainstream, we'd already allowed technology to shape our cultural tastes.

As recently as the 2000s, we still sought out lots of the culture we consumed. We'd buy a book, a cinema ticket, an album. Sometimes we still do.

But increasingly, culture just arrives - in an endless stream, sorted and served by an algorithm that is constantly predicting our tastes.

At first glance, this sounds convenient. The work's being done for us. But as the role of the algorithm goes up, so the role of humans goes down.

"There's the mythical figure of your big brother's friend or something, who passes on good music taste to you," says Chayka, whose book Filterworld explores the impacts of algorithms on culture. "And now we rely on algorithmic recommendations to do that same thing for us. To introduce us to new things."

I recognise this from my own habits. Back in the 1990s, when I started collecting dance music, I'd find new music through record shops and recommendations from people I trusted. I can still do that, and do. But these days the algorithm's doing a lot of that work for me - and it can be really helpful. I'll find tunes I wouldn't have discovered otherwise.

To an extent, I am letting technology guide me.

Chayka thinks algorithms have made us lazy, and "prevent us from going deeper" in our cultural taste. Sometimes we might find a piece of art that requires work - a long, difficult book, perhaps, or a weird-seeming movie. "It might alienate us initially, but eventually it inspires us," Chayka says.

"I think that kind of culture has fallen by the wayside in favour of culture as content to consume that's not going to change your life, it's just going to turn your brain off for a few hours."

And it's a self-reinforcing loop; creators adapt their work as they seek out the attention the algorithm can provide.

And here's the key point: this shift - to discovering culture via algorithms - is one we've already largely accepted. So when AI starts making books, films, and music in large numbers - might we just shrug and accept that too?

Back in 1986, in Washington DC, protesting teachers lined the streets outside a convention centre. They weren't angry about their wages or budget cuts. In this case, the object of their ire was the calculator. Maths teacher John Saxon had taken up the cause. "The kids are not learning their math facts because they're becoming calculator hooked," he proclaimed. " If they had given me a black box, I wouldn't know that… six times eight's 48 'cause it rhymes, and seven times nine is 63 'cause it does not."

We all have our ways of remembering times tables.

Needless to say, this is an argument that Saxon lost. But some of those arguments feel familiar.

Of course, some things are definitely out of range of technology, at least for now. Think of my sweaty DJ night in Falmouth a few weeks ago, with 250 other ravers.

Alex Mahon says she's noticed an uptick in appreciation for in-person experiences like these - perhaps as a backlash to the amount of our lives now spent on a smartphone screen.

She's chief executive of Superstruct Entertainment, one of the world's leading festival and live entertainment groups.

"People want to go to more live things," she says. "They want to have things that are unforeseeable… unpredictable. The special moment is live. The excitement, the discovery is hearing it in person with others."

In the case of culture, when is it OK to outsource to technology, and when is it not? The more I look at this, the less I'm sure we can assume what choices we'll make.

Each of us will have to decide when it matters if something is made by a human.

Three friends on their student debt: One paid off, one chipping away and one creeping up

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 23:17:03 GMT

When Lizzy, Libby and Charlotte met as freshers in 2012, their main responsibility was making it to lectures on time after early morning sports practice.

Their student debt, growing with interest from the day they took out their loans, was the last thing on their minds.

"The conversation was just so much less relevant at that time," says Charlotte. "As our careers have gone on and our paths have diverged more and more... those conversations start to come more to the forefront."

The friends, now in their early 30s, went to the University of Newcastle in the same year tuition fees tripled to £9,000 a year in England and Wales, and new loans called Plan 2 were introduced. Each borrowed about £37,500 to cover three years of tuition and living costs.

This year marks a decade since the first students in their year started repaying.

They may have started out in the same position, but over that time their career trajectories, life choices and earnings have shaped how much they've repaid, how much interest they've racked up, and how much they owe - with very different outcomes.

Student loans have come under scrutiny this year and there's been a particular backlash over Plan 2 loans. The government has said it wants to make the whole system fairer and campaigners are waiting to see what, if anything, changes in this month's Budget.

The anger about Plan 2 grew after the government announced updated terms in November. The income at which graduates start repaying is set to be frozen for three years, meaning graduates would start making payments sooner and pay more each month.

But it has also been brewing because the interest rate is higher than most other student loan plans, and many have seen their debts rise despite making monthly repayments.

"Since April this year, I've paid off in the region of £450 and I've accrued over £500 in interest," says Charlotte, a physiotherapist in Bristol.

She did a master's degree after uni and worked in the NHS before moving to the private sector. She earns about £50,000, but her loan is still going up.

"It makes me angry... it's just disheartening."

All three friends earn above the national average of £39,039. But research from the Institute for Fiscal Studies in February suggests Plan 2 graduates need to earn about £63,000 or more for a loan balance of £50,000 to start going down.

"I just had no concept that the debt was going to go up," says Libby, who remembers being in tears when her first student loan letter came through after graduating.

Now a project manager in a housing association and living in Worcester, she earns £72,000 and says her student loan balance has hovered at about £47,000 for a number of years. But she is currently on maternity leave and knows the interest will continue to accrue while her earnings - and therefore monthly repayments - drop.

"It feels like I will never pay it off, so it's something that I'm kind of just sucking up until the loan is written off," she says.

Her partner did the same course, starting a year before her and before tuition fees near tripled with the introduction of Plan 2 loans.

She says it is "so frustrating" that she has to pay out thousands of pounds a year more on her student debt.

Current and former students have different student loan plans depending on where they live in the UK and when they went to university. Plan 2 loans were given out in England for a little more than a decade from 2012 and are still issued in Wales.

The debt is written off after 30 years.

Lizzy, who studied economics and now works in financial services and lives in Bristol, is the highest paid of the friends, who bonded over rowing at university. She earns £85,000 a year and decided last year to clear her student debt by borrowing money from her family instead.

She had estimated that, based on her current earnings trajectory, she would repay her loan in 11 years. By paying off her debt in full early she has accrued less interest and hopes to repay her family in four years - saving about £20,000.

The amount graduates are voluntarily repaying towards their student loans has been growing. MoneySavingExpert. com founder Martin Lewis has warned that only higher earners could benefit from making voluntary repayments and most should not be "panicked into overpaying".

Finance journalist Holly Mead told the BBC it could make sense for those who are confident they will clear the debt and can make "a really significant overpayment" of tens of thousands of pounds, like Lizzy.

But smaller voluntary repayments could mean "you're just voluntarily paying more interest that you don't need to pay", she added.

Lizzy says she knows there are many "scenarios in which it doesn't pay off" for people to repay it early.

"I made a gamble on my future self to actually repay it," she says. "I'm in a very privileged position to be able to do that... Buying your way out of the system or not being in at all is in itself a luxury. It buys you freedom."

She and Libby finished their A-levels in 2011 but took a year out before going to university - Libby on a gap year, and Lizzy to resit economics after missing the grade she'd hoped for by a single mark.

Lizzy says she knew the delay would mean her fees would be higher, but "it was never explained" that the repayment terms would "look and feel very different".

"I think that's something that took me probably the best part of 10 years to understand," she adds, noting that her twin sister did start university in 2011 and had less debt as a result.

"Whether you went to uni in 2012 or 2011 actually financially has a huge impact, and it shouldn't," she says.

There's been lots of discussion about what teenagers were told about Plan 2 loans before they took them out. In March, a BBC investigation found the Department for Education (DfE) had compared monthly repayments to £30-a-month phone contracts in presentations at schools in England a decade ago.

An inquiry by MPs then concluded that this amounted to "mis-selling" because it was inaccurate for higher earners.

Last month, the government said university applicants in England would be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out.

All three friends follow the Rethink Repayment campaign on social media. It was set up by Oliver Gardner, who says the first Plan 2 borrowers are grappling with competing financial pressures such as getting on the property ladder and starting families.

"Maybe in your 20s, you can get away without saving as much, potentially. But now people are like, 'we need the savings to do these big things that we want to do with our lives'," he says.

The campaign wants a lower Plan 2 interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse that decision to freeze the threshold at £29,385 in England for three years from 2027 - which, while it is not the first freeze, sparked this year's debate.

Gardner said the government was "engaging much more openly and honestly" but "the onus is very much on them in the upcoming October budget to take this by the reins" because graduates would not accept "minor tinkering around the edges".

The DfE said it was "taking decisive action to improve the student finance system and break down barriers to accessing university" by increasing maximum maintenance loans, reintroducing targeted maintenance grants and having "raised the repayment threshold for Plan 2 loans for the first time since 2021".

"We will continue to look for ways to make the system fairer for students, graduates and taxpayers in a financially sustainable way," it said.

Lizzy, Libby and Charlotte feel grateful they met back in 2012, and say that if they had their time again they would go back to university.

"I still wouldn't change my university experience," says Charlotte, "but would go back and do something different in the sense of my course and my career trajectory? Probably."

Number of known species of giant waterlilies almost doubles

New Scientist October 08, 2026

Giant waterlilies are not exactly inconspicuous plants. But in the past few years, we have discovered no fewer than three new species, taking the total to five. The latest species to be described was identified with the help of social media, satellite photos and a mad jungle dash in the dark.

“I think it’s incredible that we find something so new, which is so large, in this world where we think everything is already known,” says Maarten Christenhusz at the Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland, who has helped describe two of the new species.

Why rediscovering extinct species can actually be a bad thing

Giant waterlilies are famed for their massive leaves, which grow up to 3 metres wide. For many decades, just two species were known: Victoria amazonica and Victoria cruziana. Then in 2016, Carlos Magdalena at the Royal Botanic Gardens in Kew, London, noticed that giant waterlilies grown from seeds from Bolivia were a bit different, with even larger leaves. In 2022, Magdalena and his colleagues published a paper showing that this was a new species, Victoria boliviana.

Advertisement

Magdalena hasn’t stopped there. In 2021, Jeremiah Harris, who runs a carnivorous plant business in the US, posted pictures online that he took while swimming near the Inírida river in Colombia next to what he assumed was V. amazonica.

Magdalena was struck by the photos because scientists had thought there were no giant waterlilies in this region. “This river is geographically completely separated from the Amazon, and has been for millions of years, and that is why this is such an interesting find,” says Christenhusz.

See Chris Packham at New Scientist Live 2026

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their team examined satellite photos and found telltale green dots confirming there really were giant waterlilies growing there. They then organised an expedition to the region. The team found two plants but neither was flowering – and analysing the flowers is a crucial step in establishing whether a waterlily really is a new species.

At 11pm on the last night of the expedition, with the plane due to leave at 9am, the researchers seemed to have failed. Then one of the guides, Gustavo Melo from the Indigenous Tucano community, said he knew where some more giant waterlilies were growing. The team set off by boat in the dark, and found five plants in a small lake just before sunrise, including some that were flowering.

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues have now published a paper describing the new species, which they have named Victoria colombiana. It differs from V. amazonica in the orientation of the spines beneath the leaves, and in the shape of its flowers and fruits. The spines are a defence against manatees and plant-eating fish, Christenhusz says, so they vary between species depending on which herbivores are most prevalent.

Botanists have finally proved what Charles Darwin was unable to nail down – that a genus of plants known to catch insects also digests them, suggesting the extent of plant carnivory has been underestimated

As far as the team is aware, V. colombiana is found in only one small area. A single event, such as a pollution spill, could wipe out the entire species, says Christenhusz. But the team is planning to try to collect seeds to help ensure the species survives.

Meanwhile, Magdalena also realised that the giant waterlilies growing in the Pantanal region of South America, hundreds of kilometres to the south-east of Colombia, must have been isolated from other populations for a very long time. Sure enough, genetic studies revealed that they are another distinct species, despite looking very similar to V. cruziana. Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues will publish a paper soon to describe this fifth species, which they have decided to name Victoria mattogrossensis.

The big unanswered question about Russia’s ‘plague’ death

New Scientist October 08, 2026

The recent death of a lab worker at a plague research institute sparked fears of another pandemic. But on 7 October, Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said it was ending precautionary measures and that most of the nearly 200 people put under quarantine have been released, after tests found no dangerous pathogens.

Was this all much ado about nothing? After all, we still don’t know what caused the pneumonia that killed the lab worker, nor, if it was plague, how she became infected. And the most pressing question of all: why did Russia respond so dramatically to her death? The measures taken went beyond what would be expected for a case of plague. There are two broad possibilities: conspiracy or colossal screw-up.

Nearly 200 people isolated after lab worker in Russia dies of plague

What we know is that Daria Shipilova, a 28-year-old lab worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia, died of pneumonia on 2 October, three days after being admitted to a local hospital. A “DN Shipilova” is an author on an abstract from a conference earlier this year about testing plague strains for antibiotic resistance, suggesting Shipilova worked directly with the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis.

Advertisement

After her death, nearly 200 people who might have had contact with her were placed in quarantine. Around 60 employees at the institute were reportedly locked in for days, and Federal Security Service officers escorted ambulances carrying those quarantined. The head of Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, is said to have travelled to Irkutsk – a 6-hour flight from Moscow – on 2 October for an emergency meeting about “a particularly dangerous infection”, and some local companies imposed mask mandates.

The thing is, there are many plague cases around the world each year and they don’t trigger this kind of response. This is because basic hygiene measures can prevent the spread of the bacterium, while prompt treatment with antibiotics can stop people who might have been infected from developing any symptoms.

DNA evidence shows that plague bacteria devastated a community in Siberia more than 5000 years ago, challenging the idea that there were no major disease outbreaks before the advent of farming and large settlements

For instance, in 2025, a young man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague – where Y. pestis infects the lungs – acquired from sick cats. The 46 people he had potentially been in contact with were given a seven-day course of antibiotics, in line with guidelines from the World Health Organization. End of story.

So why did Russia quarantine all contacts? One explanation is that health officials knew Shipilova was exposed to something more dangerous than a natural strain of Y. pestis.

“Physical lockdown indicates it cannot be controlled with prophylactic antibiotics, implying engineered pan-resistance or that it isn’t plague at all,” biologist Kevin Esvelt at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology posted on social media. The response “clearly indicates that Russia believes an epidemic is possible – and that the responsible agent is likely a pandemic weapon or otherwise embarrassing for the government”.

Free newsletter

Esvelt created the first artificial gene drive capable of wiping out an entire species, and has since pivoted to preventing bioterrorism. He may well be right. There are certainly good reasons to suspect a cover-up.

We know that the Soviet Union had a massive bioweapons programme that included trying to make Y. pestis resistant to antibiotics (the “engineered pan-resistance” Esvelt mentioned), and it had a long history of denying related accidents. For instance, in 1979, at least 68 people died after the accidental release of anthrax from a bioweapons facility in the city of Sverdlovsk. The Soviet Union claimed the deaths were caused by food poisoning.

What’s more, a 2006 paper by Raymond Zilinskas at the Center for Nonproliferation Studies in California says the Irkutsk institute was involved in bioweapon research, though this was only “a small portion” of its activities. Bioweapons research has continued in Russia and probably expanded recently, though there is no evidence the Irkutsk institute is still involved.

Plague, leprosy, smallpox and other diseases didn’t jump from animals to humans when we thought. Ancient DNA is revealing where they come from and how they changed history

The other explanation is a secondary screw-up: that the officials who imposed the quarantine measures didn’t know what killed Shipilova and leapt to the conclusion it was something nasty. It can take three days to test for Y. pestis, after all, so the results might not have been available on 2 October. Even if the results were known, officials might not have believed them, given Russia’s history of lying about such things.

Alternatively, maybe Shipilova had a strain of plague that could have been treated with antibiotics if they had been given early enough (all the strains that were tested in the abstract linked to her were susceptible to these drugs), but officials overreacted because they weren’t aware of the appropriate procedures.

What really happened may never be clear. After all, Russia doesn’t have a reputation for being trustworthy – so even if it tells the truth, we won’t know it.

AI or ‘super intelligence’? Trump isn’t the only one who is confused

New Scientist October 08, 2026

In the decades since the field began, most of the debate surrounding artificial intelligence has been about the intelligence part: can machines really think like we do? But in recent weeks, US President Donald Trump has kicked off an argument about the other part – and joined a long tradition of shifting the goal posts when it comes to AI.

“The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing,” said Trump during a speech at the UN General Assembly on 22 September. He is calling for artificial intelligence to be rebranded as “super intelligence”, backing this move with an executive order signed on 29 September and the launch this week of a body called the Super Intelligence Force for coordinating US AI policy.

The most interesting mathematical discoveries in OpenAI’s 722 new papers

Putting aside the fact that “Super Intelligence Force” sounds like a Saturday morning cartoon, what are we to make of this attempted rebrand? Trump isn’t actually alone in seeking to distance modern AI systems from the original conception of AI in the 1940s and 50s. Last year, Meta CEO Mark Zuckberg published a note declaring that “superintelligence” (one word) is now in sight. Reaching further back, the word was originally popularised by philosopher Nick Bostrom as the title of his 2014 book.

Advertisement

For me, Trump’s super intelligence and Bostrom’s superintelligence have distinct meanings that are worth preserving. Trump’s rebrand is an effort to cement US dominance in the field of AI – his executive order states that “the term ‘Super Intelligence’ more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies”. But superintelligence as envisioned by Bostrom goes far beyond the capabilities of our current AI systems. To understand why, we need to dig into history a bit more.

Long before the birth of ChatGPT, AI researchers distinguished between weak AI and strong AI, terms first defined by philosopher John Searle in a 1980 paper titled “Minds, brains, and programs”. Loosely speaking, he considered weak AI to be a computer simulation of a human mind, but not an actual mind itself, whereas he felt strong AI describes actual cognition emerging from software. Searle dismissed this latter idea as ridiculous: “No one supposes… that a computer simulation of a rainstorm will leave us all drenched. Why on earth would anyone suppose that a computer simulation of understanding actually understood anything?” Decades on, I find it hard to disagree.

In the wake of Searle’s influential paper, weak and strong AI underwent their own Trump-style rebranding, as people began to discuss differences in AI capabilities rather than AI consciousness – perhaps because the former is much easier to measure and moves the arena of debate from the philosophy department to the computer science lab. Weak AI merged with another term, narrow AI, to mean a system capable of human-level performance at a specific task. We have been living with narrow AI for decades, depending on how you want to define it, encompassing everything from spam filters to chess playing to driverless cars. In some sense, once something becomes achievable by narrow AI, it is just software – a phenomenon known as the AI effect.

Strong AI, meanwhile, gave way to general AI – a system capable of human-level performance at any task. A general AI is a highly desirable goal because it means that, rather than having to build a new system for every possible task, the AI would be able to transfer learning from one domain to another, just as a human can. In 2002, general AI morphed into “artificial general intelligence”, or AGI, largely due to Shane Legg (who would go on to co-found the firm DeepMind) popularising the term.

Most of the big AI companies, including DeepMind and OpenAI, were founded with the stated goal of achieving AGI. In the 2010s, this was seen as a slightly wacky and sci-fi research goal. Today, it is a business model, with trillions of dollars of investment riding on building an AGI in the near-future.

Despite this, definitions of AGI are woolly. OpenAI’s charter defines it as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. An agreement between OpenAI and Microsoft that was leaked in 2024 defines it as a system capable of generating $100 billion in profit. OpenAI isn’t yet profitable, with expenditure far exceeding revenue, but that didn’t prevent its president, Greg Brockman, from saying “welcome to the AGI era” with the release of its Astra model in September.

However you define AGI, it isn’t the same thing as superintelligence. Bostrom defines this plainly in his book as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest”. In other words, a superintelligence must be more cognitively capable than any human scientist, artist, philosopher or other cognitive performer that ever lived. It isn’t enough to be better than Albert Einstein or Marie Curie – you must also beat William Shakespeare, Leonardo da Vinci, Steve Jobs, Jane Austen and many, many others. Clearly, we haven’t achieved superintelligence. A real superintelligence would probably transform the world in ways we can’t imagine.

There is one problem running though all of these definitions, though, and it lies in the second part of AI: what actually is intelligence, and how do we measure different levels of it?

The standard answer is intelligence quotient, or IQ. Attempts to measure the IQ of various high-end AI models (by having them produce answers to IQ test questions) give ranges of 130 to 150 IQ, although this is complicated by the fact that the tests themselves may have formed part of the models’ training data. Human IQ scores have reached over 200, often in young children because the scores depend on age, but higher scores are increasingly difficult to measure reliably. More pressingly, IQ is now widely considered to be a flawed measure of intelligence, rooted in eugenics, that ignores many aspects of human capability. Attempting to apply it to AI feels fairly fruitless, then.

As an alternative, some computer scientists have tried to come up with AI-specific intelligence tests. One of these is ARC-AGI, which looks not only at the capabilities of a model, but also at the cost of running it, meaning that less computationally intensive models can score higher. The test is now in its third iteration, and one of OpenAI’s latest models, GPT-6.1 Sol, scores 96.2 per cent, completing the test at a reasonably cheap $3800. Does that make it AGI? I don’t think so, and I would expect a fourth version of the ARC-AGI test to come along soon, resetting the bar that models must exceed.

Does this mean we will never achieve AGI, and then superintelligence? Despite the certainty of the AI firms that we will – which is probably half real belief and half marketing – I think at this point, it is impossible to say. The meanings of these terms and our methods for evaluating them are constantly shifting. What seemed liked magic in 2022 – a computer that could answer you back – is now an annoyance in 2026, with Google’s AI Overviews often producing confidently incorrect information at the top of your search results.

Today, the most impressive achievements in AI seem to come from mathematics, but perhaps that will soon become passé. My feeling is that, if AGI ever comes, there won’t be one moment in which we declare it has arrived, but rather a gradual realisation that it is already here and we’ve just started calling it something else.

OpenAI mistranslated mathematics into code for its Navier-Stokes proof

New Scientist October 08, 2026

OpenAI appears to have made a subtle error when publishing its proofs of the Navier-Stokes problem, a team of mathematicians has claimed. The error doesn’t mean that the proofs are incorrect or that OpenAI hasn’t correctly solved the problem, but it does call into question whether mathematical results generated by AI models can always be relied on.

“What has to be done with all of these large language model-generated proofs is that they will have to be read by humans, and this creates an enormous extra burden on mathematicians,” says Anders Hansen at the University of Cambridge.

On 8 September, OpenAI announced that it had found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the most famous open problems in mathematics. It published the proof in two versions – one written in “natural language”, meaning a combination of English and mathematical symbols, as a human mathematician would write, and another written in the computer code Lean. The Lean proof is meant to be a formalisation of the natural-language version, allowing a computer to mechanically verify that all of its logical statements are true. The problem is, say Hansen and his team, that they don’t match.

Advertisement

“This formalisation process is trying to replace peer review,” says team member Fabian Circelli, also at the University of Cambridge. “Peer review would mean that human eyes look at the proofs. But what we’ve shown in this paper is that using this type of AI auto-formalisation can’t serve the same purpose.”

The most interesting mathematical discoveries in OpenAI’s 722 new papers

To be clear, the researchers aren’t saying that OpenAI has failed to solve the Navier-Stokes problem. It is entirely possible that both the natural-language proof and the Lean one provide a solution, just as there are hundreds of valid proofs of Pythagoras’s theorem. Instead, their point is a more subtle one: that OpenAI’s model has “mistranslated” when converting into Lean.

“We are not saying that the natural-language proof is wrong,” says Hansen. “Nor do we say that it is correct.” The issue is that OpenAI presents the two proofs as identical, stating on Github that “This repository contains Lean 4 formalizations of the results presented in [the paper] ‘Finite time blowup for Navier–Stokes’”.

This mistranslation occurs because the AI has to produce a Lean proof that “compiles”, meaning that the computer code is fully self-consistent and doesn’t produce an error, says Hansen. If, in the process of auto-formalisation, the AI finds a section of the proof that doesn’t compile, it will attempt to find a workaround even if it means diverging from the proof as written in natural language.

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

The team’s specific claim hinges on part of the proofs called Lemma 8.6. In the natural-language proof, an equation in this part requires that a certain value be below m + 4, where m is a whole number. In the Lean proof, the equivalent value is required to be below m + 5, which is mathematically weaker.

To understand why, imagine being asked to solve the equation x + 3 = 6, to which the answer is x = 3. It is possible to write a proof that x must be less than 4, and also that x must be less than 5. Both of these are perfectly true mathematical statements, but they say different things. The latter proof allows more possible answers for x, making it mathematically weaker.

OpenAI told New Scientist that it is aware of the mismatch between the natural-language proof and the Lean code, and that this doesn’t mean that either proof is invalid. It says it will rectify any errors in the natural-language proof as they are found, and will also continue the process of formalising the 722 maths papers the firm released this week, only some of which are accompanied by Lean proofs, which themselves haven’t been checked by hand.

Finding the divergence involved a slightly surreal process of asking ChatGPT to look for potential discrepancies between the natural-language and Lean proofs, then checking them by hand. Many of the discrepancies suggested by ChatGPT turned out, on inspection, to be consistent after all. “Going through all of these things manually was a nightmare,” says Hansen.

In all, it took the team about two weeks to identify a true discrepancy, compared with the 88 hours OpenAI said its agents spent generating the proofs. “OpenAI boast about how quickly they were able to generate this result, but that’s only part of the process,” says team member Alexander Bastounis at King’s College London.

Answering the question of whether AI models can accurately auto-formalise mathematics is essential if mathematicians are to trust these results. Anders and his team have demonstrated that it is possible for ChatGPT to produce a Lean version of a proof that doesn’t match the original natural language one, with the AI silently altering the logical argument in the process to cover up any errors. “It is trying to help me, but by doing that, it is not helping,” says Hansen.

Subscriber-only newsletter

If this were to happen for a long and complicated proof, it would be very difficult for anyone to notice without inspecting both versions in detail. This issue is only more pressing because of the batch of 722 papers OpenAI just released. If we think ‘all of this is now true, the only thing we need to do now is read the paper’, then that is dangerous, says Hansen. “The purpose of doing science is that mankind should have an understanding of how the world works so we can make educated decisions. If we lose that understanding, what are doing?”

Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London notes that in discussions like these, it is important to distinguish between the statement of a theorem and its proof. For example, the statement of the famous Fermat’s last theorem is that for positive whole number a, b, c and n, aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ only if n is 1 or 2. This is easy to convert into Lean and can easily be checked. Once you are happy that a statement in Lean is correct, if the proof of that statement compiles, you can be confident the proof is true.

The issue, as Hansen and his team have pointed out, is that this tells you nothing about the natural-language version of a proof published as a PDF document. “I am confident that the Navier-Stokes problem has been correctly resolved,” says Buzzard. “I am far less confident that the proof described in the PDF is correct.”

Hansen says he hopes OpenAI will take the team’s work “very seriously” and that more work must be done on developing robust auto-formalisation techniques. “Do we have the solution? Not yet. Is it possible to do this in a controlled way? Yes, it will be, but the optimal and the ultimate way of doing this is completely unknown.”

Two large asteroids found spinning as fast as a fairground ride

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Large asteroids have been found spinning so fast they should break apart, suggesting they might be stronger than we thought.

Dmitrii Vavilov at the University of Washington in Seattle and his colleagues analysed some of the first data collected by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began a 10-year survey of the sky in June 2026. From a sample of more than 9000 asteroids, they measured the rotation of 260, based on a change in their brightness caused by the spinning asteroids’ irregular shapes.

Of these, 66 were deemed to be super-fast rotators, spinning quickly enough to complete a rotation in less than 2.2 hours, a limit at which asteroids should no longer be able to hold themselves together under their own gravity.

Advertisement

Strange three-lobed asteroid seems to have its own tiny moon

Two space rocks in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter were even more unusual ultra-fast rotators. Each was larger than 2 kilometres wide, but completed a full spin once every 5 minutes, something never seen before for such big asteroids.

“On the scale of billions of years, asteroids of this size should hit each other and reaccumulate,” says Vavilov, forming loose conglomerations of material known as rubble piles that would break apart when rotating rapidly. The high rotation speed suggests that these asteroids aren’t rubble piles, but instead monolithic objects at least 30 times stronger than clay, says Vavilov.

This probably means our models of how asteroids have smashed together over the 4.6-billion-year history of the solar system aren’t correct, he says. That might mean these are pristine objects from the early solar system.

See Catherine Heymans at New Scientist Live 2026

Other fast-spinning asteroids have been spotted before, but nothing as large as these two. Standing on their surface, a person would travel at more than 100 kilometres per hour (over 60 miles per hour), much slower than Earth’s equatorial rotation of 1670 km/h (1040 mph). But because of the smaller size of the asteroids, it would feel “like a rollercoaster”, says Vavilov, and clinging to the surface would be difficult.

The asteroids might have been spun up by the sun heating their surfaces and giving them torque, known as the YORP effect, but that in itself is uncertain because of their large distance from the sun. “That’s another mystery,” says Vavilov, who hopes to study the asteroids in more detail in future.

Does each new covid-19 variant pose a significant threat?

New Scientist October 09, 2026

A seasonal rise in covid-19 cases in Europe and North America has focused attention on a group of variants called XFG, which has dominated worldwide over the past year. A string of covid-19 variants has arisen since the virus emerged in 2019, but do we need to be concerned every time we hear of a new strain? Or have our past covid-19 infections and vaccinations given us a baseline level of protection?

Six years on from the height of the covid-19 pandemic, “we’re in this weird, uncharted territory”, says Danny Altmann at Imperial College London. “It’s not as good as we hoped, where we would just barely notice it, like the common cold. But it is not as bad as some of my colleagues feared, where we’re brewing the next disaster.”

mRNA covid vaccines spark immune response that may aid cancer survival

In lab tests, XFG (sometimes known as Stratus) is better at evading antibody protection than previous covid-19 variants, which is thought to be why it has become dominant globally. But for most people, existing immunity from previous vaccinations and infections appears to be enough to protect against serious illness, leaving researchers counselling both calm and caution.

Advertisement

All covid-19 variants circulating today are descendants of Omicron, the last major strain to be named, which emerged in 2021. The virus “continues to evolve”, says Ian Mellis at Columbia University in New York, creating a succession of new variants that outcompete previous ones, causing waves of infection.

XFG was first detected in early 2025, and the World Health Organization started officially monitoring it that June. It now makes up around 60 per cent of sequenced covid-19 cases worldwide.

It emerged from an exchange of genetic material between two subvariants of an Omicron lineage called JN.1, says Mellis, perhaps when they both infected the same person. Earlier this year, Mellis and his colleagues reported the results of lab tests where they tested a range of covid-19 viruses, including XFG and another variant, nicknamed Nimbus, against antibodies found in human populations.

They found that although both variants bound to host cells slightly less well, this was more than offset by a greater ability to evade covid-19 antibodies, compared with past variants.

AI predicted that a forgotten breast cancer drug could be repurposed to treat many respiratory and gastrointestinal viruses, and subsequent animal tests suggests it may be right

That ability to evade the immune response, on top of how widespread XFG is, may mean that more people will be susceptible to serious infection, says Altmann. “That may play out in a few more hospitalisations.” So far though, no evidence of increased disease severity, hospitalisations or deaths has been reported.

In the UK, for example, 1638 covid-19 cases were identified in hospital settings in the first week of October, a rise from 1328 cases the week before. But that is part of an expected seasonal rise, and lower than at the same time last year.

“We’re not seeing any evidence that [this year’s variants] are making people more ill or spreading faster than before,” says Alexander Allen at the UK Health and Security Agency, “and this year’s autumn [covid-19] vaccine has been specifically designed to protect them.”

Aris Katzourakis at the University of Oxford points out, however, that real-time assessment of the impacts of a virus can be very difficult. “It takes time for something that sweeps through to turn into hospitalisations and for those to be recorded.”

Free newsletter

Earlier this year, Leena Azhar at Fakeeh College of Medical Sciences in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and her colleagues reviewed what we know about XFG, concluding that it exemplifies “quiet” evolution, more consistent with fine-tuning “than a shift toward greater virulence”.

Even though the virus is gradually drifting further from the original form, and many people in the UK haven’t been vaccinated for several years, “we’re making do with the immunity that we’ve got on board”, says Altmann. “That’s keeping a lid on it.”

That’s a very different situation compared with when Omicron emerged, he says. “It was so different, it seemed devastating.” But with the latest variants, “I’m not unduly excited or alarmed”, he says. “We’re still where we thought we were.”

Getting covid-19 for the first time slightly increased the risk of heart inflammation, blood clots and bleeding disorders among children, whereas being vaccinated against the virus was much safer and sometimes protective

This doesn’t mean a more dangerous strain couldn’t emerge in the future, for example, if many mutations accumulate in a single, immunosuppressed individual, which is how Omicron originated. “There is a risk that a new strain could emerge that causes a wave of infections again,” says Mellis.

There is also now far less monitoring that could provide early warning of such an event, he says. In particular, the amount of sequencing data has “fallen dramatically” over the last year.

Governments around the world also have worryingly “lackadaisical” attitudes to vaccine boosters, says Altmann. He points out that most children who are starting school have never been vaccinated, and it’s unclear what the consequences of that may be.

Tattoos could be turned on and off with light

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Tattoos could be radically reimagined following the development of inks that can be turned on and off by exposing them to light. This could be used medically – or to hide the butterfly on your ankle from a judgemental relative.

“You can simply turn the tattoo off whenever you don’t want to see it and it disappears from view,” says Carson Bruns at the University of Colorado. “If you never want to see it again, just never turn it on again.”

Ancient Siberian ice mummy is covered in ‘really special’ tattoos

Bruns has had a tattoo of fish scales using this method for the past two years, and says he has experienced no known side effects. “I get a lot of compliments on the fish scale tattoo,” he says. “After over two years in my skin, I haven’t seen any obvious fading yet.”

Advertisement

Instead of traditional inks, which people have used for thousands of years to decorate their bodies, Bruns and his colleagues employ photochromic dyes, which change from a transparent state to a coloured one when exposed to certain wavelengths of light. They call the new technology, which has been tested on silicon, “PhotoTat”.

There is little mechanical difference between a traditional tattoo and the new inks, says Bruns. Both are pigment particles implanted in the dermis with a needle, he says. They also both stay there permanently and are applied with the same machines and methods.

The difference is the pigment, says Bruns. With PhotoTat, “ultraviolet light writes the colour in, bright visible light erases it, and the cycle can be repeated”, he says. “The tattoo is permanent, but its appearance is not.”

Free newsletter

This could be useful in medical applications, such as for the tattoos used by doctors to guide radiation beams, which leave many patients permanently marked, says Bruns.

The light-sensitive tattoos can currently be made from 16 colours, which are clearly distinguishable from each other. From these colours, there are at least 300 different shades. White is unavailable because it reflects light, rather than absorbing it, so can’t be switched on and off like other colours. The researchers have also been unable to develop a true cyan.

Another issue is that the blue ink gradually develops a permanent, purplish colour as the dye slowly photo-degrades over many on/off cycles. Someone with one of these tattoos would also need to apply sunscreen to prevent the colour activating when they are exposed to sunlight.

In terms of safety, Bruns says the polymer that encapsulates the dyes is non-toxic and has a long history of use in permanent biomedical implants. “The colour-changing [dye] toxicity is unknown, but the toxicity of most tattoo pigments is equally unknown,” he says.

A temporary graphene tattoo that monitors blood pressure has been awarded the highest possible accuracy grading for such a monitoring device

Still, extensive safety studies need to be carried out before the tattoos will be available to the public.

Signe Bedsted Clemmensen at the University of Southern Denmark says tattoo ink in the body is a foreign substance, which has been linked to cancer, regardless of whether it is visible or invisible. “Therefore, many of the same health considerations and concerns that apply to traditional tattoo ink are also likely to apply to invisible tattoo ink,” she says.

Earlier this year, it emerged that red tattoo ink caused one man to lose all his hair and stop sweating. Tattooing has also recently been linked to localised damage to the immune system.

Nearly 1 in 10 young adults could have fatty, narrow arteries

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Nearly 1 in 10 younger adults have plaque in their arteries, according to a study of almost 17,000 people. Known as atherosclerosis, the build-up of fatty plaque can cause narrowing that reduces blood flow, leading to heart attacks and strokes. Atherosclerosis is more common in people aged over 50, so younger individuals may be assumed to be at low risk.

“The most important message is that atherosclerosis is already present in a meaningful fraction of people in their 20s and 30s,” says Olli Raitakari at the University of Turku in Finland, who wasn’t involved in the study. “Atherosclerosis is a lifelong process, not a disease of old age.”

The profound effect the heart-brain connection has on your health

Previous studies have already suggested that atherosclerosis can occur surprisingly early. In 2025, Raitakari and his team found plaque in the carotid arteries – which supply blood to the head, face and neck – of about 5 per cent of Finnish adults aged under 30. But there hadn’t been large-scale investigations spanning multiple adult age categories that examined several artery locations.

Advertisement

To fill this gap, Borja Ibáñez at the Spanish National Centre for Cardiovascular Research in Madrid and his colleagues recruited almost 17,000 adults, aged 18 to 70, in Denmark and Spain. They divided the participants, who had no known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, into five age groups, starting at 18 to 29. The study was made up of around the same number of men and women.

Free newsletter

The researchers looked for plaque using CT angiography, which creates detailed 3D images of blood vessels, for arteries supplying the heart. They also used ultrasound for arteries in the neck and legs. Overall, they found “silent” atherosclerosis in 57 per cent of the participants, including 63 per cent of men and 51 per cent of women. This is defined as plaque that isn’t causing any symptoms, but may lead to cardiovascular issues down the line.

In the youngest group, 9 per cent of the men and 7 per cent of the women had some degree of atherosclerosis.

Among those in their 30s, 35 per cent of the men and 21 per cent of the women had atherosclerosis. The numbers continued to rise with each decade, with women beginning to catch up with men around the age of menopause.

A newly discovered collection of neurons suggests the brain and heart communicate to trigger a neuroimmune response after a heart attack, which may pave the way for new therapies

Atherosclerosis was generally more common among the participants with known risk factors, such as higher LDL cholesterol and blood pressure or a family history of the condition. But these factors didn’t reliably predict the presence of plaque, particularly among the younger adults.

The findings suggest that measures to detect plaque could identify people who seem to be at low risk of atherosclerosis, but might benefit from earlier preventive measures, such as medication or dietary changes.

But the presence of plaque doesn’t necessarily predict a future heart attack or stroke, says Raitakari, and there is no evidence that screening people without known health problems would prevent such events. The researchers also state that it is unclear if the results apply outside of Denmark and Spain.

Rising water is creating inland ghost forests in the US

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Millions of trees seem to be dying in the US, both near the coasts and inland near lakes, thanks to rising water levels. The finding may force a re-evaluation of how much carbon is stored in forests, which are important carbon sinks for mitigating the more severe effects of climate change.

Rising sea levels and intense storms linked to climate change have driven widespread tree die-offs along the US Atlantic coast, creating armies of skeletal dead trees known as ghost forests. North Carolina, for example, is thought to have lost 21 per cent of its coastal forest between 1985 and 2021 because of waterlogged soil and higher salt levels resulting from rising seawater.

To see how widely this is happening, Henry Yeung at the University of Virginia and his colleagues used aerial imagery from the US National Agricultural Imagery Program. They analysed images captured between 2012 and 2023 to map dead trees within 10 kilometres of the Pacific, Gulf and Atlantic coasts of the US, as well as along the US shorelines of the Great Lakes, down to a resolution of about 1 square metre.

Advertisement

Lake levels are rising across the world and climate change is to blame

They have identified more than 260 million dead trees and found that more than half of the mortality was concentrated in just 10 per cent of the mapped forests. These hotspots weren’t only in low-lying coastal forests prone to flooding, but also in high-elevation inland wetlands, far from salty water.

Over the decade they studied, tree mortality tripled in low-lying coastal forests, where water inundation was combined with increased levels of salt.

But mortality rates also doubled around expanding freshwater lakes, including the Great Lakes, and in inland wetlands, which have experienced more precipitation.

“This is the first map of ghost forests that covers the entire US. It’s also perhaps the first comprehensive study that takes the concept of sea level rise killing trees and applies it to more inland locations,” says Matthew Kirwan at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. “As a coastal scientist, I immediately think of salt as the culprit. These authors have extended it to water in general.”

Hear from three of the world’s leading climate scientists at New Scientist Live 2026

Arya Iwantoro at the University of Plymouth, UK, says it is striking how widespread the pattern is. “Prolonged inundation and salinity are already known to stress and kill trees, but the study suggests that water-related forest mortality may be more widespread than is usually recognised,” he says. “That broadens the issue beyond sea-level rise alone.”

Yeung and his colleagues found that between 2013 and 2020, high levels of precipitation and water runoff drove record-high levels in the Great Lakes, and they suggest that this led to sustained waterlogging, increasing the chances of nearby trees dying.

“The study provides convincing evidence that changing hydrological conditions are an important contributor to the mortality patterns, but I would be cautious about attributing every tree death directly to inundation or salinity,” says Iwantoro, adding that tree mortality is often influenced by other interacting factors, including storms, drought, pests, local drainage and soil conditions.

Deforestation could trigger Amazon tipping point in the 2030s

He says the work adds to evidence that the water-related effects of climate change could accelerate ecosystem shifts.

As the climate warms, the melting of ice means global mean sea levels are rising at about 4.1 millimetres per year, and saltwater intrusion is expected to affect nearly 77 per cent of the world’s coastlines by 2100. What’s more, climate warming also fuels heavier rain and snow, because for every 1°C that atmospheric temperature rises, the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere can increase by about 7 per cent.

This means that in coastal and lakeside areas, forests may retreat as conditions become more suitable for wetland vegetation, with knock-on effects on carbon storage, says Iwantoro.

In cities such as London, trees are already struggling with hot and dry summers. Botanists warn that we need to start replacing them with drought-adapted species

“Tree mortality and decomposition releases carbon into the atmosphere, and if the forest does not recover, then these areas may not regain their capacity to sequester carbon, and it could represent a more long-term carbon stock loss,” says Michelle Sims at the World Resources Institute, a global non-profit.

However, the ecosystem that replaces the forest may also accumulate carbon, says Iwantoro. “The important question is how carbon storage changes as the landscape transitions, rather than simply how much carbon is lost when trees die.”

Grief and tech collide in uneasily brilliant sci-fi film The Remotes

New Scientist October 09, 2026

The promise of much modern technology is that it will make our lives easier and take some burdens off our shoulders. An AI chatbot can tweak your emails; a delivery service can spare you the walk to a restaurant. But when does wanting to let go of something burdensome cross into giving up control? In John Torres’s The Remotes, grief, control and technology ominously intertwine on dark roads near Manila in the Philippines. A fast favourite of this year’s film festivals, it is a stunning and transfixing film that disorients and enthralls in equal parts.

Told in four parts, each of which feels as intimate as if some of its footage were documentary, The Remotes follows detective Mijares, who is trying to solve a series of car crashes where drivers’ bodies seem to have been controlled by a mysterious app. “You saw a ghost again,” a colleague tells him early on, except that the ghost once lived on the app store. “Were you fully in control of your body?” Mijares asks an older woman as she sits in her car after an accident. Something has clearly gone wrong here, and Torres builds a sense of a supernatural unease and visceral dread from the film’s first frame.

Notably, Mijares is not only haunted by this nearly unbelievable case, but he is also grieving his late wife. He narrates this grief as much as he narrates the case, through an often-poetic voiceover, until the film shifts focus to two sisters. Eva and Gill Cantero run seminars for delinquent and unsafe drivers. The ghost in the sisters’ lives is their dead mother, but they are also spectres in Mijares’s investigation; in their seminars drivers use an app that tells them how to drive, sometimes in a kind voice, sometimes sternly. In one emotionally resonant scene, after the seminar the students gather over drinks and recount how nice it is to drive with the app and listen to the voice, how good to temporarily relinquish control. The narrative threads start to intertwine, and Torres hints at something like resolution. A few scenes show motorcyclists explicitly losing control of their limbs once they punch into the app; Mijares seems to be vindicated and the sisters indicted.

Advertisement

But Torres isn’t interested in quick or easy conclusions and most of The Remotes isn’t told in order. Even though the film is over 2.5 hours long, parts of the story seem to be deliberately left out. This moodiness and nonlinear quality make the film both impactful and, at times, also deeply frustrating. As the connections come together, some of the emotional punches of that convergence are dulled by the sheer difficulty of following the story. I found the cinematography incredibly beautiful and pleasurable, but I also really wanted to pull out a notebook and try to sketch out a timeline. In a room full of critics and journalists at the New York Film Festival, I got a sense that I was meant to understand the story by feeling it more than by understanding each beat of its plot.

Though challenging, Torres’s commitment to lingering in this uncertainty and discomfort is also what recommends The Remotes the most. This is the feeling of grieving, and it is also the feeling of living in an uncertain world, one where we are constantly inundated by information and choices with inscrutable consequences. The increasing number of documented cases of people turning to AI chatbots for advice or tragically ending up in a state of psychosis after spending too much time talking to one speaks to how – much like in The Remotes – the temptation to offload some responsibility and control on a technology that talks back is very real.

In all its knottiness, this film is a good reminder to think about it twice, maybe even to say no to ghosts in the app store more often.

How a struggling Taranaki sheep farm became a global orchid business

New Zealand Herald October 11, 2026

Taranaki orchid grower Eric Lander. Photo / RNZ, Sally Round

By Sally Round of RNZ

Eric Lander’s eye for on-trend colours has helped him turn a struggling Taranaki sheep farm into a large orchid nursery which sends off exotic blooms to top florists in New York and around the world.

The 80-year-old still works a full day at his four large greenhouses, brimming with cymbidium orchids, their colours ranging from blood red, bronze and orange to lime green and yellow, trained up elastic thread to keep their stems as straight as possible for discerning overseas markets.

Lander has been growing orchids since 1980 when he was searching for a way to improve the income from what was then a struggling sheep farm, not far from Hāwera.

“I was looking for something different to sort of boost the finances, and my sister took me along to visit an orchid nursery up in Whakatāne, and I looked at it, and I thought, oh, well, I might be able to do that.”

His orchids could even be found in New York’s Trump Tower at one stage, Lander told RNZ’s Country Life.

He exports 95% of the flowers and, in 2025, sent off more than 3000 boxes via his Auckland-based wholesaler, carefully cut, inspected and nestled in sheep wool.

Wendy Holt is among a small team that picks and packs the orchids twice a week from late May to early November.

“Especially when they go to America, and we get the really big ones, you think what do they do with them? How do they display them? Who has them? I guess it’s like hotels and that, big hotels … big corporate businesses, I suppose.”

Adjusting the elastic on each of the 30,000 plants at least once a week is another task, Lander said.

“We need them straight, otherwise they won’t fit into the boxes, and the buyers want them straight too.

“It’s quite a job.”

Breeding and growing orchids is a long game, involving decades of selection, with Lander pollinating by hand to get the colours he thinks his customers will like.

“It takes seven years before you’ve got a production plant and then if it’s a good one, you can keep it, but if it’s a bad one, you throw them all out.”

“That’s the only way you get exclusive varieties.”

A recent stroke has affected Lander’s sight, and he relies on his team to inspect for tiny pests, but it hasn’t affected his discerning eye for colour.

“You can see a good apple or a bad apple, you know, it’s the same thing, but somehow I’ve got judgment that most people don’t have about what will sell, especially overseas.”

Lander feels pride and a sense of achievement in the business, Lander Orchids, now nearly half a century old.

“A little place in Taranaki away from everywhere and me that never grew anything before,” he said.

“It’s still a challenge to me, and it’s still a pleasure, and it keeps me getting up every morning.”
