New Zealand Herald October 11, 2026

BB Vietnamese Street Food owner Thuy Tran says allegedly fake Google reviews featuring rats (inset) are damaging her Christchurch restaurant's reputation. Photo / Rafaella Melo

A Christchurch restaurant owner says she fears for her business after photos allegedly manipulated with artificial intelligence to show rats at her premises appeared in a Google review.

Thuy Tran, who owns BB Vietnamese Street Food on Cashel St, believes her restaurant has been repeatedly targeted by fake reviews and prank calls involving claims about rats.

The latest incident happened on October 1, when a two-star Google review appeared with a photo apparently showing two large rats near the restaurant’s entrance.

Manager Ly Dinh said CCTV footage showed a man approaching the restaurant, taking a photograph using a mobile phone and leaving without buying anything.

The Herald has viewed the footage, which shows the man looking around before briefly taking a photograph and walking away.

About an hour later, the review appeared, Dinh said.

She believed the incidents were linked and that the rats were added to the image using AI.

“On the CCTV footage, we couldn’t see any rats,” she said.

“We just want to know what his purpose was. He’s not our customer. Why would he do that?”

Dinh said it was not the first time the restaurant had faced such allegations.

About two years ago, another Google review claimed the restaurant served rat meat and had live rats on the premises.

Dinh disputed the claims, saying the accompanying photographs showed flooring that did not match the restaurant.

She said the business had also received repeated prank calls asking whether it served rat meat.

“They call and then do it again after two or three months, and then again and again.”

The business employs three staff members, and Dinh said continued attacks on its reputation could put their jobs at risk.

“A single online comment accompanied by a photo can seriously damage a small business’ reputation and potentially threaten its survival.

“If they keep attacking the business and it goes broke, what happens to our staff?”

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

Tran, who moved to New Zealand from Vietnam seven years ago, having previously run a restaurant in her home country, opened BB Vietnamese Street Food about two and a half years ago.

She said the allegations were particularly worrying because tourists often relied on Google reviews when choosing where to eat.

“It’s not fair for us. It’s affecting our reputation.”

Tran also fears the allegations could affect her second Christchurch business, BB Vietnamese Takeaway Fish & Chips, on Centaurus Rd.

She said she wanted people to visit and judge the restaurant for themselves rather than rely on online allegations.

“I just want everybody, instead of seeing a fake review and believing it, to come to our shop, experience what we serve and see for themselves.”

Tran said cleanliness was a priority at the restaurant, where staff arrive an hour before opening each day to clean and prepare the premises.

She said the restaurant had been fitted out with new equipment and staff paid close attention to cleanliness.

“Everything we use here is brand new and sparkling clean. We take care of the details.”

A Christchurch City Council food safety verification report dated June 2025 found the restaurant’s premises and equipment were generally clean and in good condition.

The report rated its overall food safety verification outcome as acceptable, including a positive assessment of pest control.

Tran reported the latest incident to police and expressed frustration with the response.

Police confirmed receiving a report about 1pm on October 2 concerning an incident at a Cashel St restaurant about 11.30am the previous day.

“Following careful consideration, the file has been closed, but it can be re-opened and reviewed at any time should further information become available,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

Police said further information could be provided through 105 or its online reporting system.

“I am extremely disappointed with the way this matter has been handled by the police,” Dinh said.

“We placed our trust in the authorities to investigate this serious incident, especially when we had actual images and evidence that we believed could help establish what happened.

“As a small business, we pay taxes and contribute to our community. It is deeply frustrating that, despite repeatedly providing evidence and updates to support the investigation, the case has been closed without us receiving any further updates or a clear explanation of the outcome.”

Rafaella Melo is a multimedia journalist with more than 10 years’ experience in Brazil. She spent two years reporting for Hawke’s Bay Today before joining the NZ Herald’s Christchurch team in 2026.

‘Worst time for business owners’ coming in three months

New Zealand Herald October 11, 2026

81% of accountants say cash flow may affect clients' on-time tax payments. Photo / 123rf

By Susan Edmunds of RNZ

New Zealand is three months out from the “worst time for any business owner”, and businesspeople are being warned to be proactive to avoid the crunch.

A new survey of New Zealand accountants has found the provisional tax system is out of step with how businesses earn, spend and manage cashflow.

John Cuthbertson – New Zealand tax and financial services leader at Chartered Accountants Australia New Zealand – said one survey respondent had said January 15 in particular was the worst time for a business owner.

This is the date that both GST and income tax payments are due, while revenue was often down because business had been slower over the Christmas period and many clients were just coming back from holiday.

He said the payment dates did not reflect commercial reality and there was misalignment with business cashflow.

“The good news is the system doesn’t need to be rebuilt from scratch. Practical changes to improve flexibility could make a significant difference for businesses and the accountants who support them.”

The research showed 81% of accountants thought their clients’ cashflow constraints could affect their ability to pay provisional tax on time. Seventy-seven percent cited that January 15 date as particularly challenging.

In total, 98% of accountants had dealt with a payment issue in the past 12 months including missed payments, clients being charged use of money interest or cashflow-related difficulties.

Tax Management New Zealand (TMNZ) chief executive Matt Edwards said the biggest barriers were not in tax knowledge.

“They’re about timing, visibility and having the right tools to act on information quickly.”

Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand said the January 15 date should be revised, there should be flexible payment options and better use of technology.

Edwards said too many businesses did not treat their tax obligations as part of their cash flow. “I wish they did.”

He said the solution could come from more proactivity and enabling accountants to do more without additional investment.

“It is difficult for an accountant to have a single page view of exactly where all their clients are sitting in regards to their tax obligations. That requires an investment of time. If their engagement doesn’t cover that, it’s an invsetment of time they are not remunerated for and generally you don’t se enough proactivity around that.”

He said the survey showed the system was not broken but there was room to optimise it.

“Tax policy always changes over time and is optimised over time. But I think it’s not systematically broken, and I think that’s proved in the data. It’s the administration burden, particularly on the accounting fraternity to actually manage it that creates the problems. And I think that can be solved through technology rather than necessarily just tax policy.

“I think the tools are there to make this easier. I just don’t think we’ve deployed the tools in the most productive way at the moment.”

"I just refuse to believe that New Zealand has become twice as sick in the last 10 years, or that we have become twice as bad at getting people to say, 'actually, no, you could work'".

"Have we got some sort of health crisis here, or have we maybe got our policies wrong?"

Questioned if it could be because of a mental health crisis and if he had evidence to support his point, Seymour referred to the numbers.

He suggested a mental health crisis could come from the Government telling people they can not work.

"If Government policy says, 'Oh, yeah, don't you worry, you just stay home', then you really do get a mental health crisis because people lose the social contact, the purpose, all of the things that come from working."

Act Party leader David Seymour says raising the age of eligibility for NZ Super “has to happen” and will likely be driven by events, rather than a political party.

The party has announced it wants to increase the eligibility age by three months every year, reaching 67 years by 2035.

Seymour was asked on Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast whether that plan would ever get anywhere given NZ First in particular was opposed to the idea.

“When you look at the, say, $4.6 billion that it costs to pay people Super at 66 and 67 when a huge number of those people are actually still working, I think that the change has to happen, and I suspect that it will be events that drive it rather than any particular party,” he said.

“It may be that as bond rates head over 5% the pressure on government budgets becomes unsustainable and some of the unreasonable people come to the table.”

On the weekend NZ First announced plans to boost Working for Families and permanently increase the minimum wage - but Seymour said the party didn’t have a costed budget for such policies.

“Every year we've been in opposition and every election year, the Act Party puts out our numbers and they all add up. That's the only way to be responsible. Everything else is just soundbites and slogans.”

With a month to go before the election and a fortnight before enrolment closes, more than a third of young people who are eligible to vote are not enrolled.

A man died in a suspected drowning at Christchurch’s Sumner beach yesterday despite efforts from local surfers to try to save his life.

Police were called to Scarborough at around 12.10pm yesterday to reports that a person in the water may have suffered a medical event.

“Coastguard Sumner assisted in bringing the person to shore at Sumner, where sadly the man was unable to be revived,” police said.

Hato Hone St John received a call at 12.12pm about an incident in Scarborough and responded with an ambulance and two operations managers. It referred further inquiries to police.

Contact our South Island newsroom

The Press reports that a local paddleboarder and three surfers went to the aid of the man about 200m-300m from the shore.

“He was rag doll blue in the face,” paddleboarder Alan Kerr told The Press.

Coastguard Sumner volunteers said they responded to “an unresponsive paddleboarder” off Scarborough and that surfers found the person and tried to help them.

Coastguard Sumner’s jetboat, HamiltonJet Rescue, was returning from training and reached the scene within minutes.

Volunteers brought the person aboard and back to the boat ramp, where they gave CPR, oxygen and defibrillation for an extended period.

“Sadly, the person couldn’t be revived,” Coastguard Sumner said in a statement.

Sixteen Coastguard volunteers responded, on the water and onshore. They were joined by two medical professionals from the public, a Surf Life Saving medic, a Fire Emergency New Zealand first response unit and Police.

“Coastguard’s thoughts are with the family and the local community.”

The beach was a busy place yesterday as the city basked in 23C.

“Police extend our sympathies to the man’s loved ones,” a police statement this morning said.

His death has been referred to the Coroner.

By Sam Sherwood of RNZ

This story discusses details of long-term sexual and physical abuse.

For about four decades a South Island predator carried out the most horrific offending against those close to him, including raping his daughter, step-granddaughter, sisters and former partners. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood reports.

Standing inside the dock at the High Court, the man stood quietly in his prison clothes as his lawyer formalised the guilty pleas and discussed arrangements for sentencing.

There was no mention in the brief hearing of the extent of his offending before he walked back out of the dock to be sent back to prison where he will stay until he is sentenced later this year.

Inside a court document released to RNZ is the full story of the man’s offending, detailing 20 charges he has pleaded guilty to, with offending that began in the 1980s through to the 2020s.

It includes eight charges of sexual violation by rape (seven of which are representative), a representative charge of rape, and eight charges of sexual violation by unlawful sexual connection (six of which are representative).

He also pleaded guilty to a representative charge of making objectionable material, a representative charge of doing an indecent act on a young person and one charge of wounding with intent to injure.

His offending includes raping his daughter, his step-granddaughter, two of his sisters, and two ex-partners. He also committed indecent acts on a distant relative.

The man now in his 50s has interim name suppression. RNZ is not reporting the locations of his offending or the court in which he is being sentenced, to avoid the victims being identified.

The court document begins by discussing the man’s offending against an ex-partner who he began dating in the early 1990s when she was 17. It did not take long before he became violent, “physically, emotionally and sexually”.

The woman, who had four children with the man, left about 2015.

“During the relationship, which lasted around 20 years, the defendant offered violence towards the victim by hitting, pushing, and kicking her. On one occasion he smacked her in the face over making a coffee.”

In one incident, while pregnant with her first child, the man punched her in the eye and kicked her in the stomach, telling her he hoped her baby died.

The woman thought she was going to die during one assault when he put his hands around her neck, squeezing so it was difficult for her to breathe.

The summary of facts says by the mid-2000s the man raped her multiple times.

The man also pleaded guilty to a representative charge of sexual violation by rape in relation to another former partner.

The woman was 15 when she began a sexual relationship in 1990 with the man, who was then 21.

“The victim recalls feeling controlled by the defendant. She recalls the defendant being a jealous person. He didn’t like her joking or laughing with anyone of the opposite sex.

The summary of facts refers to three occasions where the man raped her.

The relationship ended when she turned 16.

The man also offended against one of his children.

The summary of facts says his daughter lived with him in several different houses from when she was born until she was about 16 and left home.

The offending started about 2006/2007 when she was 5 and lasted until she was 15.

“While [she] was around 5 to 6 years old, she recalls her father raping her whenever he had the opportunity.”

After the first attack, he told her what happened was “secret between them, and she wasn’t allowed to tell her mother”.

The court document refers to one incident when her father was driving down a gravel road.

“Knowing what was going to happen, she jumped out of the car and ran off. He then drove away leaving her there frightened in the pitch black.”

The man started letting his daughter go out drinking alcohol with friends between the ages of 13-15.

“She recalls getting home drunk on several occasions, where he would proceed to rape her while she was intoxicated. [She] described him as thriving off any situation she was intoxicated.”

In the early 2020s, the man also offended against his step-granddaughter.

The girl was 2 when her mother began dating the man’s son.

The relationship lasted about five years before she and her mother moved to another city.

Since then, the girl travelled once a month to stay with her stepfather and the man who lived in the same house.

She would often sleep in the man’s bedroom, which had a second mattress prepared.

When the girl was aged between 6 and 8, he raped her for the first time. He also took multiple photos of the victim being raped by as well as other photos of her.

The man also raped two of his sisters.

One of his sisters recalled living with the family at a property when she was about 13 in the 80s.

“It was here the defendant carried out the sexual activities he wanted with her on a frequent basis until she was around 18 years old.”

He started assaulting another sister when she was about 11 until she was 17.

“The victim recalls the defendant often saying disgusting comments to her including ‘old enough to bleed, old enough to butcher’.”

When the victim, then in her mid-20s, was about eight months pregnant with her first daughter, the man drove her to deliver something [firewood] after a family gathering. The woman reluctantly went with him after her father insisted.

On their way, he took her to an area where he had previously raped her when she was a child and asked to have sex with her.

“The victim told him to ‘f.. off’ and that he was a ‘disgusting creep’. The defendant replied that ‘the other girls still let me do it’.”

She again told him to “f... off” and said he was “sick in the head”.

“To which the defendant replied ‘I know I am’ while smiling.”

The man also admitted a representative charge of indecent act on a young person under 16 in relation to a distant relative.

In response to questions from RNZ, police confirmed the investigation into the man began following an in-person report on January 18, 2024.

“The defendant was arrested and charged with sexual violation offences related to that report on 7 May 2024.

“Further investigations uncovered additional victims and resulted in 94 charges laid in total.”

Christchurch double homicide: Former Devils Henchmen president among dead

New Zealand Herald October 11, 2026

Former Devils Henchmen Motorcycle Club president Glen "Lizard" Tukaki is understood to be one of two men killed in Christchurch on Saturday.

Tributes have flowed for a former motorcycle club president understood to be one of two men killed at a Christchurch social housing complex early on Saturday.

Police were called to the complex at about 12.50am. Two other people were seriously injured.

Contact our South Island newsroom

A 58-year-old man is due to appear in Christchurch District Court today, charged with two counts of murder, attempted murder and wounding with intent.

Glen “Lizard” Tukaki, a former president of the Devils Henchmen Motorcycle Club’s Christchurch chapter, is being remembered by loved ones for his caring nature.

Nigel Robinson is understood to be the other man who died and has been named in social media tributes. His friends and former associates expressed their disbelief, saying he would be missed.

Police have not formally confirmed either man’s identity and have said any gang connections were historical and were not considered a factor in the incident.

Facebook tributes remembered Tukaki as a colourful character with a caring side.

“One of a kind who was a kind, caring fulla deep down,” one person wrote.

Another recalled his generosity, saying he had “the biggest heart”, while a friend remembered him as someone who was “never short on offering a helping hand”.

“My brother, my president, see you over there some day,” another wrote.

Another remembered Tukaki as a “hard man” who rarely smiled.

“When you did, it was a shock,” he wrote. “But you did me no harm. I had a lot of good nights at the club with you. I will never forget you.”

His “little sister” Jayne Tukaki wrote: “Rest easy, Glen, love you always.

“It doesn’t seem real, just can’t fathom it. So many memories from our childhood to treasure forever.”

Another poster said: “My world will be so different without you brother.

“The true, hilarious, fun laughs we shared which were many ... [It] truly was an experience having you as a mate, friend & ally.”

Robinson, also known as “Rooster” and “Big Red”, was remembered as a generous man who lived life on his own terms.

One person described him as having “one of the biggest hearts I’ve ever known”.

“The type of person who would give his last dollar if he had it, even if it meant going without himself,” they wrote on Facebook.

“You lived a colourful life, that’s for sure ... You were one of those people who left an impression without even trying.”

Another person said: “You wore your heart on your sleeve, and always had the backs of those you loved.”

“You definitely lived a few lives in the one my bro ... Will miss ya BIG RED.”

Robinson’s daughter, Stella Robinson, paid an emotional tribute to her father on Facebook.

“Your quirky, loud personality and loving soul will echo through generations,” she wrote.

“Thank you for being my Dad no matter what ... I love you to the moon and back.”

The Devils Henchmen Motorcycle Club was founded in Christchurch in 1973 and became one of New Zealand’s original outlaw motorcycle gangs.

The Herald reported in 2024 that the Devils Henchmen appeared to be making a comeback in Christchurch, although police believed its membership remained small.

The killings happened at Guthrey Courts, a social housing complex owned by Ōtautahi Community Housing Trust.

A neighbour told the Herald she heard “a lot of screaming” followed by sirens and the arrival of armed police.

“[There was] a lot of chaos ... I just heard a lot of screaming ... then we heard heaps of different sirens and saw armed offenders [squad members] turn up.”

She said several surrounding streets were blocked off and residents were told to remain inside their homes.

The woman described the complex as generally quiet, although parts of the street could get “rowdy and busy” at times.

“It’s just a bit concerning how something like that can happen so close to home,” she said.

My suburb was sold to me as a bush paradise. Too bad about the heavy construction vehicles

Sydney Morning Herald October 12, 2026

Give anyone free access to subscriber-only stories when you subscribe.

My first experience of Brisbane was World Expo 88. Visiting from Sydney with my Dad, we zipped around on the monorail, watched the nightly laser light shows, and marvelled at the bright future of a rapidly changing “BrisVegas” – entirely unaware that I would, eventually, be calling this city home.

The following year, when I was just 22, I bought a modest, one-bedroom flat in Kedron. No New South Wales bank would give me a mortgage at that age, but a Queensland bank backed me, and I became what would later be known as a “rentvester”, owning in Brisbane but living in a rented unit in Harbord – now Freshwater – on Sydney’s Northern Beaches.

Back then, there was no way I could afford to buy anything on that expensive slice of the coast, and I kept my Kedron unit for 13 years, finally selling it to buy my first home in Belrose.

But Brisbane wasn’t done with me. Decades later, I needed to escape a volatile situation on those same Northern Beaches. I fled to Queensland, initially looking at new townhomes in Norman Park. Then I realised I could buy a brand-new house-and-land package in a masterplanned community called Ellendale, Upper Kedron, for the same price. Sold.

So it’s a tale of two Kedrons, in fact.

The common misconception is that Upper Kedron must be right next door to Kedron. But the two suburbs are some 15 kilometres apart, separated west to east by Keperra, Mitchelton, Everton Park, Stafford Heights and Stafford. The explanation? We get our name from Kedron Brook, not Kedron proper.

The waterway notwithstanding, Kedron is highly urbanised, powered by the pumping artery of Gympie Road. Upper Kedron, by contrast, is surrounded on three sides by D’Aguilar National Park. Back in 2019, Canvey Road was a remarkably quiet place.

Not so today. The masterplanned reality has manifested as a dense sea of massive, two-storey family homes increasingly crammed onto microplots.

Despite having worked as a fact-checker in print and broadcast media, focused on truth-seeking, I managed to buy a suburban display home based on a developer’s glossy brochure that singularly failed to mention they were situated right on what would become the primary arterial road through the expanding estate.

Instead of quiet bushland bliss, I have heavy dump trucks rattling my windows six days a week, pounding past until 6.30pm. This endless line of heavy construction vehicles treats my “peaceful haven” like a major highway. I’ve been forced to install a double-glazed uPVC entryway just to keep the din out.

The Pensar water reservoir project is providing important infrastructure to the estate and while “every effort will be made to minimise impacts to the community”, the official masterplans tell me the work will continue until late 2027.

Despite the noise, I am grateful to be in my own home, far away from the turmoil of the Northern Beaches.

I am an outlier here – a self-proclaimed spinster librarian living with my cat Chloe in a heavily family-centric suburban estate. Conveniently, the Arana Hills library is just around the corner from the pool, allowing me to borrow books and converse with like-minded librarians.

As an avid animal lover, pet-sitting has become my passion, giving me a wonderful sense of productivity and purpose. Bushwalking on nearby trails is a fabulous stress reliever, and being so close to the native bush brings back pleasant memories of my childhood in Beacon Hill.

Honeyeaters dart frantically through the canopy, and scrub turkeys prowl the ground level, completely indifferent to the changing landscape. They offer a fleeting escape from the suburban sprawl.

In 2024, when Ellendale Village shops finally opened, we could hardly believe it. It was a long time coming. The car park is always full, but I prefer the walk as it’s so close to home. I seem to be in the IGA every other day. Their friendly staff always greet customers with a smile.

We have a chemist right next to our Upper Kedron Medical Centre. Now I can walk down to see my new GP, too. When I need it most, kind neighbours often step in to help me.

One of my warm-hearted neighbours has even been helping me with my gardening. This gentleman has trimmed my hedges, whipper-snipped the edges and donated cuttings. All this from a gent who has the most beautiful front garden in Canvey Road! Amazing to have neighbours who are so kind and giving living close by.

For Upper Kedron, I believe that peace will eventually return. But it might not be until after the Brisbane Olympics, when the new builds are finally complete, and the big trucks no longer dominate our horizons.

McLarens, Mar-a-Lago and machine guns: Introducing Gina Rinehart’s controversial new frontier point man

Sydney Morning Herald October 12, 2026

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Ricardo Lopez Tugendhat believed he was going to die and wanted the world to know who he thought was going to kill him.

The former manager at a mining company linked to Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart spelt out his fears in a chilling letter to an Ecuadorian news outlet.

“Being familiar with the character and temperament of Mr Carlos de Miguel III, I am deeply concerned that the threats I have received from him … are carried out,” read the letter, published by the outlet.

“I hereby publicly hold the aforementioned Carlos de Miguel III responsible for any attack against the life or physical integrity of my family or myself.”

Carlos de Miguel is Rinehart’s man on the ground in Ecuador – the chief executive of Hanrine Ecuadorian Exploration and Mining, a subsidiary of Hancock Prospecting.

He is a former US serviceman who instilled fear in some workers. Some former workers claim de Miguel would saunter around Hanrine’s sites in northern Ecuador with an assault rifle and flanked by menacing-looking dogs.

He loomed as a central character when this masthead spent a month in Ecuador tracking Hanrine’s controversial activities in the Latin American country.

The investigation examined hundreds of pages of government documents, company records, court files and research papers, and spoke to dozens of villagers, environmental activists and experts, who detailed allegations of human rights breaches, irregularities in the concessioning process and a pattern of violence and harassment towards local villagers.

Former Hanrine workers detailed allegations of exploitation and abuses at the company’s site in La Merced de Buenos Aires, including hiding workers without contracts from authorities conducting compliance checks, serving raw meat to labourers, forcing employees to work while sick and a culture of threats and intimidation.

Most workers this masthead spoke to were too scared to be quoted on the record, fearing retaliation from Hanrine, which categorically denies any wrongdoing and maintains it complies with “relevant laws and regulations”.

The claims raise serious questions about the company’s operations, which have been a subject of sustained controversy, and which critics say highlight the lack of accountability and oversight for Australian subsidiaries operating overseas.

Julien Vincent, an experienced climate change governance campaigner and former winner of the Goldman Environmental Prize, which recognises grassroots activists, says there should be an expectation that Australian companies and their subsidiaries operate to a higher standard overseas than they would at home.

“That’s because they’re not just doing business, they are representing Australia in another part of the world,” Vincent says.

Local media have chronicled de Miguel’s career from working as a security contractor for former Ecuadorian president Rafael Correa to handling security for WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange at the Ecuadorian embassy in London in 2012.

The mining executive said in interviews with local media outlets that he has had a decade-long association with Hancock Prospecting, beginning in 2015 when the company became interested in diversifying its portfolio into Latin America.

De Miguel shares Rinehart’s conservative political views and her support for US President Donald Trump. He made a US$250,000 donation to the Trump-Vance inaugural committee and attended the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), where Rinehart is a regular attendee.

De Miguel was among several Hancock Prospecting executives who toured the US with Rinehart in early 2025. He later attended the Starlight Ball in Washington to mark Trump’s inauguration, where Rinehart was photographed talking to Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa and his wife, Lavinia Valbonesi.

De Miguel posed on a red carpet while wearing a velvet suit and aviator sunglasses at the Hispanic Prosperity Gala in Florida, where the mining executive owns a $US1.4 million home. The event, held at Mar-a-Lago in February, was sponsored by Hanrine, Trump Vodka and the Gina Rinehart Foundation.

De Miguel is also a car aficionado and the owner of a silver McLaren GT that he occasionally races. The car is nicknamed Maverick in a reference to the Top Gun movies.

Luis Fausto de la Cruz remembers when he fell out of love with working for Hanrine. It was 2022 and the farmer turned labourer was at the company’s camp on the edge of La Merced de Buenos Aires when, he says, a ute pulled up.

De Miguel, surrounded by security guards and flanked by two menacing-looking dogs, had walked out of the vehicle armed with a sophisticated assault-style rifle, de la Cruz says.

“He spoke about having been to war; I don’t know how many wars,” de la Cruz says. “It hurt my soul.”

De la Cruz, a father of six, believes this was an attempt to intimidate staff. It made him furious but he felt helpless.

“There was nothing one could do; if you spoke up, you were treated like a criminal,” he says. “So much for the claim that they are trained, educated people … you don’t come to [deal with] humble folk with weapons.”

De Miguel did not address questions about this alleged conduct directly but “categorically rejects” any allegation workers were mistreated.

De la Cruz says he worked carrying building materials and doing manual labour for Hanrine for about eight months, before staff were fired en masse and the company withdrew from the area. He claims the working conditions were brutal.

Workers would be sent to the mountains around La Merced de Buenos Aires for 20 days at a time, and left incommunicado from their family, he says. No phones were allowed on site, which also meant workers could not take photographs of their living conditions.

Staff slept in bunk beds in large tents, and the food served, he claims, often arrived cold, spoiled or raw. De la Cruz remembers one occasion when staff were given a special Christmas meal of roast pork that made several people sick.

“We aren’t dogs that eat raw meat,” he says.

He says staff who became ill were denied leave and made to work.

Lucia Chicaiza, the president of La Merced de Buenos Aires parish, says many workers were too scared to report their working conditions to authorities.

As previously reported by this masthead, several villagers in the parish claim, including in a judicial council report, to have been assaulted, stabbed and harassed by Hanrine staff for their anti-mining views. The company is also accused of hiring illegal miners as security guards, who were often armed.

Another former Hanrine employee, who spoke anonymously because of safety concerns, claims de Miguel was permanently armed and kept weapons inside company premises.

“He told us he had a permit to carry a weapon and that the police couldn’t even touch this gun,” the former employee alleges.

Local anti-mining protesters who had blocked the company from accessing its concessions in the parish would often be referred to by Hanrine staff as “chunchos” – a derogatory term that roughly translates to “savages”. Chicaiza was often called Lucifer.

Chicaiza says reports about Hanrine’s camps were so concerning she asked authorities to carry out a compliance visit.

“That’s when they hid us,” de la Cruz claims. “I was there.”

One morning, de la Cruz says, casual workers were told to leave the camp and head “for a walk” in the mountains. Staff were made to “hide” away from the camp while officials from the department of employment inspected the site.

Another Hanrine employee also claimed staff were told to leave the company’s facilities whenever authorities conducted compliance checks.

Manuel de la Cruz, a potato farmer who also worked as a manual labourer for Hanrine, says staff would be hidden from officials “because they weren’t paying the daily wages legally as they should”.

Former Ecuadorian employment minister Patricio Donoso told a human rights committee of non-government MPs in Ecuador’s national assembly in 2023 that the company was twice sanctioned for blocking department officials conducting compliance checks, and failing to present employment contracts for its workers.

It is unclear how many locals were employed by Hanrine. De Miguel has previously claimed in the media to have hired up to 200 people, many from the local community. Donoso placed the figure close to 300, although 169 contracts had been terminated at the time he spoke to the committee in 2023.

Hancock Prospecting has publicly acknowledged in its annual reporting on its modern slavery obligations that its operations in Ecuador are its highest risk jurisdiction.

This masthead is not accusing the company of breaching those obligations, only noting that it has stated repeatedly its awareness of potential labour issues in the country.

In a statement, de Miguel denied all claims workers were treated poorly. He said he had received “numerous messages from staff expressing their appreciation for Hanrine, its workplace culture and the opportunities the company has provided” and shared two undated messages from unnamed employees praising the company.

“In countries like Australia it can be easy to underestimate just how significant the opportunity of employment can be for people living in poor areas,” de Miguel said.

The average annual GDP per person in Ecuador is estimated at $10,000, according to anti-modern-slavery organisation Walk Free.

The letter Ricardo Lopez Tugendhat penned to news outfit La Fuente: Periodismo de Investigacion in 2020 highlights just how feared de Miguel was by some who had crossed paths with him.

Lopez Tugendhat had previously worked closely with de Miguel as assistant manager, handling security for Hanrine, until their relationship soured early that year.

Hanrine and Lopez Tugendhat were caught in a messy dispute that led to both parties taking each other to court, and Lopez Tugendhat reporting de Miguel to authorities for alleged intimidation.

Part of the dispute involved claims by Hanrine that Lopez Tugendhat had used a fake disability card to claim benefits he was not entitled to. Lopez Tugendhat claimed he had been unfairly dismissed by the company.

Hanrine later dropped the disability card case after signing an agreement with Lopez Tugendhat, and the court found him not guilty this year. The unfair dismissal claim was settled and Hanrine paid $US20,000 to Lopez Tugendhat in 2022, according to court documents.

At the time he sent the letter, Lopez Tugendhat was worried an article published by the news outlet would draw the ire of his former boss.

The article suggested Lopez Tugendhat, a three-time shooting world champion, could have tipped off the police to a stash of firearms and ammunition hidden in de Miguel’s home gym.

Police had raided de Miguel’s property and arrested the businessman the previous month on the basis he did not hold valid permits for three of four firearms found, which included a high-powered rifle used by elite police and military officers. Investigators also found 9500 rounds of ammunition, several magazines, an air rifle and a training gun, according to court documents and local media reports.

In the letter, Lopez Tugendhat claimed de Miguel had threatened to kill him and his family, and he provided a case number to track his report of the alleged threat through the prosecutor’s office.

This masthead was able to find a record of the original report Lopez Tugendhat filed against de Miguel for alleged intimidation in January 2020, but it did not contain any findings.

“The only report I’ve made against Mr Carlos de Miguel III is for intimidation and death threats, of which me and my family were the victims of,” Lopez Tugendhat pleaded in his letter.

“I expressly request that your prestigious media outlet clarify and correct the record.”

The weapons case against de Miguel was dropped 10 months after the raid, after it was determined the businessman was in the process of renewing the expired permits.

The decision was partly informed by Lopez Tugendhat’s evidence that de Miguel was a member of his recreational shooting club and the ammunition found in his home had been bought through the club.

De Miguel later said the raid was part of a plot to discredit him as a mining executive and derail Hanrine’s bid to obtain a lucrative copper project near its concessions in La Merced de Buenos Aires called Llurimagua that the company was offering to acquire for US$400 million.

When contacted by this masthead, de Miguel said it was not uncommon in Ecuador for allegations to arise in the context of employment disputes.

“The unfounded workplace allegations against myself that you reference were categorically dismissed and did not result in any charges or adverse findings against me,” de Miguel said.

Lopez Tugendhat declined to comment when contacted by this masthead.

On a clear morning, you can see the Colombian border from the top of Luis Fausto de la Cruz’s land.

Motilon trees – a high-altitude Andean species that produces a deep purple berry used to make “colada morada”, a thick smoothie-style drink used to commemorate the Day of the Dead festivities – grow in the small valleys that form between the hills undulating through his land.

Bears and guans, a large chicken-like bird native to the Andes, are regular visitors to the property, which is also home to a waterfall and walking trails.

De la Cruz, yellow shin-high rubber boots on his feet, walks through the overgrown paths with a machete in his hand. He wants to turn part of his land into an ecotourism venture with huts, bird lookouts, a zipline and horseriding routes.

“There’s a lot of birds here,” he says. “I am going to fight little by little to do something.”

De la Cruz says he doesn’t regret working for Hanrine. It was an eye-opening experience. But he feels locals were taken advantage of and promises of new homes, roads and services that lured locals like himself to work with the company were never fulfilled.

He says he isn’t afraid that speaking out will make him a target.

“The only thing I fear is God, no one else.”

Canelo Álvarez ‘fears nothing’ and will fight in Riyadh despite deadly attacks, Al-Sheikh says

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 20:42:20 GMT

Álvarez vows to fight in Riyadh despite deadly strikes

Airport attacks leave at least 12 dead, hundreds hurt

Mexican seeks redemption after Crawford defeat

Canelo Álvarez intends to go ahead with his world title fight in Saudi Arabia later this month despite a series of deadly attacks on airports and other infrastructure in the kingdom, according to Turki al-Sheikh, the Saudi official who has become one of boxing’s most influential power brokers.

The Mexican superstar is slated to challenge the unbeaten Christian Mbilli for the WBC super-middleweight title in Riyadh on 31 October, three weeks after Saturday’s missile strike on the Saudi capital’s main international airport killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300.

Al-Sheikh, the chairman of Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority, said on Sunday that Álvarez had personally assured him he remained committed to the bout regardless of the fraught security situation.

“Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Al-Sheikh wrote on social media. “He fears nothing. My country is home to the two Holy Mosques, land of peace, safety, rich civilization, deep history and kind-hearted people. Thank you to everyone who checked in and showed support. Hard times reveal true friends.”

The reassurance came as Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensified their attacks on Saudi territory. A second projectile struck a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, according to the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen. Authorities reported further injuries but did not immediately provide a figure.

Saturday’s strike, which hit the same airport complex, was the deadliest attack on a Gulf Arab country since the outbreak of the war with Iran. India’s embassy subsequently reported that one of its citizens had died from injuries sustained in the attack, potentially raising the death toll to 13.

The airport remained closed on Sunday, while the US government has urged American citizens to avoid the facility and its surrounding area. Several international airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia amid the mounting threat to civilian aviation.

The Houthis, who have claimed responsibility for attacks on airports and energy facilities across the kingdom, have warned airlines and travelers against entering Saudi airspace. The escalation has raised concerns about the safety of major international events in a country that has invested heavily in establishing itself as a destination for global sport, entertainment and business.

Saudi Arabia has become a major force in professional boxing under Al-Sheikh, staging a succession of high-profile bouts in Riyadh and using its considerable financial resources to attract some of the sport’s biggest names. The kingdom’s expanding sporting ambitions have also drawn scrutiny over its human rights record and accusations of sportswashing.

The latest attacks threaten those ambitions at a particularly sensitive moment. Saudi Arabia is hosting an international energy conference this week, with further major business gatherings scheduled, while the widening conflict has raised the possibility of greater US military involvement. US president Donald Trump said on Saturday that he was considering action against the Houthis and planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

Álvarez, 36, has a professional record of 63 wins, three defeats and two draws, including 39 knockouts. The 31 October contest would mark his return to the ring for the first time since losing a unanimous decision to Terence Crawford in September 2025. He previously fought in Riyadh in May of that year.

Speaking on a Zoom call with the Guardian and other reporters on Tuesday, Álvarez admitted that his focus had wavered in the days leading up to the Crawford fight, despite what he described as a strong training camp.

“When you lose, you always look back and look [at] your mistakes,” Álvarez said. “I did a very good preparation for [the] Crawford fight, but in the fight week, my mind wasn’t there.”

The former undisputed super-middleweight champion has been preparing for his comeback on Spain’s Mediterranean coast, training at the same facility used by Oleksandr Usyk. He has also adjusted his schedule to account for the time difference in Saudi Arabia, having struggled to acclimatize during his previous visit. Álvarez said he now believes he needs 21 days to adjust fully to the change in time zones.

Mbilli, who has won all 29 of his professional fights, 24 by knockout, represents another formidable challenge. Álvarez described him as a relentless, high-volume puncher whose aggressive style should make for a crowd-pleasing contest.

Álvarez, who turned professional at 15, also declined to put a timetable on his retirement when asked how much longer he intended to compete.

“I don’t know how many more fights,” he said. “I don’t know because I feel really good.”

Impervious Manchester City shrug off chaos and controversy to silence Anfield

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 20:02:08 GMT

What had been billed as a day of reckoning for the Premier League champions turned into a Sunday afternoon stroll

Anfield welcomed Manchester City to their new reality, a sullied place where every touch is accompanied by cries of “cheat”, any favourable decision is considered proof of further conspiracy and every victory hollow. But Welcome to Hell this was not. The only body of irrefutable evidence in City’s favour since the guilty verdicts landed is that Enzo Maresca’s league leaders appear immune to prosecution and persecution.

That may well change depending on the outcome of City’s appeal and any punishment that eventually arises, likewise the merits and value of a commanding 3-0 win on Liverpool soil. The sight of Erling Haaland savouring a statement victory in front of City’s supporters after the final whistle, while chants of “going down” echoed around the rest of the stadium, captured the schism at the heart of this Premier League season.

City were transformed by the introduction of Jérémy Doku and the dismissal of the Liverpool midfielder Ryan Gravenberch. They were never intimidated, always composed and look a genuine threat to Arsenal’s defence of the title. And yet this could prove their last Premier League appearance at Anfield for the foreseeable future.

It may be difficult, nigh on impossible, to sustain this level of motivation and desire knowing that relegation beckons. Knowing that no one outside City will give them credit for another title triumph did not affect them here, however.

In the 17 days since news of City’s guilt first emerged, and the gestation period of a prolonged international break, their return to action in a Premier League undermined and distorted by their 114 breaches had been built up as a chastening day of reckoning for Maresca’s side. It proved nothing of the sort.

Anfield can still make its voice heard to seismic effect and in the frantic start when Liverpool flew at City, with a fired-up Ronald Araújo whipping up the crowd after winning a challenge against Antoine Semenyo, the collective sense of injustice at a club pipped three times to the title by those in sky blue inspired Andoni Iraola’s players. But bear pits rarely feature in the corporate packaged world of Premier League entertainment 2026.

The “reception committee” for the City team coach before the game was populated by fans carrying selfie-sticks and club shop carrier bags, not an incensed brooding mob. At half-time the Kop was asked to cheer on corporate guests of the club sponsor Standard Chartered as they took part in a penalty shootout, many clearly kicking a ball for the first time in their lives.

There were incessant chants of “you cheating bastards” and various banners of damning judgement, many with an Oasis twist that may have been appreciated by Noel Gallagher in the away end. “And after all you really robbed us all” read one. “All of your stars are fading away,” read another. “A generation of supporters cheated,” cut to the heart of the issue confronting not only Liverpool but the Premier League itself.

The City support responded in kind. “In Khaldoon we trust – we’ve won it all!” proclaimed the away flags. The visitors, while performing the Poznan before kick-off, also reclaimed one of the “Cheat” flags that had been doing a healthy trade outside the ground before the game. The inflatable bananas that were once part of the City fanscape also made a comeback, a throwback to more innocent days when their club was not in the dock for inflating sponsorship deals. There was more bickering than tangible animosity. The four men who walked on to the pitch carrying the Premier League hoardings before kick-off received a more hostile reception than City’s players when they appeared for the warm-up.

The decision for City’s team coach to arrive by a different route ensured a tame reception for the visitors. All eyes were on the usual entrance on Anfield Road as City were ushered in from the opposite side of the stadium – so. It meant even the referees’ chief Howard Webb could walk in almost unnoticed. The hostility cranked up as soon as the contest started and City, using their vast experience to telling effect, gradually drained the venom from the atmosphere and the threat from a depleted Liverpool team. But it was the 62nd-minute dismissal of Gravenberch that had the greater bearing on the outcome.

Doku proved a devastating substitute for Iliman Ndiaye and tormented Liverpool from the left, being involved not only in the red card but all three City goals. The hosts, minus their two most potent attacking players this season in Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak, plus a hamstrung Dominik Szoboszlai, had no answer with Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola largely anonymous.

The Kop made no calls to be handed the trophies lost to City – and what would that really mean now anyway? – but took solace in demanding that punishment be served in the form of relegation this season. “No trophies for 50 years, que será, será,” the home crowd chanted. But there was no immediate retribution for Liverpool here. City dealt with the chaos and the controversy serenely.

Andy Burnham to publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 19:49:28 GMT

Move comes after criticism of remarks in support of football club’s owners following financial regulations breach ruling

Andy Burnham has said he will publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City in his previous mayoral role after his intervention in support of the football club’s owners raised eyebrows.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative party leader, had urged the prime minister to publish everything related to his work with the club as Greater Manchester mayor and the Liberal Democrats wrote to him asking him to release minutes of meetings and declare all hospitality gifts received from owners of Manchester City.

City has been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. The club has maintained its innocence and appealed against the verdict.

Burnham said last month he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club after the finding, crediting them with being “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”.

Downing Street sought to clarify his comments afterwards, saying the prime minister was clear the judgment was serious and that where wrongdoing was established, those responsible should face the consequences.

Burnham said he would “put out there” everything he had done to work with the club’s owners as mayor in an interview with the Rest is Politics podcast to be released on Monday.

He said “the football issues are different from the investment issues”.

“But I see now people trying to conflate these things. I’ve been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I’m happy to do.

“I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester.

“None of it is recent … in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting … and that was in 2021. That is right and I will put that all out there.

“But the football issues, they are serious and have to be dealt with, and the process is independent and it has to run its course. But I think everybody should separate the investment issues because they’re not the same thing.”

The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees.

The commission found that the remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan’s Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development Ltd, which owned the club.

The shadow sports minister, Louie French, called for Burnham to also “come clean” about any meetings since becoming prime minister and urged Lisa Nandy, the secretary for digital, culture, media and sport, to respond to questions.

“The prime minister must publish every contact between his ministers, officials and Manchester City since he walked into No 10, the prime minister must also explain why he inappropriately intervened in this case, and Lisa Nandy must answer the questions I have put to her in full.”

Spectre of ghost football hangs over Manchester City win of unknown significance

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 19:11:36 GMT

Football felt secondary on the first weekend of action since club were found guilty of breaking financial rules

The Cimbri are heading menacingly south, but in Rome life goes on. The asteroid is definitely coming this way, but people go to work, eat, drink, plan as usual. The White Walkers are approaching the Wall, but the squabbles between the great houses go on. Everyone in the Premier League knows the crisis is approaching, thinks – hopes, fears? – it may be apocalyptic, but until it arrives, what can you do but carry on?

After any break, there’s always an awkward moment while everybody resets. What was the cliffhanger we left the soap opera on? What new plotline had just been seeded? This is one of the reasons international weeks are so disruptive. It’s not just that the Premier League story slows for a while, it’s that we are reminded that these entities are not eternal but alliances of convenience between paid employees who have a life outside the soap opera.

But there has never before been an international break so disruptive as this, never such a sense of unreality about a weekend of Premier League football. It’s not that, the 2022 World Cup aside, this has been the longest international break in history. Nor can anyone, surely, be unaware of the dominant narrative of this window: between 2009 and 2018, Manchester City cheated. Perhaps an away game at Anfield for City is not quite the event it was when Pep Guardiola and Jürgen Klopp were at their peak, but it should still be a great footballing occasion. Yet this was an afternoon when the football felt secondary.

City continue to protest their innocence, clinging to the now-familiar formula that they have a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that will somehow clear their name, if only people wouldn’t keep refuting it. They have launched an appeal, but if that fails the sanction is likely to be unprecedentedly severe. Do their games matter? Will they be annulled before the season’s end? Was this victory just the difference between finishing the season on -100 points and -97? Could they be expelled from the league? Until sentence is announced, there will an air of provisionality about everything they do. It’s the seconds after an incident that everybody knows VAR will check, the ghost football that might be cancelled, but extended for weeks.

This, though, is not only an issue of the present; it’s an issue of the past. The sanction may or may not strip City of their titles. Many City fans will ignore such a punishment, continue to claim those honours, will point out that memories cannot be so easily extinguished. But even if City’s appeal is successful, or even if the sanction does not relitigate the past, there will be asterisks there in the minds of those who are not City fans, and perhaps also in the minds of some of those who are. Add in Chelsea’s offences, and the Premier League is coming to the end of an 18-year period in which very little was quite as it seemed.

The inflatable bananas brandished by City’s support at Anfield on Sunday may have harked back to an earlier, more innocent era, but there is no going back. City are not the club of Imre Varadi any more; as it stands they are the club guilty of the greatest act of cheating in English football history. Their fans can do the Poznan in a spirit of resistance, but they cannot turn their back on the shame their leaders have brought upon them.

What that means for the longer-term credibility of the league can only be guessed at. The basis of sport is faith. Incredible finishes mean little if nothing can be believed. Why go through the emotional agonies if a result might be struck off a decade later for offences committed in the air-conditioned offices of a distant state? Will the City decision undermine faith, or reaffirm it, come as proof that cheats do not prosper, that they will – eventually – be exposed, that the Premier League, almost alone in this grubby world of compromise with and abasement before the mega-rich, is prepared to do what is right?

after newsletter promotion

City were booed, there were some chants of “going down” and there were a handful of banners, but Anfield was not the seething pit of disgust many had anticipated. Nor was there much City-related fury at other grounds, although Manchester United fans, erasing all the silverware of the past 15 years, reinstituted their counter on the Stretford End recording the length of time since City last won a trophy. The general sense is of bafflement and bewilderment; what does this mean? What might happen?

It is as though the scale of City’s offences have not yet been fully grasped, that no one quite knows what might happen next. City fans, similarly, seem set on a policy of defiance, as though the scandal is something that has been done to them, rather than the result of the actions of their own directors. To an extent, that is understandable. Until the sanctions are announced, until the result of the appeal is known, the sense of unreality, the phoney war, will go on. The crisis is coming, but its impact has not yet been felt.

Exeter finally find first win despite Christian Wade’s hat-trick for Newcastle

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 18:04:23 GMT

Prem Rugby: Exeter 34-28 Newcastle

Wade becomes second player to score 100 top-tier tries

Amid the current gushing torrent of Prem tries here was a reminder that winning still trumps all else. Exeter finally have their first, relieving, victory of the campaign but there were times when it seemed Newcastle might conceivably secure a first away league success in almost four years. In the event the Red Bulls fell just short despite Christian Wade running in a hat-trick to become only the second player to score 100 top-tier tries.

Exeter will be suitably relieved to have edged a curate’s egg of a contest, ultimately made safe by a late try from their Georgian prop Bachuki Tchumbadze. The Chiefs’ Italian international back-rower Ross Vintcent also contributed two ­first-quarter tries to steal some of the prolific Wade’s thunder. The 35-year-old retains a poacher’s instinct and is now closing in fast – in every sense – on Chris Ashton’s all-time Prem career haul of 101.

A game of nine tries, slightly below average for this season, was also notable for a promising debut display from 18-year-old Jake Dalziel, the youngest player to represent Newcastle in the Prem and the premature departure of England winger Immanuel Feyi-Waboso with a tweaked hamstring. “I don’t think it’s a catastrophe but he said he doesn’t feel right,” said Rob Baxter, Exeter’s director of rugby. “It’s more of a concern than a long-term worry.”

The same, for now, applies to the meagre attendance of 7,071 on a grey but relatively mild afternoon. This week Exeter slashed ticket prices in most categories between now and Christmas and still there were ­thousands of empty seats around the ground. The quality of the product matters but so, increasingly, does value for money in these difficult economic days.

For the first time in recent years for a league fixture here there was not a soul on the North Terrace behind the posts, a real sign of the times. Just 8,682 showed up for Exeter’s opening weekend West Country derby against Gloucester and here a stadium with a maximum capacity of 15,000 was more than half empty.

There are plenty of other outdoor activities available in Devon at this time of year but, otherwise, people are either preferring to watch from the comfort of their own sofas, save up for Christmas or they’re not overly bothered. Which, given Chiefs made the Prem final in June, it is a concerning state of affairs for all involved in marketing and selling the professional game.

Those who did turn up, however, were treated to an eventful tussle with five tries in the opening quarter alone. The eager Vintcent collected two of them, the first inside 40 seconds after a chargedown with the help of a (legal) headed assist. Wade was also productively busy, running in an easy first and then unselfishly releasing Max Hicks for a second in the same right corner.

Jason Gilmore claimed his Harlequins side restored pride despite a third successive loss of the Prem campaign against Sale in Salford.

The Sharks snatched a 28-24 win with a 73rd-minute penalty try after they had been outplayed for long periods by a Quins side smarting from last weekend’s 48-0 humiliation against Gloucester.

“It’s disappointing. We probably created three chances in the first half which we didn’t take which came back to bite us,” said the Harlequins head coach. “Fair play to Sale. They got themselves back into the game with their set piece but I’m really proud of the boys’ efforts up here.

“Two bonus points on the road up here is, I wouldn’t say pleasing, but I’m just happy for the boys that they got some reward out of their work. If you’re prepared to go to dark places for us and win those collisions, then you’re going to get selected. If you’re dipping your toe in one week and then not the next, then we can’t tolerate that.

“You can’t be up one week and then down the next week like we had last week. Performance will dictate the shirts.”

Marcus Smith impressed with two tries on his return after injury and Harlequins hooker Sam Riley also touched down twice.

But Sale, who trailed 17-14 at the break, fought back with Ben Bamber adding to first-half tries from Elia Canakaivata and Gus Warr before the decisive late penalty try.

Hicks is an interesting arrival in the Prem, having grown up near Ethan Roots in New Zealand and even worked on the same building site as his opposite number. He is also English qualified as is the Red Bulls No 8 Hoskins Sotutu, which helps explain why the national head coach Steve Borthwick made the trip to Devon.

With the autumn block of the Nations Championship just around the corner this was a timely moment, therefore, for Henry Slade to slice through a big gap behind Werner Kok and score from 40 metres out. The centre also converted his own score from wide out but it was still the visitors who led at the interval.

Having lost Roots to the sin-bin for a no-arms tackle on Harrison ­Obatoyinbo, the Red Bulls now had the youthful Dalziel pulling the strings and the teenager’s beautiful offload outside to Sammy Arnold created the platform for Wade to accelerate away for his second. Dalziel, the son of the British & Irish Lions assistant coach John Dalziel, is highly rated in Scotland and looks to have an extremely promising top-level future.

After a stern half-time lecture from Baxter about their lack of defensive energy, Exeter appeared to revive slightly and the former Bath full-back Sam Harris, on his Chiefs Prem debut, finished off a sharp blindside break from Stephen Varney. ­Unfortunately for the hosts, two misjudgments from Slade then muddied the waters, a loose offload allowing Wade to pounce for a third time and a midfield forward pass causing a potential try for Varney to be scrubbed out by the television match official.

Instead it required a fine long-range penalty into the wind with 16 minutes remaining by Slade to nudge the Chiefs back in front before Tchumbadze rumbled over from close range. Those who had paid to attend were suitably grateful, though whether this performance frightens their next opponents Toulouse, the French Top 14 champions, is another matter. The likely unavailability of Feyi-Waboso will make it an even tougher assignment although Chiefs do now have their forceful Wallaby back-row forward Tom Hooper back for this weekend’s opening round of the Champions Cup.

Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 17:21:39 GMT

Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure

Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.

In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.

He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.

Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.

Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.

There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.

The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.

The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.

The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.

The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe, reported on Sunday that the US is ⁠threatening ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons to ‌press Kyiv to halt its ‌deep strikes on ​Russian energy infrastructure.

The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.

On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.

Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.

Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.

The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.

He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”

Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”

Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.

Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.

Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.

Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.

Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.

Every vantage point was taken, with spectators standing on walls to get a glimpse of the enemy, only for the coach to sneak in from the opposite side of the ground to avoid confrontation.

The subterfuge defused a volatile situation that could have turned into an incendiary one. Tensions were high on Merseyside. Since the City takeover in 2008, Liverpool have finished second to their rivals on three occasions, although only one of those falls within the parameters of the investigation into City’s financial breaches of Premier League rules. Liverpool supporters are aggrieved, feeling they would have won more trophies had City not circumnavigated the rules to help sign elite players.

References to the verdict were not difficult to find at stalls outside. For £15 – haggling took it down to £10 – it was possible to buy a “Guilty 114” flag, including an AI image of the City squad in prison uniforms or a “Cheats” banner in the style of the Oasis logo.

Many supporters, however, were content with the traditional – and much maligned – half and half scarf to commemorate such an occasion. The fashion conscious could pick up T-shirts with a similar motif. There were more frugal offerings, with homemade banners carrying the blunt message being paraded around the ground.

There was a sense of injustice and thousands wanted to express it. A solitary City fan, clad in sky blue, stood among the sea of red. He was unbothered by the commotion around him but was left alone because he is not at fault.

Social media chatter suggested City merited a “bus greeting” on Anfield Road and police were prepared for such an eventuality. There was toxicity and hostility on both sides in the buildup, with away supporters chanting their anthem of “City’s going down with a billion in the bank” while waving inflatable bananas, the latter a tradition that goes back to the 1980s. It provides a reminder that City existed for 114 years before Sheikh Mansour’s investment and will continue to do so regardless of what happens in relation to potential sanctions. Many have witnessed City drop to the third tier and win the Champions League, so have experienced both ends of the spectrum already.

The police flew a drone above the route the City bus planned to take into the ground, while officers walked up and down filming those in attendance as the decibels and anger grew.

Every vehicle was treated with suspicion, as theories of subterfuge from City, not for the first time, were discussed. The prospect of sneaking the players and staff into the ground were gossiped about among the crowds but there was no Trojan horse. Instead the official team bus, with full livery, came up the other side of Anfield Road and around the back of the stand that bears its name.

The Liverpool bus arrived to cheers, chants and plenty of red smoke just before 3pm. The eyes stung as the wind blew. The police presence grew closer to the anticipated arrival time on the bus.

There was mild heckling from home fans in earshot but, like with the bus, it passed without incident. The cheering and jeering carried on while the travelling fans waited to enter the ground but it was nothing out of the ordinary for a football match between two rivals. Calmness had descended.

As City walked on to the pitch for their warm-ups, they were loudly booed by the majority inside the ground, every player’s name mentioned on the public address system receiving the same treatment. But for how long they stay at the summit or even in the league when their punishment is served, nobody knows.

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 16:49:05 GMT
