An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire and causing injuries, according to Saudi authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week.

The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq.

After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.”

The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.

In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.

The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties.

Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike.

On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.”

On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details.

The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others.

The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued.

“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X.

Trump said he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, on Saturday night, after the previous attack on the airport.

The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis.

Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit.

It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump faces the prospect of midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home, threatening his party’s performance at the polls.

Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children.

Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the last month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island.

The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier.

The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.

The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.

Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said.

The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.

“Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.”

The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March.

On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom.

The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles into Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low.

The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government.

Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US.

Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

The Guardian view on mental health: overdiagnosis is not the problem facing young people

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 16:27:06 GMT

Parity of esteem with physical healthcare remains a distant prospect. Ministers must do more to tackle rising distress

Perhaps the single most important finding of the independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism in England, published last Friday, is that mental distress across the population, and particularly young people, has substantially worsened. Its chair, Prof Peter Fonagy, told the BBC that the former health secretary Wes Streeting had been “completely wrong” to suggest that conditions and disorders were being overdiagnosed.

Mr Streeting acknowledged his mistake. But some rightwing politicians and commentators have leapt on the notion that medicalisation of ordinary states of mind is behind the huge rise in young people seeking help. This review should bury that idea. Instead, this should be a moment to face facts. First, that the rises in psychological distress, and the need for support with neurodevelopmental differences, are real and tied to social changes. Second, that current services are not up to what is being asked of them.

Fifteen years after the phrase “parity of esteem” gained prominence – the idea being that people with mental ill health have equivalent entitlements to those with physical illnesses – it is a long way from being realised. Years-long queues for mental health care and neurodevelopmental support are not even included in official waiting-list figures.

The difficulty comes in deciding what to do about this, particularly given the fiscal rules under which the government has chosen to operate. One proposal already accepted by ministers is for stronger regulation of ADHD and autism assessments. Currently, many of these are delivered by private providers, with no common standards in a market with low barriers to entry; such a situation should never have been allowed, though long waiting lists have driven the demand for their services.

There is no straightforward fix to the wider set of problems. The experts are right to say that access to services should be based on need, not labels. It is reasonable to challenge the way that a diagnosis has become a “door to support”, both in mental health and special educational needs contexts. But the more important question is how this situation came about. The answer is that demand overwhelmed services, and diagnosis-based thresholds became a form of triage. On the critical question of resources, the report has less to say.

It recommends stronger accountability for mental health in the Department of Health and Social Care – an excellent idea, and probably a precondition of improvement – and suggests that this and other proposals should be incorporated in the upcoming mental health strategy. Beyond that, it argues for a 10-year plan, one aim of which would be to roll mental health and neurodevelopmental support into one service.

This is an ambitious agenda, which deserves a serious response. But while Prof Fonagy may be right that some reordering of waiting lists could be managed at relatively little cost, it is inconceivable that broader reforms can be achieved without new funds. And while the report refers repeatedly, and rightly, to the need for investment, it does not explicitly state that budgets should increase as a proportion of overall health spending; nor does it make the case for waiting list targets.

Did the authors fear that such demands would be ignored? So far, Yvette Cooper has followed her predecessor as health secretary in saying relatively little about mental health and young people. Now is the time to show that she is listening.

The Guardian view on the US, Russia and the international criminal court: Trump’s assault on the rule of law intensifies

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 16:25:39 GMT

A fuel deal with Vladimir Putin, and sanctions against the legal institution, ram home the president’s belief that might is right

On Friday, Donald Trump drove home his belief that might is right and the rule of law is an obstacle rather than an essential foundation stone of international order. First came the escalated assault on the international criminal court (ICC), sanctioning the body itself. Then he announced a deal with Russia to buy diesel.

The US has long chafed at the notion of being bound by the rule of law that it espoused publicly. That hypocrisy now appears as a lesser vice. The president has declared that “my own morality” is all that constrains him. His brazen flouting of the law, embrace of dictators and rhetorical attacks all undermine global standards.

Weeks before the midterms, Mr Trump blames Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities for high diesel costs. It is his own unlawful war on Iran that has raised prices. The weekend’s attacks on Riyadh’s international airport, suspected as the work of Tehran-backed Houthis from Yemen, underscored that he cannot simply park that conflict when it suits him.

The Moscow deal is unlikely to produce significant shipments; the Russian military runs on diesel. But Ukraine is supposed to heed its message to make life easier on Vladimir Putin. It is Mr Putin (for whom the ICC has issued a warrant) who launched the illegal war, and whose troops launched lethal attacks on civilians this weekend. But in a world turned upside down, Mr Trump blames Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to cut a peace deal and says the democratically elected leader should go.

It is similarly perverse to wield measures designed to target human rights abusers and war criminals against those who seek to defend their victims. Mr Trump’s attack on the ICC was fuelled first by its Afghanistan investigation – though it has suspended consideration of US actions there – and then the issuing of arrest warrants for Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant. The court has been preparing for these measures. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said that companies have six months to wind down ties and that US allies must rein in the court: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”

In stark (and intentional) contrast, the Nobel committee on the same day announced that this year’s peace laureate is Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and chair of the UN commission which last year concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. It was not only a recognition of a remarkable career that began in apartheid‑era South Africa, but a reminder that institutions defending universal principles are under increasing pressure, and must be defended. “Peace requires justice,” the committee said.

As the ICC says, it cannot stand alone. The UK, EU and others too were right to criticise the US decision and declare their commitment to the court; invoking blocking statutes against sanctions would add heft to the rhetoric. They must show similar resolve in standing with Ukraine.

The nakedness of Mr Trump’s hostility to the rule of law has one benefit: no one can explain it away, or assume it is narrowly bounded. The war on Iran, kidnapping of Venezuela’s president, extrajudicial killings of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and threats over Greenland and Canada have shown how far he will go, and overturned assumptions that allies will be safe. It is clear that the problem is not a “rogue court”, as Mr Rubio has claimed, but a rogue superpower.

Do we really ‘hold tension’ in our hips?

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 16:00:30 GMT

The idea is popular in wellness circles, but experts say there’s no evidence that trauma uniquely affects the hips. Here’s what causes hip tightness and what can help

In yoga classes, on TikTok and throughout other wellness spaces, you’ve probably heard the saying: your hips hold tension. These joints have a reputation of being emotional storage units of sorts – but is it true that they are affected by old traumas and painful memories?

Pain and muscle tension hit harder when you’re going through a difficult time. But should tight hips make you question your mental health? And what can you do to reduce hip tightness? Here’s what you need to know.

When you sense muscle tension in your body, it’s probably caused by one of two things.

The first possibility is not clearly related to stress and involves muscles resisting stretch even when they’re relaxed. Stiffness like this is a mechanical property that reflects how your tissues are built and used.

The other possibility is that your muscles and nerves are engaged in some low-level activity more often than they need to be; this does often happen when people are under psychological stress.

Neither of these causes map cleanly on to what people actually feel, nor the anatomical location of the problem. For instance, when people refer to “tight hips”, they may be feeling pain, an unwanted pulling sensation or stiffness – and the sensation may be coming from the buttocks or the back rather than the hip.

But there is no particular predisposition for a stress-tightness link in the hips. In fact, the evidence linking mental strain with musculoskeletal tension is strongest for the muscles of the shoulders, jaw and pelvic floor. “There’s nothing special about the hip,” says Greg Lehman, a physiotherapist, chiropractor and biomechanics expert who teaches clinicians about pain science.

People who have experienced trauma, especially in childhood, are more likely to have chronic pain and tend to be more sensitive to pain in lab tests. But again, there’s no evidence this is more true for the hips.

Unpleasant sensations in the joint can arise from anatomical issues. For example, people with very shallow or very deep hip sockets tend to have more pain, says Abby Cheng, a sports medicine doctor who specializes in hip disorders at Washington University School of Medicine in St Louis.

Another anatomical cause is irritation in the tendons or their fluid-filled cushions on the outside the hip, called tendinitis or bursitis. It’s especially common in middle-aged and older women.

Other causes are harder to pinpoint. Cheng and other clinicians believe that hip and back pain can be caused by muscles in the front of the hip that are shortened by sitting, as well as other imbalances in muscle strength and length. Having said that, studies haven’t conclusively linked short hip muscles to pain, and many other factors that accompany a sedentary lifestyle may contribute to hip discomfort in desk workers, says Lehman.

Overall health may factor into hip discomfort. An anatomical problem can “nudge up your chance of having pain”, says Lehman, but stress, poor sleep, inactivity and anxiety often tip it over.

Furthermore, how tight your muscles feel doesn’t reliably predict how tight they actually are. Lehman sees it in the clinic: dancers complain of tight hamstrings, “and their foot is behind their head”.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

Start by moving more. If walking, gentle stretching and other exercise eases the tightness; it’s probably muscular and nothing dangerous, says Cheng. In these situations, she says, “motion is lotion”.

Don’t stretch too aggressively, though. It’s possible to stretch too much, says Cheng, and going beyond the gentle range can hurt more than it helps, especially if your hip discomfort is related to hip socket depth. In that scenario, she says, “you’re really just banging two bones into each other.”

Get regular aerobic exercise, and strength-train at least twice a week. For people with hip discomfort, Cheng focuses on glute-strengthening moves like clamshells and “monster walks”. These may help by increasing your hips’ ability to tolerate use, and they may also help you age better: in older adults, strength training increases bone density in the hip, which lowers the risk of a dangerous hip fracture.

Take steps to improve your health more broadly, which Lehman says can reduce your sensitivity to pain. Anything that makes you healthier helps, including meaningful activities and time with friends, he says.

Get help if hip tightness doesn’t improve with more movement or gets worse the more you move, says Cheng. Look for a clinician who examines your whole body and asks about your stress and sleep.

X-rays and MRIs can occasionally clarify the cause of your symptoms, but both experts said imaging typically doesn’t indicate where you hurt or point to the source of your discomfort. Structure is “not irrelevant, but it’s not destiny”, says Lehman.

If discomfort lingers despite your best efforts, try to make peace with it. “It’s OK to look for a fix, but sometimes accepting some pain is easier,” says Lehman. “And then the irony is, it helps.”

How to tackle serious safeguarding gaps in nurseries

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 15:52:49 GMT

Tulip Siddiq and a parent urge the government to take a number of steps to keep children safe, in response to an editorial

Your editorial on early years provision (The Guardian view on nurseries: some things are going right for under-fives, 4 October) ends by referring to the horrifying case of Vincent Chan, who worked at Bright Horizons nursery in north-west London. We write as the MP representing the constituency in which the nursery is situated and as the parent of children who attended the nursery and were victims of Chan. We believe his case exposed serious gaps in the safeguarding system that urgently need addressing by government.

First, CCTV should be mandatory in nurseries. When used with appropriate safeguards, it can provide both a deterrent and an important source of evidence when allegations are made.

Second, implementing a “flare” system that goes beyond Disclosure and Barring Service checks, allowing parents, carers and nurseries to report safeguarding concerns, and connecting allegations and relevant employment information across early years settings and over time.

Third, the law governing sexual and exploitative images of children needs examination. One family affected by this case has discovered that photographs of their child found on Chan’s devices did not meet the existing legal threshold for an indecent image. We should ask whether current legislation adequately protects children from exploitative or sexualised imagery that falls short of this threshold.

Finally, early years settings need clear, enforceable standards governing electronic devices, backed by Ofsted inspection. Nurseries hold large quantities of photographs and other sensitive digital information about vulnerable children. The rules governing how devices are used should reflect that responsibility. Had this been in place, Chan could have been caught sooner.

We urge the urgent attention of the prime minister and the government on these matters. Tulip Siddiq MP Labour, Hampstead and Highgate, Parent A Parent of children who attended Bright Horizons, Finchley Road, London

A two-tier food system for people living in poverty

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 15:52:34 GMT

Jane Middleton says the question we should be asking is not how can we use up surplus food, but how we can ensure that no one has to rely on charity to eat

Charlotte Hill (While British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolution, 6 October) conflates two separate problems. One is food waste; the other is domestic food insecurity. If, as she suggests, we use the former to address the latter, we are simply creating a two-tier food system where people living in poverty do not have the dignity of making their own choices.

While the work of food-waste charities such as the that one Hill heads is commendable as a sticking plaster, in the long term it entrenches poverty and removes any incentive for large corporations to tackle the food waste they create.

The right to food, established in the United Nations charter, includes the right of individuals to acquire food by socially acceptable means – in effect, having enough income to buy it in the same way as everyone else. The question we should be asking is not how can we use up surplus food, but how we can ensure that no one has to rely on charity in order to eat.

People on low incomes are not there to make large corporations feel good about themselves via charitable donations. Hill says that “unavoidable surplus food” is generated in our farming system. If this is the case, then consider coming to an arrangement with schools, hospitals and prisons, but please don’t view people struggling to make ends meet as a repository for your waste products.

In a country with food surpluses, we should be battling against the institutionalisation of food aid, not encouraging it. Jane MiddletonBath

Why plan for judge-only trials in fraud cases is wrong

Andy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendum

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 15:33:15 GMT

PM says he asked question upon entering No 10 but does not reveal who gave him ‘clear answer’ Russia meddled

Andy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street.

Burnham said he had asked whether Moscow had attempted to influence the referendum and received a confirmation that it had.

Speaking on the podcast The Rest is Politics, Burnham said: “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”

Burnham’s comments mark a significant departure from the position taken by past Conservative governments, which insisted there was no evidence of successful interference by Russia in the referendum vote.

The prime minister did not disclose who had given him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or whether any interference had affected the result of the vote.

A report by parliament’s intelligence and security committee in 2020 criticised the government and intelligence agencies for failing to properly investigate potential Russian interference in the referendum.

The cross-party committee found that ministers had failed to seek a full assessment of Moscow’s activities, despite evidence of attempts to influence British politics through Russian state-backed media outlets and social media accounts.

It said the government had not provided any post-referendum assessment of Russian attempts at interference, in contrast to the investigation undertaken in the US after the 2016 presidential election.

The committee also said that whether a hostile state had sought to influence a democratic process was important regardless of whether those efforts had succeeded.

Burnham said Britain needed to be more open about attempts by hostile states to interfere in its politics, particularly as European leaders grapple with the rise of the far right.

Last month the prime minister attacked Russian information warfare during a speech to the UN general assembly, saying there was evidence Moscow had tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.

Burnham told the podcast: “These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.

“I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that, actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.”

He said he had discussed the threat posed by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, on a visit to Berlin this week. Burnham said Merz raised concerns about the party’s links to Russia.

Record-breaking quartet put Australia in full control against South Africa

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 15:29:05 GMT

Australia 390 & 33-0; South Africa 284

Starc, Hazlewood, Cummins and Lyon share nine wickets

As a fractured news environment demonstrates, observations can be made from just about any perspective. One view of Australia’s Test team could focus on age, with the principal bowlers all having more than 33 years to their names. Another could focus on them all having more than 300 wickets.

At the first Test in Durban, an unprecedented achievement by Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon is continuing, one that they began in Mackay two months ago: being the only quartet in history to walk on to Test fields as members of the 300 club. By the end of day three they had taken another nine, South Africa bowled out for 284, trailing by 139 runs by the time bad light stopped play with Australia 33 without loss.

Beyond individual feats, those players are defined by the work they have done together: 38 Tests and counting as a group blitzes the previous record, however you define frontline bowlers. So it went through the first session of the third day. Hazlewood had already taken out Ryan Rickelton with a trademark dismissal the previous evening, but the morning looked set to be South Africa’s. A nice breeze, a snoozing surface, and a bushel of boundaries for Aiden Markram and David Bedingham, the latter taking three in a row from Starc.

But Starc was the one to flip the story, the left-armer around the wicket to draw Markram’s edge from a big drive on 37, the ball lifting to cause the error. Temba Bavuma followed cheaply, caught at slip reverse-sweeping Lyon, then Bedingham went for 49, Cummins now the bowler getting lift to tease another nick. The scorecard reflected team effort: Cummins one for 18, Lyon one for 14, Starc one for 37, Hazlewood one for 35.

That was the 31st over, before Wiaan Mulder bedded in with Tristan Stubbs. The match looked to be drifting by the 46th, as Australia turned to Travis Head, and Mulder immediately belted the part-time spinner for six and four. But at the other end was Cummins playing the middle-overs enforcer, as he so often does, finding a way when batting difficulty softens with the ball.

The breakthrough bouncer was the wrong line, outside off-stump, but the length and the sense of threat initially made Mulder shape to play. The pace and sharpness of bounce meant his attempt to bail out was too late, frozen in the first half of his shot when the ball lobbed up for a catch. In Cummins’ next over, the bouncer ploy snared Stubbs, mindlessly hooking to fine leg. A 55-run stand had fizzled out with both participants gone in the 30s.

The story of Australia’s four bowlers is also a story of Steve Smith’s catching. This innings took him back to the top of the Test catching list, in the game of statistical nip and tuck that he will continue to have with Joe Root for as long as they both play. Of Smith’s 223 catches so far, 150 have come from the current bowling quartet. His first three on this day were spectacular.

For the Bedingham dismissal he dived across from second slip, instinctively poaching a ball heading to first. When Bavuma shaped for the reverse hit, Smith had the fleetness of thought and foot to sidestep a couple of metres, putting himself in the path of a ball that would have flown by. At six down, Kyle Verreynne hit the same shot more sweetly, but Smith moved early again, this time putting himself in range for a full dive to his right and a one-hander. It was beyond the norm, Smith’s victory lap showing that even he rated the effort among his best.

Marco Jansen’s free swinging was fun but futile, his 26 from 20 balls far less useful for his team than Lyon’s 27 from 91 the day before, leaving South Africa 197 for eight after Jansen bashed Hazlewood to mid-off. What’s my first decision as CEO? I’m giving myself the day off

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 15:00:29 GMT

A life coach has helpfully pointed out that we’re all chief executives of our own existence. So let’s start enjoying the perks

To-do lists are done, apparently: the latest tactic to motivate and galvanise yourself is a “CEO hour”. The rationale for this method, courtesy of career and life coach Eva Katzler, is that you are the chief executive officer of your own existence, so you should routinely sit down and check in, just as they do in other businesses, reflecting on the past week and setting intentions for the next. Regularly having a formal meeting with yourself may be the kind of behaviour that makes people start worrying about you, particularly if you power dress for the occasion, but at least you can be sure you’ll get all the best biscuits.

Katzler is against the to-do list because she sees it as “our fast track to feeling like we’re completely out of control, because we can never get through it. When you never get that sense of achievement, what you’re left with is a feeling of failure.”

Instead she suggests asking yourself what your wins were from the last week, which tasks you’ve been avoiding, and how you’re managing your energy, time and workload. Also, noting any eureka moments you had, how well you took care of yourself, and what support you need.

Scoff all you like, but for me even the idea of a CEO hour was impactful, because I noticed that my immediate instincts were to wonder how low the bar was for what constituted a win of the week (does “lived to tell the tale” count?) and worry about a boardroom coup. My company felt much more unfortunate Apprentice candidate than Fortune 500.

But then came one of those eureka moments I’m meant to be looking out for: I don’t have to do this well. In fact, there’s absolutely no point making any effort at all. I’m already the CEO, baby! There’s no position higher – I’ve already climbed to the top of the ladder. Ah, the sweet smell of success. I think I’ll give myself the rest of the day off, and if I’ve got a problem with that, I’ll have to take it up with me.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

Zack Polanski signals Green party overhaul after row over Zionism vote

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 15:00:29 GMT

Rapid growth means structures need to change and give leaders greater control, Polanski says in Guardian article

Zack Polanski: How we’re transforming British politics

Zack Polanski has signalled a potential overhaul of the Green party’s cherished grassroots democracy, calling for leaders to have greater control over strategic direction after a divisive vote equating Zionism with racism.

The Green party leader has also questioned whether political parties should seek to define what members believe, in his strongest criticism yet of a motion that has provoked bitter divisions, international condemnation and calls for his resignation.

Writing for the Guardian after his defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, Polanski suggests the party’s focus on defining Zionism has been misguided, even though he agrees with the substance of the motion.

Appearing to accept criticisms of his leadership over the issue, he admits his priority was “fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party” and accepts that his own colleagues and members may feel “let down” by his decision to not make an intervention last week.

He adds: “I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.”

Polanski says the party’s rapid growth means its democratic structures need to change, including giving leaders more responsibility for setting its political direction.

“Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible,” he writes.

His intervention marks the clearest indication yet that he believes the party’s internal structures need reform, after senior Greens raised concerns that its system of policymaking gives disproportionate influence to a small minority of members.

Under the Greens’ existing rules, policy is decided by members at party conference rather than by its leadership, a system that has increasingly come under scrutiny as membership surged.

The controversy intensified last weekend when 1,022 members representing about 0.4% of the party’s total membership voted in favour of a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism and backing a single Palestinian state.

The motion, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813, was opposed by four of the party’s five MPs and prompted criticism from the European Green party, whose position supports a two-state solution.

Ellie Chowns, the Greens’ Westminster leader, said the party must not become vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists, arguing the vote demonstrated the urgent need to modernise its policymaking structures.

Polanski, who is Jewish and grew up in a Zionist household, writes: “It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians.

“This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the Holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion.

“At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up with identity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic.

“There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with, such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel and Palestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone the Green party – to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.”

The comments go beyond Polanski’s previous objections to elements of the motion, which largely centred on its call for a single Palestinian state rather than leaving Palestinians to determine their own political future.

The controversy exposed divisions within the Greens and raised questions about the party’s ability to manage its rapid expansion under Polanski’s leadership.

The Guardian previously reported that senior Greens feared the existing structure allowed a small number of highly motivated activists to determine policy for the wider membership. Some argued members should set broad political priorities while smaller bodies developed detailed policies.

Yes, it’s been a tough week for the Greens: but don’t lose sight of how we’re transforming British politics

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 15:00:28 GMT

We must now have unity and a discussion about party democracy. And let me be clear: as leader, I will never tolerate antisemitism

When I stood for leader of the Greens in 2025, our party was at a crossroads. The transformative leadership of Carla Denyer and Adrian Ramsay had taken us to an electoral success we’d never seen before. I knew we had even greater potential – and that the country was crying out for the bold politics we could offer.

We have seen unprecedented wins this year – from our first ever parliamentary byelection win to our landslide council and mayoral victories in former Labour strongholds.

Those victories have moved Labour. Our electoral successes helped topple Keir Starmer, seeing him replaced by a prime minister unarguably to his left. They forced a change in tone in the government’s relations with Israel. The government has even rowed back on some of its cruel anti-migrant policies.

Our work isn’t done. But the next phase for our party takes place in a landscape that is clearly more challenging for us. Andy Burnham is enjoying a honeymoon phase, and hasn’t yet had to make the “difficult decisions” that will reveal exactly who will lose out under his government – unpopular choices he will probably start making at his fast-approaching first budget.

Of course I wanted to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. But our result shows, as the polling expert John Curtice has said, that our party represents a greater threat to Labour in places like this than ever before. We tripled our vote share in a seat that Labour has comfortably held since 1983 and forced it to campaign hard in a constituency it would once have taken for granted.

We have transformed the electoral landscape and, as the first nationwide serious threat to Labour on its left in modern political history, we are here to stay.

The result also came at a difficult moment for our party. A motion voted through at our conference, “Zionism is racism”, has stirred up strong feelings among many members and the wider public too. And I know there have been questions about my approach to the motion.

I’m a Jewish man who grew up in a Zionist household. The story I was told about Israel was one of destiny and safety: a land without a people for a people without a land. But since then I have learned about the people who did live on that land – and what has happened to them. The Palestinians driven from their homes; slaughtered en masse; and those who remain, living under an apartheid system that denies them fundamental rights, including that of self-determination.

It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion.

At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up with identity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic.

There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with – such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel and Palestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone the Green party – to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.

Before the vote, I made it clear that there were amendments I would like to see made, and I am disappointed that those did not pass.

I have been asked why I was not present for the vote. The answer is that my priority was fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party. I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.

after newsletter promotion

My responsibility now is to bring our party together to achieve our full potential. This starts with an assurance from me: under my leadership, I will not tolerate antisemitism. No one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith or where they worship. I will meet any group within our party that fears victimisation to understand exactly what they need in order to feel safe and welcome.

Second, our party has grown to a size none of us could have anticipated when I became leader. Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible.

Above all, that unity must be deployed in the service of changing this country for the better. This government is on course to preside over the worst parliament for living standards in modern times. Energy bills are expected to rise again this winter; rent increases are forecast to speed up. Meanwhile, Burnham is offering no concrete support for bills and ruling out any controls on rents, and Reform UK is still using cost of living pressures to stir up division in our communities.

The Green party’s bold, principled ideas have never been more needed. From an emergency brake on rents to full public ownership of water companies, we are offering solutions that this government won’t go near unless we force it to. We have work to do – and I will bring my party together to get it done.

Zack Polanski is the leader of the Green party of England and Wales and a member of the London assembly

Resurgent Verstappen holds off Leclerc to seal dominant F1 Singapore GP win

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 14:19:26 GMT

Red Bull driver claims second victory in a row

Kimi Antonelli third and closes in on title

Delivering an emphatic reminder of how imperious he can be when he has the car beneath him, Max Verstappen was untouchable in victory at the Singapore Grand Prix.

It has taken Red Bull most of the season to deliver said ride, however, and the title is beyond the Dutchman. In his wake at the Marina Bay circuit the champion in waiting, Kimi Antonelli, did enough to move to within a race of taking the crown.

The race under the floodlights certainly belonged to Verstappen, who with a commanding run from pole to flag took his first victory at Marina Bay, on the occasion of his 250th race.

He was enthused, understandably. Having wrestled with a recalcitrant car for so long, the Red Bull was purring in Singapore. He took pole and the win in the sprint race and then pole and victory in the grand prix.

His second win in a row this season was taken with consummate calm even given a malfunctioning radio, where all the team could hear from him was the garbled, distorted static beloved of the more vociferous noise metal outfits.

The victory, beating the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc into second place with Antonelli taking third, was of greatest import in that he and the team have proved able to bring performance to the car that they can feed into next year’s model.

On this form they can expect to open 2027 in a far more competitive position, from which Verstappen will expect not to be on the sidelines of a title fight, a fight that this time around has been absolutely bossed by Antonelli.

His third place in Singapore, along with his Mercedes teammate George Russell coming back to take only ninth place, having started from 19th, was enough to ensure the 20-year-old has one hand on the title.

His lead over Russell is now 102 points and he can mathematically win the title at the next round in Austin if he takes victory and Russell finishes ninth or lower and Lewis Hamilton, who was sixth in Singapore and is 111 in arrears, is fifth or lower.

The Italian reacted with surprise when told he could seal it and become F1’s youngest champion as soon as Texas. He was counting no chickens but there was, for the first time, an acknowledgment that his dream is within reach.

The manner of how he reached this point was demonstrated in Singapore, where he ground out the best he could with a car that was not competitive at the very front while notably enjoying, as all champions do, a little good fortune as well.

In what was a largely pedestrian race on a track where passing is remarkably tricky and with Verstappen in a class of his own out front, Antonelli understood that banking points from fourth on the grid was all that mattered and proceeded to pound round in a strategic fight with the Ferraris of Leclerc and Hamilton and the McLaren of Lando Norris.

He complained of feeling liquid at his feet and losing his brakes at one point but held his nerve with the steel of a veteran. Solid but unspectacular, he was in fifth for much of the race until the final stages when Hamilton’s decision not to pit under a virtual safety car came back and bit the Ferrari driver.

Hamilton had started third but took his pit stop early in the race after which Ferrari appeared to be undecided as to fully commit him to a two-stop strategy, notably not calling for Leclerc to move over for him.

Finally, a helpful intervention in the ‘overdiagnosis’ wars. But where’s the money to answer this tragedy?

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 14:10:35 GMT

There is much to agree with in the Fonagy review into mental health support. Without serious public funding, however, its approach won’t work

Back in late 2025, when Keir Starmer’s grip on the Labour party was loosening and Reform UK was still in its pomp, the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, commissioned what the government called its “Independent review into prevalence and support for mental health conditions, ADHD and autism”.

Here, it seemed, was not just an inquiry into England’s ever-extending waiting lists for the diagnosis of mental illness and neurodevelopmental conditions, and the dire lack of support for people who experience one or both of them. The review would also dovetail with two other huge issues: mounting claims of “overdiagnosis”, which Streeting had appeared to partly endorse, and the government’s drive for the reform of so-called welfare. An apparently well-briefed piece in the Times seemed to speak volumes: work led by the renowned psychologist Peter Fonagy, it said, was commencing just “as Labour seeks a fresh crackdown on welfare spending” amid diagnoses “which have become the most common reason for a sickness benefit claim”.

Last Friday saw the publication of the 600-page final report Fonagy had co-authored with Gillian Baird – a specialist in paediatric neurodisability – and the psychiatrist Simon Wessely. And, as so often happens with such inquiries, its interpretation suggested the media’s equivalent of a Rorschach blot. One of the Guardian’s headlines was “No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real”. The Mail, by contrast, yelled out a rather different message – “Rush to diagnose ADHD and autism can damage children” – while the Telegraph went for “ADHD surge fuelled by benefits, report warns”.

Such are the perils of producing a very nuanced mixture of analysis and recommendations. When he appeared on Radio 4’s Today programme, Fonagy said that Streeting had been “completely wrong” to agree with suggestions of the common overdiagnosis of mental health disorders. When it comes to autism and ADHD, he and his colleagues’ report says that “if present trends continue we are clearly entering a phase in which the balance of risks is changing, from previous merited concerns with under-recognition and underdiagnosis towards an increased risk of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis”. But it also insists that right now, “we cannot conclude that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale”, and points out that any data that might settle this festering argument “largely do not exist”. This is not the kind of stuff that suits a world that craves simple binaries and polarised shouting, but it speaks an undeniable truth.

For the most part, in fact, it is hard to disagree with what the review points out. But among its conclusions lies one troubling proposal – that provision for both mental illness and so-called neurodivergence can and should often be led by observations of need rather than formal diagnosis. In making that suggestion, I have no doubt that Fonagy and his colleagues’ intentions are benign. But our systems of power and politics and the government’s increasingly anxious view of public spending could yet make it very dangerous indeed.

First, though, the undeniable positives. In a very elegantly written and often moving introduction, Fonagy – who is 74 – completely rejects the popular idea of a new generation of wilting wimps falsely claiming to be suffering from mental ill-health. “The cacophony of voices now available to a young person – most of them digital, many of them confident, few of them accountable – has made the ordinary developmental process of understanding oneself far harder than it was for me,” he says. He goes on: “Young people today are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced. They are not fragile. They are outnumbered.”

These are mental health issues. When it comes to autism and ADHD, Fonagy and his two colleagues’ insistence that overdiagnosis is currently not happening “at scale” and that “the evidence does not show that people presenting today are less impaired than those presenting previously” is very important indeed. When Streeting commissioned the review, among the most in-vogue books was The Age of Diagnosis by the neurologist and epilepsy specialist Suzanne O’Sullivan, which made the absurd suggestion that the overdiagnosis of autism might have reached the point where it was partly to blame for rising rates of anxiety and depression among the young, linked to her claim that “the stigma of autism has been associated with low self esteem among children”. (If autism is still stigmatised, O’Sullivan publicly calling it an “illness” is hardly helpful.)

The review, by contrast, is altogether more calm and evidence-based: for a bundle of reasons, it says that overdiagnosis and misdiagnosis may well be a future risk, but we can guard against those dangers by more closely regulating private diagnostic clinics (which are often partly NHS-funded) and stop them advertising their services. These are proposals that many autism and ADHD insiders agree with.

On a different subject, Fonagy and his co-authors also do us all a favour by emphasising the correct meaning of the ubiquitous term “neurodiversity”: whereas O’Sullivan says that it “has a biologising, pathologising effect”, the report rightly understands that the word means the complete opposite: it crystallises the plain fact that “variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour is part of natural human diversity rather than pathology or disorder”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But what do we do when faced with genuinely diagnosable conditions that are debilitating and entail intensive support? One bit of first-person testimony in the report is heartbreaking. “When she was 12,” says an unnamed parent, “our daughter was put on ADHD medication, which lowered her mood, leading her to self-harm. She was referred to CAMHS [child and adolescent mental health services] who turned her down. Within the next month we ended up in A&E due to taking an overdose. She was then finally accepted by CAMHS, who suggested an autism assessment.

“Two years later, after receiving an autism diagnosis, little changed. School would not make any adjustments until an EHCP (education, health and care plan) was accepted, and social care said she did not meet their threshold for support because she did not have a learning disability. Our daughter was broken and unsupported and was admitted to inpatients at 15 years old.”

Herein lies one of the review’s few dangers. By way of lessening an increasingly frightening crisis that is partly centred on pitifully long waits for formal diagnoses that can easily be ignored, it suggests moving towards a more “needs-based” approach, which echoes the government’s plans for special needs education. “There should be a fundamental shift from a diagnosis-dependent system to a needs-led plus diagnosis system,” it says. Such a change, the report says, would require “increased capacity, transformation through digitally enabled care, clearer national standards and sustained investment”.

They are my italics, with very good reason. The government responded to the report by saying that the health and social care secretary, Yvette Cooper, “has asked NHS leaders to urgently examine how people can access advice, assessments and treatment more easily”. But without sufficient money, “needs-based” help is likely to amount to very little at all. Coincidentally, the Fonagy review arrived on the same day as reports that the prime minister and the chancellor had rebuffed Cooper’s requests for money to fund a pay rise for NHS staff including nurses, porters and midwives. So what chance of a huge cash injection to tackle what the report so starkly highlights?

Meanwhile, the Department for Work and Pensions still has a culture built around crackdowns and pushing people into work. Councils repeatedly fail to meet their responsibilities for the care and education of neurodivergent people. And, in the absence of properly funded change, both they and people suffering mental illness only stand even a faint chance of pushing their way through an almost impossible mess of bureaucracy and obstruction if they have pieces of paper confirming that their condition – or conditions – are real and true.

This is what makes politicians who talk of “overdiagnosis” look so crass, and the likely fate of such a definitive and in-depth report so tragic. It is an all too familiar story, indicative of our current defining national predicament: the government simply cannot afford what it proposes, so one of our cruellest modern crises looks set to grind on.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

‘That’s when I begin to scream’: Mick Fanning on punching a great white shark

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 14:00:28 GMT

The Australian surfing champion was monstered by a great white shark while competing against fellow Aussie Julian Wilson in the 2015 world tour event final at Jeffreys Bay in South Africa. The attack was broadcast live on TV. Here, in an extract from his memoir, All Heart, he relives the encounter

I’m locked in on my take-off spot in the J-Bay lineup, scanning the horizon, biding my time. Assessing my position against the rippling lines of the oncoming set, I decide to move slightly further inside.

As I move, there’s a big splash behind me. Glancing over my left shoulder, I catch a glimpse of a huge dark shape in the water. A jolt of fear grips me. What the hell is that?

Instinct kicks in and I haul myself up on to my board to shield my body. There’s a violent lurch directly beneath me. Suddenly, I’m yanked off by a wild tug on my leg rope. I quickly scramble to get back on my board and that’s when I see it. The unmistakable fin of a shark.

There’s a split second of full-body panic. Then: THWACK! The shark’s tail whips out and wallops my left cheek. My head jerks back as a white flash of pain explodes in my skull. Then I’m being dragged down into the churning water, the force almost tearing my leg from its socket. Consumed with terror, I’m suddenly released and break through to the surface, gasping for breath. Has the shark got tangled in my leg rope and bitten through it?

Suddenly, the shark jackknifes around. It’s like a torpedo hurtling straight towards me. That’s when I begin to scream.

The shark crashes into me from the side and I blindly lash out with my fists, yelling, punching, kicking. It shrugs me off like a leaf. I fall backwards into the waves again and as my head surfaces, I see it swimming away from me towards the horizon.

Flailing in the water, head on a swivel, I swim away hard. I can see Jules about 25 metres away now.

Got to warn him. Now. “Shark! Shark! Go in! Go! GO!”

Jules keeps paddling towards me. “Go in!” I yell.

“There’s a bloody shark.” He keeps coming.

Just then, I imagine the shark circling back around. If it comes for me now, it’ll get me from behind. I’ve got no board, it’ll go at my legs first. There’s no way to defend myself. Fuck that.

There’s no way I’m going to let that happen. I stop swimming. Force myself to turn. Fists clenched, I tread water breathing hard, trying to get as high as I can, scouring the water for the shark’s return. The world goes mute and I’m so focused that I don’t notice the jetski until it’s right by my side.

“Mick! Mick! Get up here!”

I scramble up on to the sled it’s towing, looking around for Jules. “Jules? Where is he?”

“On the other jetski. He’s fine. You OK?”

Wait, am I OK? Hastily, I scan my limbs. Check my hands and fingers, feet and toes. I seem to be alright. I just need to stop hyperventilating.

“Yeah, I’m OK. But what the fuck?”

Seconds later, the jetski pulls up by the bigger boat. Jules is on board. His eyes are wild. “You right?” he stammers.

“Yeah, you? I was telling you to go in! You crazy bastard.”

He shrugs and then gripping each other by the shoulders, we both start laughing manically, shit-faced on adrenaline and pure relief. “That was so gnarly. So fucking gnarly.”

“Whoah! I can’t believe that actually happened.” And it’s like we’ve survived the biggest scare of all time. Like we’ve won a war, cheated death, escaped the jaws of a great white! Somehow, we’ve got away scot-free. There are high fives and backslaps. Hoots and howls. Everyone on the boat is talking a mile a minute, pumped up with a mix of exhilaration and hysteria.

“If you’re both OK, we’re going to get you in now,” says Peter Mel, the field commentator who’s been calling heats from the water.

“We can probably just surf in, yeah?”

Peter stares at me as if I’m insane, then he speaks to me with the sort of soft tone you’d use to address a small child.

“No, Mick, that was a big shark. We’re going to escort you in.”

Whatever. I turn to Jules. “I can’t believe you fucking swum towards me. You’re fucking crazy!”

“What was I gonna do? Watch my mate get eaten by a shark?”

On the shore, we’re bustled straight into a white Volkswagen van and continue our postmortem. When Jules hears that I punched the shark, he convulses in giggles. I laugh too, because it’s all so crazy. Jules still looks utterly wired, his pupils dilated like two black holes.

“Mate, that was wild!” he says shaking his head.

I start laughing again. It’s like my nervous system has got whiplash. Then the doors of the van open.

Standing outside are Jarrad and Fletch, plus my mates: Otto, Ace and a bunch of other touring surfers. I’m expecting more high fives and wild-eyed grins. Instead, they’re deathly quiet. They look shell-shocked and upset. In fact, most of them are in tears.

OK, maybe I’ve misread the situation here …

I’m engulfed in a tearful hug from Ace [Australian world tour surfer Adrian Buchan]. He’s more distraught than I am. Then Fletch embraces me [Rip Curl team manager Ryan Fletcher]. Then Jarrad [former tour surfer and Mick’s coach at the event]. Immediately, I start explaining what happened. How the shark grabbed my leg rope. Bit through it. How I landed a punch or two.

“Someone was looking after us,” I say.

Jules and I are led up to the commissioner’s office. Inside, they’re all completely rattled too. I get hugged by more people. I agree to an interview with Ronnie who is there in his role as an event commentator for the WSL broadcast. It hadn’t occurred to me yet that this whole thing has been beamed live all around the world. As Fletch suggests: it’s the easiest way to let everyone back home know I’m OK.

Before the interview I’m asked by the tour commissioner, Kieren Perrow, if I’d like to see the footage.

“Yeah, I think I’ve got to,” I tell him. “Cause I don’t think I’m processing this the same as everyone else.”

In Kieren’s office, a bunch of us gather around a big-screen TV. And then, I watch the replay.

There I am waiting for a wave, oblivious. Then the splash behind me, the shark’s fin, the flurry of whitewater as I try to scramble away. The next moment, a wave obscures the camera. For eight long seconds no one can see the frantic tussle that almost cost me my life. The camera even pans back as if wanting to protect the viewer from the worst-case scenario.

“We all thought you were gone,” Jarrad says. “The last thing we saw was you being knocked off your board, then that set rolled in. Next thing we saw was your board heading out to sea … ”

Watching the footage, what’s most terrifying is the size of the shark. It must’ve been at least three-and-a-half metres long, with the girth of a submarine. Suddenly, I don’t feel invincible any more. I just feel very, very lucky. A shark that big can do whatever the hell it wants.

“Oh fuck,” I stammer.

And suddenly it dawns on me that Mum was watching the final live back home.

“Can someone please call Mum? Let her know I’m OK.”

Then I realise the quickest way to let her know is to jump on the broadcast, which is still going. I do the interview with Ronnie. The adrenaline is starting to wear off now, the cold horror of what happened is kicking in. The conversation is a blur. I’m just about holding it together, wiping away the odd tear.

“The commissioner’s office has decided that there’ll be no final run today,” Ronnie says.

“Is that even a concern for you at this stage?”

“Mate, I’m happy to not ever compete again. I just want to let all my family and friends know that I’m OK. Right now, I’m just tripping out.”

The interview finishes, and as I walk off camera, standing there is Kelly Slater. He’s my arch rival, the man I’ve battled against so hard on so many occasions. He walks towards me and just embraces me in a giant hug.

I walk downstairs surrounded by security. Parko is standing at the bottom with Ace and Bec, his wife. Bec’s emotional – she knows how bad it could’ve been. She hugs me and my legs just buckle. That’s when it all sinks in and I’m overcome. I burst into tears as reality hits like a tsunami.

Ronnie notices me crumble. “Righto mate, we better get you out of here now.”

This is an edited extract from All Heart by Mick Fanning (A$36.99, Simon & Schuster)

Wildlife park confirms tiger will not be euthanised after man mauled to death

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 13:48:21 GMT

Ed Miliband, whose constituency includes the park, offers ‘deepest condolences’ to family of visitor who entered enclosure on Saturday

A wildlife park in Yorkshire has confirmed the tiger that mauled to death a man who entered its enclosure will not be euthanised.

A man, who has not yet been named, was seen entering a tiger enclosure at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, located near Doncaster, before police were called at 1.35pm on Saturday.

South Yorkshire police said the tiger “subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury” and despite the efforts of emergency services, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement on Sunday, the wildlife park thanked those who had expressed concern after the “tragic incident” and said their “thoughts and heartfelt sympathies” remained with the family of the man who lost his life.

“The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support,” the statement read. The park also confirmed that the tiger, named Altai, was “safe and well and will not be euthanised” after the incident.

The foreign secretary and MP for Doncaster North, Ed Miliband, said he was “deeply saddened” and sent his “thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died”.

“I am very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded,” Miliband added.

One visitor at the park, Marie Miller, wrote in a Facebook post that she had seen the man before the incident and he was “happily enjoying” his visit. Miller said the man had asked a stranger to take a picture of him.

“The man who I saw on the bridge with his earpods in dancing was happily enjoying seeing the tiger,” the post read.

“He asked a total stranger to take a picture of him with the tiger in the background.”

Another visitor, who did not want to be identified, told the South West News Service that it was “frightening and confusing” when the park was evacuated after the incident.

She said: “At first, we were all scared and confused because we had no idea what was going on. Different routes had been closed off, and staff were positioned around the park directing visitors where to go.

“The scariest part was not knowing what was happening.”

The visitor said she heard people saying the man was 22, but was unable to confirm this. “As we walked past the police near the tiger enclosure, we saw officers surrounding a young man in the tiger enclosure,” she said. “We saw an air ambulance outside the park, although, from what we observed, it didn’t take anyone away.”

South Yorkshire police said the man’s family was made aware of the incident on Saturday and were being supported by specialist officers. The force has encouraged people not to share videos of the incident that have been circulating online.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011. The attraction is on a purpose-built 2-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.

Flu cases higher than usual in England during September, experts say

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 13:32:58 GMT

UK Health Security Agency notes above-average activity and urges at-risk groups to get vaccinated

Flu is striking earlier than usual in England, experts have said, insisting that vaccination is the best way to blunt its impact.

According to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), flu is at low levels, but various metrics, such as the proportion of positive tests and GP consultations for influenza-like illness, suggest it is on the rise, with the number of emergency-department attendances for influenza-like illness above seasonally expected levels.

“Flu activity throughout September has been higher than in the same period during all past four winter seasons,” UKHSA reported, adding that flu trends had been rising since August.

Prof Sir Andrew Pollard, the director of the Oxford Vaccine Group, said: “There is one simple action for all those who are at risk because of age or their underlying health conditions, which is to get vaccinated as soon as possible and before we reach the peak of transmission.

“Everyone can benefit from being vaccinated but free vaccines are only available for children and those in higher-risk groups.”

He added that those who were not eligible for a free flu vaccine via the NHS might be able to access them for free through their workplace, while vaccines were also available privately for anybody able to pay for them.

A private flu vaccination costs about £20 at most high street pharmacies, and some retailers offer them for under £10 as part of membership schemes.

Pollard said an earlier flu season did not necessarily mean a worse flu season. “We don’t know for certain why the timing varies each year.” He believed an early rise was due to a combination of factors, including the weather, the particular strain of the virus that is around and its ability to spread, the immunity of the population to the circulating strain, and aspects of behaviour – for example, the number of close contacts people have.

Antonia Ho, a professor of infectious diseases at the University of Glasgow’s Centre for Virus Research, said it was important to get vaccinated as soon as possible as it took a few weeks for the vaccine to provide full protection.

“An early rise in influenza cases may indicate a more intense influenza season overall, because earlier onset is associated with a longer period of community transmission and higher cumulative case numbers,” she said. “However, onset timing alone doesn’t determine severity.”

Data from UKHSA has suggested the increase in flu is being driven by cases among young people aged 18 to 24, and that a mix of two flu A subtypes – H1N1 and H3N2 – is circulating in England. “The flu vaccine covers both subtypes and also influenza B,” said Ho.

While UKHSA has noted that the H1N1 subtype of flu A appears to have changed or “drifted” a little from the strain that was used to make this year’s flu vaccine, Ho said it was too soon to say if that would affect how well the vaccine worked.

According to data from UKHSA, the vaccination programme in England last winter is estimated to have prevented about 100,000 hospital admissions and 7,000 deaths, despite the flu season again starting earlier than usual.

John Tregoning, a professor of vaccine immunology at Imperial College London and author of the book Infectious: Pathogens and How We Fight Them, said: “Last year is a good example where [we] also had an early start to the flu season, and then because of that, probably people slightly changed their behaviours and went and got vaccinated, and then it comes down again.”

Experts have urged those eligible for a Covid jab to get vaccinated, with UKHSA data suggesting levels of Covid are rising. Tregoning also emphasised the importance of vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

Ho said that while vaccination against respiratory diseases was important, there were additional measures people could take if they started to feel unwell.

“If you have flu-like symptoms, ideally stay at home, practice good hand hygiene, avoid contact with others,” she said.
