‘I want to do everything I can to head off dementia’: why demand for the shingles vaccine is soaring

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 13:00:27 GMT

Could a drug intended to prevent painful rashes also protect our brains as we get older? The signs are promising – but not conclusive. Yet that’s enough to be driving a boom in shingles jabs

When Jenny, a 50-year-old marketing and branding professional from Cambridge, went for her shingles vaccine last year, an entirely different disease was on her mind. Having witnessed three of her four grandparents succumb to dementia, with all the distress that brought, she wants to avoid the same fate. She hopes the shingles vaccine might help.

Jenny is far from alone. Britain’s high street chemists have reported a rise in demand for the shingles vaccine, at least some of which is driven by people more worried about dementia than shingles. And while the vaccine is free for some on the NHS, most under-65s pay around £450 for the full two doses.

The trend follows a flurry of studies that suggest, but do not prove, that the shingles vaccination might offer some protection against dementia. How much protection? It depends on how the study is done, but scientists have reported as much as a 20% reduction in risk, with the strongest effects in women. On a brutal disease that has no cure, the impact could be profound. “Imagine a vaccine that became a medicine for dementia,” says John Todd, professor of precision medicine at the University of Oxford and one of the scientists involved. “Wow. Wouldn’t that be amazing?”

Recent figures from Boots show that bookings for its shingles vaccination service more than doubled over the past year, after rising 30% in the year before. A similar trend has played out at Superdrug, where bookings are up 41% year on year.

Of course, many who go for their shots simply want to avoid shingles. It’s a painful rash, triggered by reactivation of the chickenpox virus which lies dormant in the nervous system after a childhood infection. The vaccine is not approved for any other condition. But dozens of people who contacted the Guardian said preventing dementia was at least part of their reason for getting the shots.

“I want to feel as if I’ve done everything I can to try to head it off, in terms of risk factors and preventive measures that are available to me now,” says Jenny. “If there’s a potential for this to give me more time without the onset of dementia in 20 years’ time, then God, I’ll take it.”

Nearly 60 million people live with dementia globally, but the figure is set to rise with population growth and ageing. By 2040, more than 100 million people are projected to have the disease. In England and Wales, it’s expected dementia could affect 1.7 million people that year, with the annual cost reaching £90bn.

The most common form of dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, is associated with the abnormal buildup of proteins in the brain. Plaques (clusters) of amyloid accumulate between neurons, and tangles of another protein, tau, form inside the nerve cells. New drugs can clear amyloid plaques and slow the disease, but so far the impact on patients appears small and the side-effects can be serious.

The wave of work on the shingles vaccine was spurred by suspicions that the virus that causes chickenpox and shingles, varicella zoster virus or VZV, might somehow contribute to dementia. After a chickenpox infection, some virus remains in the body, lying dormant in neurons. As the immune system weakens with age, or is suppressed through medications or stress, the virus can reactivate and travel down nerve cells to the skin where it causes shingles. In the brain, the virus can drive inflammation, nerve cell stress and the accumulation of amyloid and tau.

In an influential paper in Nature last year, researchers at Stanford University in California focused on a natural experiment that arose in Wales during a shingles vaccination programme. The vaccine on offer, Zostavax, was a live-attenuated vaccine, meaning it contained a weakened version of the varicella zoster virus. It was made available from 1 September 2013, but anyone who was 80 or older on that day was ineligible, because it becomes less effective the older a person gets.

The age-related cutoff split the older population into two groups: those who could get the vaccine and those who could not. This allowed scientists to compare dementia rates in thousands of people born on different sides of the eligibility line.

When the Stanford team ran the numbers, they found that dementia rates were 8.5% lower in the vaccine-eligible group over seven years, in women, but not in men (the gender disparity in this experiment remains unexplained). Since only about half of the group went along for their shots, the researchers concluded that the vaccine lowered dementia risk by nearly 20%. They have since reported similar effects in Australia and Ontario, Canada.

“We have a really compelling body of data from these studies,” says Pascal Geldsetzer, an epidemiologist on the Stanford studies. “We’re much more confident that what we’re looking at is cause and effect rather than just correlation.”

More evidence came in 2024 from the University of Oxford, when Todd teamed up with psychiatrists Maxime Taquet and Paul Harrison to study Shingrix, a newer and more potent shingles vaccine that has largely replaced Zostavax. Shingrix is not a live-attenuated vaccine but contains viral proteins and an adjuvant – an additive designed to strengthen the body’s immune response and so make the vaccine more effective. In this case, the adjuvant is made of tiny fat-based particles called liposomes that are filled with various compounds that stimulate different parts of the immune response.

The Oxford team analysed health records for more than 200,000 US citizens who were vaccinated for shingles. About half had Shingrix and half Zostavax. Over the next six years, dementia cases were 17% lower in those who had Shingrix compared with Zostavax, amounting to an extra 164 days lived without the condition. Women fared better, with a 22% lower risk compared with 13% for men. (Women have a higher dementia risk, which seems mostly down to them living longer.) One benefit of the study was that it compared Zostavax v Shingrix rather than vaccinated v unvaccinated people. That reduced the risk of the results being skewed by the “health vaccinee” bias, whereby people who get vaccinated are generally more health conscious and do more to reduce their risk of dementia in other ways.

“I thought wow, I’ll just book the vaccine online,” says Todd. “If by chance it does lower the risk of dementia, I’m 68 – why wouldn’t I take that? And also, it’s really effective against shingles.” Todd is a consultant for GSK, the manufacturer of Shingrix, but the company had no involvement in any of the studies.

More recent work hints at other potential benefits of the vaccine. In August, the Oxford team published a paper showing a reduced risk of heart attacks and stroke after the Shingrix vaccination. The effect is small, but across the population it could prevent thousands of deaths per year. Separate work at Kaiser Permanente, the US healthcare giant, found a similar effect.

The results are exciting, but none of this is proof. Critical questions remain. In July, researchers at the University of Bristol, and others including Geldsetzer, found no evidence in much larger English hospital records that Zostavax protects against dementia. That may be due to quirks in the data or how it is analysed, or a sign that the old Zostavax vaccine does not protect against dementia after all. Geldsetzer suspects hospital data is not the best for studying dementia, as most patients are managed in primary care.

Precisely how the vaccine might protect against dementia is still a puzzle. By stimulating the immune system to attack VZV, the vaccine might help to reduce inflammation and cellular damage in the brain. There may be knock-on effects whereby inflammation reactivates another dormant virus, the cold sore-causing HSV1, which in turn drives Alzheimer’s-like damage. The vaccine may also have broader effects, boosting ailing immune systems so they are better at clearing harmful waste from the brain.

One avenue scientists are exploring is whether the adjuvant, which is in Shingrix but not Zostavax, is important for protection against dementia. The Oxford team suspect that might explain why a vaccine for respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, which contains the same adjuvant as Shingrix, also appears to protect against dementia. The adjuvant specifically stimulates T-cells that are central to the immune response to the virus. “You want a really healthy immune system to do the garbage collection of damaged neurons,” says Todd.

The lack of hard proof hasn’t stopped people taking action. Jenny had already had a bout of shingles – “It looked like I’d been slapped across the face by a zombie,” she says – but it was the fear of dementia that prompted her to get vaccinated. She made the decision after reading the research for herself, wary that the press might have hyped it.

Sally, a 68-year-old former headteacher in Telford, Shropshire, cared for her mother with dementia for five years. “It does bring you up very sharply when you’re considering your own future,” she says. Sally runs marathons, watches her nutrition carefully and does all she can to protect herself from the disease. “I was going to have the shingles jab anyway, but when I saw the research saying there may be a protective effect against dementia, I jumped at it. The experience of caring for someone who developed dementia was pivotal in my decision.” She got the jabs on the NHS.

It could be a while before we have clear answers. Todd and colleagues want to do a mechanistic study to understand at the deepest level what happens to the immune system when people have the shingles vaccination. Meanwhile, two major clinical trials are under way in Finland and Denmark to see whether Shingrix genuinely protects against dementia, but they won’t report for years.

What should people do in the meantime? Geldsetzer says that while vaccine recommendations are a matter for government advisory bodies, he wouldn’t discourage people who want to get the shingles vaccine for dementia protection. Todd says: “I have been suggesting to friends and colleagues to get the vaccine if they are 50 or over – it’s safe.”

Alzheimer’s Research UK does not advise people to have the shingles vaccine specifically to prevent dementia. Instead, it recommends all the healthy habits we know promote brain health: exercise, a good diet and challenging the brain throughout life. Michael Jones, evidence manager at the charity, says: “While new studies finding these links are promising and growing in number, there isn’t enough data to demonstrate a direct cause-and-effect relationship.”

Dominic, a 61-year-old engineer in Christchurch, Dorset, paid for the Shingrix vaccine last year. His father had shingles, the classic rash around the torso, which lasted for months. His eldest sister had shingles, too. It affected her eye and caused minor damage. A cousin also developed the condition. Dominic planned to get the shot, but only acted after reading the dementia research. “I really don’t want to get shingles,” he says. “That could strike at anytime. And when does dementia start? We just don’t know, do we?”

‘It’s not just about circling things on a map’: how our journalists use and corroborate satellite imagery

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 13:00:27 GMT

From the destruction of Gaza to climate breakdown, satellite imagery has become an indispensable reporting tool. But as a recent Guardian investigation illustrates, a lot of work goes into ensuring its veracity and keeping the focus on the people affected on the ground

How to bear witness when you can’t physically go there? Journalists have always grappled with this. Whether it’s because of armed conflict, repressive regimes or prohibitive terrain, some places remain too dangerous or difficult for reporters to access.

Enter low-orbit satellites. As the technology has evolved and proliferated, satellite imagery has become increasingly indispensable. But as with all reporting tools, it requires professional judgment and painstaking work to verify things.

“When satellite images show that something on the ground has changed, there’s a lot that needs to be corroborated,” says Kaamil Ahmed, a reporter on the Guardian’s global development team who used extensive satellite imagery for an investigation we published last week into the destruction of Rohingya villages in Myanmar. “For instance, we could see from the images that people had been displaced, but we needed to verify the images, we needed to be sure about what actually happened and who was behind it, and also whether the villages we were looking at were really Rohingya villages. None of that was straightforward.”

“We have to treat satellite imagery in exactly the same way as any other type of data we look at, or any human source we speak to,” adds Ashley Kirk, the Guardian’s senior editor for visual journalism. “It goes back to basic journalistic principles of second-sourcing and triple-sourcing information. So that might involve checking that we can still see the same thing in images obtained from another satellite provider, or cross-checking things with information from the ground, such as social media posts or witness testimony, and speaking with experts.”

Kaamil has been reporting on the persecution of the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority group from western Myanmar, for more than 10 years. Myanmar has been accused of orchestrating an ethnic cleansing of its Rohingya population after a military crackdown from 2016 to 2017 led to about 700,000 people seeking refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh.

Last week’s investigation mapped the more recent destruction of Rohingya villages in western Myanmar since 2024 by a group of insurgents. It also examined the construction of detention camps and labour camps. “We’d heard for a couple of years that things were happening in that particular area, but it was very hard to stand up,” says Kaamil. “Phone lines and the internet have been down for years so there’s so little evidence coming out of the area. Often, we’d have to simply wait for people to go to Bangladesh as refugees before we could hear their testimony. So that’s why satellite imagery has been so useful.”

Indeed, it was shortly after Kaamil published another satellite-led investigation back in March – which examined attacks on a village in Darfur as part of the ongoing war in Sudan – that a source contacted him and suggested he apply the same reporting techniques to a particular area in western Myanmar.

“One of the challenges was that this was a very remote area. Satellite providers weren’t passing over it regularly so, to begin with, we were really struggling to get the quality of images we needed. There’d be big gaps in the timeframe, there weren’t images from the right day, or they weren’t the right resolution.”

All these things can hamper journalists’ efforts to make informed comparisons.

Ashley recalls facing similar issues over the summer when we used satellite imagery to assess the impact of the wildfires across Europe. “We needed to look at historical images to see the burn scars and assess how certain landscapes had changed,” he explains. “But quite often we are restrained by whenever a satellite goes around Earth and captures images of a very specific area. You’ve got to hope that it’s the right time of day and exactly the right area, and also that there are no obstructions such as cloud cover or smoke obscuring the landscape too much – which in the case of the wildfires would often happen.”

Even when our data and visual journalists manage to source clear images of a specific area on a specific day at a specific time, there is still a lot of corroboration to be done. Kaamil offers an example from his investigation into the attacks in Sudan: “There’s a lot of destruction in Darfur, but some of the satellite images of burnt landscapes were actually related to agriculture rather than the war, so we have to be very careful about checking and not making assumptions.”

Ashley points to another example from his team’s extensive use of satellite imagery to report on the destruction of Gaza over the past three years. “You would see a circular object and you might think it’s the dome of a mosque. But a circular pattern could also indicate a crater. So then, for example, we’d use images from other times of the day to see if there are any shadows that suggest a building.”

For last week’s story about the Rohingya villages, Kaamil corroborated the satellite imagery using eyewitness testimony from some of the sources he has kept in touch with during his years of covering their plight, as well as other sources of data. “For instance, on top of satellite imagery, we also used fire data from Nasa, which has sensors that detect every fire of a certain size. That helped us to verify that fires actually happened in these villages on the dates that people said that they happened. We also used conflict data because it was very important for us to be sure that these villages were not destroyed as a side-effect of shelling during battles between the insurgents and the military – that they were actually systematically destroyed. The conflict data showed us that there were actually very few battles during the period of destruction indicated by the satellite imagery, because at that point the insurgents had complete control of that particular region.”

Gathering all this supporting evidence isn’t just about corroborating things. The interactive article we published last week presents some of those eyewitness testimonies, together with photographs and video clips, alongside the satellite imagery. The result is a more immersive experience that gives audiences a fuller picture of what has been happening on the ground.

“One of the big limitations of satellite imagery is that it’s literally very distant from the human story on the ground,” says Anna Leach, a visual projects editor who also worked on the investigation. “But of course this is a very human story about the displacement of people, and we always try to show that human element in everything we do.”

“We tried to make sure the article remained connected to the people affected,” adds Prina Shah, a senior digital designer on the Guardian’s visual team who also worked on the project. “So we included photos of villagers’ faces and other images to show that people actually live here and it’s not just about circling things on a map.”

Ashley highlights another example from our coverage of the war in Gaza. Published in December, the article in question used satellite imagery alongside on-the-ground photography to chart a woman’s two-year search for safety in the ruins of Gaza. “We tried to show all of the different places that she was displaced to and how each of those places got destroyed, and so she just had to keep on fleeing,” he says. “Combining the satellite imagery with more traditional reporting techniques meant we could tell her story and also contextualize it. We showed the human story, but the satellite imagery allowed us to show, for example, all of the other tents that surrounded her tent and so you immediately see that her story is just one of thousands. Satellite imagery is really effective for giving people a sense of the scale of what’s happening alongside what’s happening to individuals.”

Given that our satellite-based interactive articles often contain multiple perspectives and narratives, our visual journalists also put a great deal of effort into honing the experience of scrolling down as you read them and see the visual evidence. “We’re thinking about how we explain quite complex imagery in a digestible way to an audience that might be viewing it on a mobile phone,” says Prina. “This can entail things like ensuring different elements pop up when they’re meant to and fall back when they need to because the audience’s attention needs to be focused on different aspects of the satellite imagery, for example, or on the personal accounts that are presented simultaneously.”

This process involves a lot of testing and fine-tuning before the article is published. “Certain issues only come to light when you’re playing with the actual interactive and refining interactive elements and animation and transitions to improve focus or understanding.”

Having spent so many years reporting on the Rohingya, Kaamil really appreciates the team’s efforts to bring the story to life: “We’ve tried to go beyond satellite images that just show destruction. People might get immune to that,” he says. “Also, the Rohingya refugee population has existed for so many years now, it can seem like a stagnant situation. Presenting things in a fresh and different way is part of how we try to make people care and ensure that our reporting has impact. So these forms of journalism help us to report on things that aren’t always on the news agenda.”

The investigation into the erasure of Rohingya villages was part of the Guardian’s Global development series, which is supported by theguardian. org.

​I’ve seen what Amazon thinks about me – and it revealed a depressing truth

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 13:00:27 GMT

From ‘has flat buttocks’ to ‘likes brunettes with muscles’, the retailer’s About You pages offer some remarkable insights into customers’ lives and tastes. Naturally, I rushed to check out mine …

There’s been a disturbing development in the surveillance capitalism space for me and other Amazon users: we can now find out exactly what the site thinks about us. The tax-agnostic shopping behemoth launched an “About You” function, which allows shoppers to see what assumptions and beliefs it has gathered from our purchases, in May, but last week things got interesting. Threads user Megan Montgomery found her “About You” page, and discovered Amazon thinks she “has flat buttocks”, prompting other shoppers to post the implacably devastating verdicts they uncovered: “husband has skinny legs”; “likes brunettes with muscles”; “cusses when scared”; “cannot keep real plants alive”; “too short to reach into a 40in-deep box” and “treats cats as biological children”. A TikTok user says hers includes “has a bad father”.

By their fruits shall ye know them, if by “fruits” you mean compression socks, shapewear, cat carriers and self-help guides. Obviously, this is bad, but it’s a well-deserved kind of bad – we’ve sacrificed privacy for convenience and this is the result. It’s also bleakly funny, so just as obviously, I was over there like a ferret up a trouser leg to find out what the stuff Amazon has delivered here over the years has caused it to deduce about my household. The results were disappointing. You don’t need a particularly sophisticated algorithm to deduce “likely lives in York”; “feeds wild birds consistently” (not in summer! I follow RSPB guidance!) and “cycles recreationally” (absolutely not, but I live with a multi-bike-owning MAMNILYBOROD – that’s “middle-aged man not in Lycra yet because of risk of divorce”).

There’s a lot our About You page hasn’t noticed or doesn’t consider important either. What about the sprays, mosses and soils that keep the houseplants I inherited from my son alive? I definitely treat the variegated monstera and temperamental calathea “like biological children”. The multipacks of cuttlefish bones and other tortoise ephemera don’t merit a mention and I’m surprised, too, that my husband’s frequent DIY-related purchases don’t feature. He sources enough widgets, pipes and sealant to open a mid-sized B&Q and I feel obscurely insulted on his behalf that all that hitting things with hammers while swearing (sorry, “cussing”) hasn’t made the cut. It would be nice, too, if my many years of Kindle purchases counted for something – I would have enjoyed a complimentary nod to all the dry histories of ideas and dense Russian classics I optimistically download, fancying myself An Intellectual (glossing over the easy novels about relationships I actually read).

Our page isn’t lacking in pretentiousness though: Amazon comments include “values specialized fitness nutrition products”; “maintains premium coffee brewing setup” and “prefers Japanese stationery brands”. If this portrait of our collective purchases were one real person, you could imagine him – it’s definitely a him – mansplaining David Foster Wallace or how, actually, you should eat nigiri sushi with your hands, on a date. Is this who we are, as a household? I hate us.

Really, the thing I hate most about us is that we’re shopping like this at all. What’s the point of taking recycled containers to the organic market, puffed up with my own virtue, when I’m coming home and buying phone chargers and creatine gummies on my phone? Driving, recently, through the vast logistical and petrochemical sprawl that is Rotterdam port after three days clearing my mother-in-law’s flat made me think this more urgently. We accumulate so much stuff over a lifetime, at such heavy environmental cost, only to have to work out how to get rid of it again. Buying from Amazon makes it worse: the company is estimated to have cost the UK £575m in lost tax revenue in 2024, is accused of unsafe and unethical employment practices and is helmed by a man seemingly intent on spending his obscene wealth on sending a flying penis into space.

The most damning thing Amazon knows about me is the simplest: I’m too lazy and disorganised to do without it – it’s the ubiquitous, inevitable, depressing answer for so many little “needs” (wants, really). I resolved to print out and put up a picture of Bezos’s rocket to shame myself into shopping around, but I’m already facing my first challenge: where the hell do I get our weird printer cartridges?

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Readers reply: Why are national anthems almost always orchestral?

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 13:00:27 GMT

The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts

This week’s question: Why is a child saying ‘Na-na, na-na-na!’ so annoying?

Why are national anthems almost always orchestral? When – and by whom – was it decided that brass and strings best represent a country’s identity? Where are the power-pop or folk varieties? Ross Gomes, by email

Send new questions to nq@theguardian. com.

Longstanding national anthems were mostly written before recorded and amplified music existed. They were often played outdoors, or in large halls. Those requirements are practically demanding large assemblies of portable instruments to play them. If it couldn’t be played by a military band, heavily staffed with brass players, a national anthem would not have lasted long. leadballoon

Anthems typically pre-date the electronic and digital eras, which meant playing them on traditional woodwind, stringed and drummed instruments. Most of them also have words, so they can be sung by the faithful and the callow. Consequently, most national anthems sound awful to modern ears, quite aside from questions over suitability in an internationalist, secular and increasingly postcolonial world.

If you’re in the mood, though, Niger’s L’Honneur de la Patrie (2023) would not be entirely out of place as the theme tune of a grand movie sci-fi. Meanwhile, Syria’s still-unofficial Fī Sabīli al-Majd (2024) is perky and evokes the feeling of a whimsical late-1800s western caper movie; they should definitely use that in place of Ḥumāt ad-Diyār, in my opinion. Dorkalicious

Just the weight of convention. Monkey see, monkey do. unclestinky

Rather than orchestral, they are usually harmonically choral, with the four parts for soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Melodically, Britain’s own is deliberately as simple as it can get, for the untrained masses to join in in unison. The simple monosyllabic words God Save the King are biblical, from the King James version. The first modern one is La Marseillaise, dating from the French Revolution. Keith Barnes

More to the point, why are some of them so dire? There’s no comparison between God Save the King and La Marseillaise; one’s a dirge, the other makes me want to march to the barricades. Goldgreen

Even if they’re originally written for strings or brass, it doesn’t mean that they’re limited to performances by those instruments. Jimi Hendrix’s version of The Star Spangled Banner, for instance, was a better representation of the US at the time than any orchestral recital (and perhaps would be even more so now). superspartan

They’re no more orchestral than, say, Greensleeves, the Londonderry Air or Abide With Me. Many have military origins, which suits mobile groups with acoustic brass, pipes and drums. Others have origins in folk song, court dances and religious hymns (most European languages use a version of the word “hymn”, meaning song of praise, for anthem). The American anthem was a drinking song, the Chinese one a film theme. alexito

Flower of Scotland was written in the 1960s and narrowly failed to become the Scottish anthem in a vote of Holyrood. It’s usually performed by a pipe band, or by a large ensemble choir of football fans. Not sure I ever heard an orchestral version. Randomusername222

Billy Connolly suggested the Archers theme tune would make a great national anthem. Now, that’s what I hear in my head whenever the UK’s dirge is played. After all, a national anthem is basically a country’s theme tune. So for me, the lyrics to Whatever Happened to the Likely Lads? are perfect.

Not only is our national anthem an awful dirge, it fails to even mention the country, its features, its people (unless you include hammering the Scots). It just drones on about the current super-rich welfare claimant with poorly diversified genes. walpole6

Gareth Malone looks back: ‘After the Christmas No 1, I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber’

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 13:00:26 GMT

The choir leader and presenter on not fitting in at his all-boys grammar, how synthesisers changed everything, and his ‘dithering’ start on TV

Born in London in 1975, Gareth Malone is a choirmaster and broadcaster. He began his career running youth and community choirs for the London Symphony Orchestra and first appeared on TV in 2006’s The Choir. He has since created choirs with Leicester schoolboys, Aylesbury prisoners, as well as the Military Wives, which produced the No 1 single, Wherever You Are. He lives in London with his wife and three children. His new live show, Sing-A-Long-A-Gareth: At the Movies, is on tour across the UK this autumn.

I was 15 and just coming into my own with my confidence, as you can tell by the double denim and the pose. The photo would have been taken at a party at my parents’ house in Bournemouth. When I wasn’t filling up guests’ drinks, I’d be playing some songs – it looks like I’m playing B flat major, so I suspect at this very moment it was Hey Jude.

For a few years prior to this, school had been difficult. We moved from a nice leafy part of Wimbledon to Bournemouth when I was 10, and until that point I had friends who were both girls and boys. Going to the all-boys grammar school in a new area was an aggressive gear shift and I struggled to make friends. There was no physical bullying, but it was a sustained period of ostracisation that went on for the first three years of secondary school and dribbled on into year 10. It wasn’t ever discussed. There was no “you’re being bullied. If you have a problem with any other boys, come and talk to us,” from the school. My parents probably knew because I wasn’t bringing any friends over. Instead I learned how to take care of my own problems, which was through music and theatre. My saving grace.

I feel so lucky that I had the music studio at school – a place to be expressive in a sea of business studies and maths. Playing the synthesisers started my lifelong passion for production and all-round music nerdery. We also had a piano at home and I used to sit at it and make sounds for what felt like hours.

Mum worked for Abbey Life Assurance and for the civil service. Dad worked for a bank. Neither of them were particularly career-minded – they enjoyed their life, their family and their house, hence friends often coming over. My grandparents were very important, too. Growing up as an only child made me very comfortable in my own company, but it did mean I wasn’t armed with some of the physical vocabulary that other boys had. I used to overreact when other kids were playing up. “Why are you speaking to me like that? No one speaks to me like that. Why are you behaving in this stupid way? No, I don’t want to play rough, or go and play football, because that’s what five-year-olds do.” I was far happier to sit and have a conversation. All of which is possibly why I gravitated towards the girls at school – they were a bit more sensible.

In my teens I got very into Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd. I was singing a lot in bands – but I was also obsessed with Kenneth Branagh in Henry V, so I decided to study drama at University of East Anglia. I have fond memories of pretending to be a pig, and doing lots of clowning and mask work. Once that was over, I went on to study music at the Royal Academy of Music in London. It was a difficult transition for me – I went from that arrogant tweeny, liminal stage, as pictured, to realising that I was, actually, just fairly average compared with my peers.

After graduating, I went back to Bournemouth. I was selling ice-cream to make some money while sending out CVs. A friend got in touch and said they had seen an advert for some youth work in Poole, and thought I’d be good at it. They wanted someone young and musical to work with local children who lived on an estate with a high level of deprivation. They had a little music room with a couple of ropey instruments that I would try to teach them how to play. That’s where my passion for giving everyone opportunities – a safe space and music – came from.

I also realised that to get people to trust me, I had to be myself. I was from a totally different side of the tracks and I was wide-eyed, naive. The kids could smell the middle-classness on me, so any pretending to be cool and aloof wouldn’t work. I had to be rigorously myself.

My job is to give others confidence, but I’ve definitely gone on a journey with my own self-esteem, especially when it comes to being in front of the camera. I was working with the London Symphony Orchestra and running a choir when I first got the opportunity to be on TV. The producers of The Choir had seen that we had a high Google rating so they got in touch. The show was about starting a choir at Northolt high school in Middlesex, and throughout, I tried to apply the same method of authenticity on camera that I’d learned with the youth group. I had been given this amazing job that I’d never done before, but I was learning to do it on national television. I was being filmed constantly. The director said: “I want you when you’re angry, I want you when you’re upset, I want you when you’re happy. I won’t make you look like an idiot.” He stuck to his word, but I remember being nervous, trying to look in control, and dithering quite a lot.

When you’re recognised it can be a great gift, but a burden when you’re, say, taking out your bins. When Military Wives got to No 1, I was suddenly thrown into a new level of celebrity: I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber. My memories of that time was that it was intense – when you have a Christmas No 1, it’s like you’ve joined a weird club with people like Noddy from Slade and Shakin’ Stevens. None of the bells and whistles has ever distracted me from the reason I got into this industry in the first place 20 years ago, however. Focusing on my passion for music and the importance of art in people’s lives. There’s something so healing about music, and singing in a choir. When people come together, they are buoyed up by it. I lost a friend at the beginning of this year and before he died he said something deeply touching to me: “We never did go for that pint.” It was brutal. Such a simple thing that felt impossible as we were both absorbed in our careers. The telly, the degrees – all of those achievements are wonderful. It’s the foundation upon which a lot of my happiness is at rest. But it’s not the main thing. People and community are.

When I was 15 I had a clear vision of what I wanted with my adult life. It involved a music studio with lots of instruments in it. The teenage me would be overjoyed to know that at the end of my garden is a little den with a piano, drums, shakers, maracas, guitars, bongos, synthesisers, a computer and speakers – that there’s never a day when I’m not doing music, half of it tinkering alone, the rest making music with other people. He’d probably be confused about the amount of hot yoga I currently do. But glad to know I still like a denim shirt.

Richard E Grant admits Traitors mistakes: ‘I never thought they would take me seriously’

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 12:15:32 GMT

Actor says he should have made a joke of his admission, he felt institutionalised there and he is not watching the series

Richard E Grant has said his early exit from The Celebrity Traitors was due to his failure to realise his fellow contestants would take him seriously.

The Withnail and I actor was voted off as a traitor after brazenly admitting his status to other contestants.

Speaking to the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Grant said revealing his true identity so early was a mistake. “I never thought they would take me seriously,” he said.

“It was a completely catastrophically idiotic thing to do. I can only imagine the faces of the producers looking at each other and mouthing ‘he said what?!’. The strategy of no strategy is the strategy, clearly.”

He revealed that his daughter told him before filming that he would be “slaughtered” as he was “incapable of hiding what you feel about people or anything”.

During the first episode, Grant appeared to be thrilled to be selected as a traitor. His enthusiasm for the role appeared to get the better of him when he was asked by his fellow contestant Joe Lycett which side he was on.

When Grant confessed to being a traitor, Lycett said: “I think you’ve done something that’s never been done in the game. It’s a bold strategy.”

Grant said he now realised he should have made a joke of his admission. He said: “What I should have done in retrospect is go round everybody and say ‘are you a traitor? Yeah. I am a traitor, I am Spartacus. I am a traitor,’ to try and make light of it, but that may have dug my grave even deeper.”

Explaining the context, he suggested contestants were treated like children and prisoners. He said: “You are so institutionalised in that thing within 24 hours, because you are isolated, kept in a room, there is a guard outside your door, your food is delivered and there’s no internet access, so you are kind of shut down.

“You are also not told what time it is and are also prescribed on a daily basis what you are going to wear. So, you are kind of infantilised and institutionalised at the same time.”

He said he had chosen to avoid watching the series. “It’s a weird thing because as an actor it is very uncomfortable to watch yourself, and if you watch yourself unscripted – which Traitors is – there’s no place to hide. That is unequivocally you.”

People smugglers are still profiting from small boats. Can the UK fix the crisis?

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 12:00:27 GMT

As ‘one in, one out’ scheme ends, refugees still want to cross the Channel despite French police aggression and hostile welcomes

The smuggler works quickly. Using a small shovel, he digs up a dinghy buried in a sand dune on a beach not far from Boulogne-sur-Mer, assembles it and affixes a motor in record time.

“I never saw anyone work like this,” says Amad, from Iraq, one of a group of about 30 asylum seekers waiting to cross the Channel. “The UK government wants to stop the smugglers, but they are smart. They have plan A, plan B and plan C, so there is always a way for them to get people across this sea. For as long as asylum seekers will pay them, there is too much money involved for them to give up.”

The wind has dropped, the waves are flat and there are no French police in sight. The conditions are perfect as the smuggler rushes everyone into the dinghy as it moves away from the shore.

Amad is one of several asylum speakers who spoke to the Guardian this week from the area of northern France known as the Jungle. They were hoping to cross the Channel to the UK in the next few days.

“This place is busier than ever,” says another asylum seeker, Omar, from Yemen. “So many refugees and so many smugglers are here. Everyone wants to cross.”

Some who have already been forcibly removed from the UK are hoping to return. They were sent to France under the “one in, one out” scheme, where one small-boat arrival is forcibly returned to France in exchange for another asylum seeker brought legally to the UK.

Now, after moving approximately 1,500 people in both directions across the Channel, the scheme has been brought to an end. Beset with problems, it could not be effectively scaled up, the British government concluded.

NGOs working on the ground with asylum seekers in northern France were unsurprised by the outcome and say the end of “one in, one out” must prompt a wider discussion about how to deal with the crisis in the Channel.

The UK government has shown little sign it is contemplating a radical shift in attitude. A Home Office spokesperson pointed the Guardian to an announcement about a refugee resettlement scheme that is likely to assist only a few hundred refugees a year and is highly unlikely to stop people crossing the Channel in small boats.

The spokesperson said: “Just last week, the home secretary announced the reopening of the UK resettlement scheme for new referrals, providing genuine refugees with a safe and legal route to the UK.”

The agencies calling for a different approach hope at least to expand the parameters of the debate.

According to workers in the Jungle, living conditions there are appalling. Those at Utopia 56, which witnesses police interventions on French beaches where asylum seekers try to board dinghies, say that since the UK increased its funding to France earlier this year on a payment-by-results basis, police violence against migrants has increased significantly.

Utopia 56 estimates a 40% increase in police violence from April to August 2026 compared with the same period the previous year. That coincided with an agreement for the UK to pay France £660m over three years to ramp up “stop the boats” initiatives.

Sophie McCann, of Médecins Sans Frontières UK, said: “The government’s increasingly brutal efforts to stop people trying to reach the UK by boat are failing. MSF’s medical and mental health teams in Calais and Dunkirk witness the serious physical and psychological harm caused by violence and harassment meted out by French police, largely funded by the UK, on people who have already fled war, persecution and extreme hardship.

“People will continue to risk their lives crossing the Channel in search of safety in the UK until the government provides safe and accessible routes.”

The Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union, which has many Home Office staff among its members, has worked with the refugee charity Care4Calais to draw up a blueprint to introduce a refugee visa-to-travel scheme for asylum seekers to travel legally to the UK.

The plan would still require asylum claims to be considered on merit and for those whose claims are rejected to be removed from the UK. But they say it would eliminate people smugglers from the equation and save lives. According to the UN’s International Organization for Migration (IMO), at least 225 people have died while trying to cross the Channel since 2018.

The scheme would be unlikely to halt irregular arrivals entirely, but Care4Calais says it could dent the smugglers’ business in a way that other initiatives have failed to do.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Charlotte Khan, of Care4Calais, said: “Consecutive governments have focused on border security measures that have only made Channel crossings more dangerous, resulting in a shocking number of lives lost, while completely ignoring the only solution that will work – safe routes.”

The PCS general secretary, Fran Heathcote, called for safe routes to be significantly scaled up. “Our members deal with the human impact of the asylum system on a daily basis and their voices must be heard. The only way to truly undermine criminal smuggling gangs is to remove the demand through a Ukrainian-style visa system, allowing people fleeing war and persecution to travel safely and legally to claim asylum.”

The Labour government has arguably made more efforts than any other to try to prevent asylum seekers from reaching the UK in small boats.

Previously, people travelled less visibly, in the backs of lorries or on planes, and so attracted less public attention. Images of black dinghies overcrowded with people in orange lifejackets, monetised for social media clicks by far-right agitators, have generated mounting hostility from some who say they are evidence that the government has lost control of its borders.

But desperate people continue to clamber into dinghies. In the six days between 2 and 7 October, 1,739 people arrived in 23 boats. Along with the now terminated “one in, one out” pilot, which government trumpeted as “groundbreaking” when it announced it in July 2025, the Home Office and the National Crime Agency make regular announcements about smugglers being intercepted and dinghies seized “upstream”.

There has been a reduction of more than 40% in small boat arrivals so far this year compared with the same period last year, probably due to a combination of UK government initiatives, windy weather and a drop in irregular migration to Europe overall. According to data published by the IMO, there has been a 39% reduction this year in these arrivals to Europe – from 98,040 during the same period last year to approximately 60,000.

Despite the reduction in arrivals, far-right agitators wearing masks and black paramilitary clothing continue to protest on the streets and try to block small boat arrivals.

None of the policy roadblocks appear to have dented the resolve of asylum seekers who want to reach the UK.

Sohrab, from Afghanistan, has been sleeping on the streets of Paris and is making his way to the Jungle. “I want to live and I will do anything to save my life from death,” he says. “I have already spent a bad day in jail in France after police caught me trying to get into a lorry heading for the UK. The smugglers are very violent, but there is no other way for me to reach the UK apart than to go to the Jungle.”

Despite the failure of “one in, one out” to deter small boat crossings, Emily Graham, of the Future Governance Forum, believes it is the way forward.

“The ‘one-in, one-out’ pilot proved cooperation based on responsibility-sharing is right in principle and has the potential to deliver results,” she said. “To reduce the number of people arriving by small boat, the government should build on the previous pilot and seek a new ‘routes for returns’ deal with European partners.”

Amad has another idea. “We would much prefer to give our money to the UK government if they allowed us to come here legally, rather than to the smugglers,” he says. “No asylum seeker would pay smugglers who beat and exploit them, or risk our lives on a dinghy, if there was another way.”

There’s more to our music than Oasis, says Manchester mayor

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 12:00:27 GMT

Bev Craig pledges £2m in funding to nurture local artists by improving access to rehearsal and production space

The Manchester mayor, Bev Craig, has said the city’s music scene is about more than just Oasis, as she announced funding to nurture a diverse range of local artists, be they “guitar bands or not”.

Craig pledged the £2m investment funding in Greater Manchester, as the city region hosted a conference for the creative industries at MediaCity in Salford.

She said there was a “real intentionality” to what Manchester was doing, in terms of growing its own music industry and attracting international events.

Earlier this year, Manchester’s Co-op Live arena hosted the Brit awards and the Mobos, Europe’s biggest and most influential celebration of Black music and culture.

“I wanted to have a major event that celebrated black music, culture and creativity,” Craig said, “and so that’s why we said, just after the Brits, we’d host their 30th anniversary, because we knew it would be the last one that the Mobos founder Kanya would be able to come to.”

“I think there’s a real intentionality around what we’re doing with our music scene,” she added. “We’re known, I think, over the world for the influence that some of our indie guitar bands have had on Greater Manchester music, but there’s more to Greater Manchester’s music scene than just Oasis.”

“I’m struck by the diversity, the creativity, the talent that we see,” Craig said. “And the job, as I see it, is making sure that that next generation of talent in an industry that’s becoming more and more middle-class, more and more London-centric, and a world where it’s more and more expensive to be able to break through, that we’re giving our local artists the hand up that they need to be able to be the next big thing, guitar band or not.”

Addressing Beyond the Music’s creative industries AI summit on Friday, Craig set out her plan for diversifying opportunities in the music industry. She also outlined commitments to support AI literacy for music professionals, and to monitor the impact of new technologies on employment, income and diversity in Greater Manchester’s music sector.

The festival that accompanied the summit featured performances from up-and-coming black and minority ethnic artists including Bawo, JayaHadADream and Alt Blk Era.

The final day of the conference was convened by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, whose love of Manchester guitar bands is well known.

The culture minister Ian Murray told the conference: “With a prime minister who picks up his guitar to murder Smiths tracks, we have a passion from the very top.

He added, joking: “That’s probably a career-limiting sentence for me.”

“We’re living and working at a time of considerable change, particularly with technology,” Murray said, “but the future of creativity will not be shaped by technology alone. It will be shaped by the choices we make today, and how we support talent, how we reward creativity and how we embrace that innovation.”

The £2m of funding Craig has set out is in addition to the £4m Culture Fund investment announced earlier this month, which will fund music projects from grassroots venues to world-renowned institutions.

The additional funding is aimed at improving access to rehearsal and production space across the city region, providing practical support and ensuring there are jobs for musicians in their communities.

Although the Manchester music scene may be about more than Oasis, the newly elected Manchester mayor did say she would be going to see the band on their sellout tour next year, which includes 11 nights at Manchester City’s Etihad Stadium.

“I will, and thankfully the price of pints are much too expensive and the clientele have aged [which] means that you’re not as cautious as to what’s travelling through the air as historically you once would [be],” she said.

But she added that “as somebody who loves all forms of music” she was “as excited about seeing [Merseyside band] the Ks at Beyond the Music as I am about seeing Oasis”.

“I’m a little bit more into my dance music than the previous mayor as well,” Craig added. “So maybe a bit more varied in my tastes, shall we say.”

Rapid showers and no flushing toilets: drought pushes Lundy island to the brink

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 12:00:25 GMT

A dry summer has left the Bristol Channel island critically short of water, forcing visitor caps and talk of evacuating its 28 residents

Tom Carr was peering up at the clouds scudding around the island of Lundy, 10 miles off the coast of north Devon. “That one’s definitely got rain in it,” he said. “The mainland will be wet at the moment. And look over at Wales – it’s getting a real soaking just now.”

But above Lundy the sky was, stubbornly, blue. No significant rain has fallen here since the start of May, leading to perilously low water levels. Restrictions have been put in place, visitor numbers limited and there has been talk of the island – home to 28 people – being evacuated.

“It’s been a challenge,” said Carr, a conservation farmer who looks after sheep, cattle and ponies. He has been here more than 20 years and reckons the combination of the climate emergency and the topography of the granite outcrop, which soars out of the Bristol Channel, is the problem.

“Climate change is here, it’s happening. We’re having hotter, drier summers. And when the rain clouds do come in, they tend to split as the approach the island and we stay dry.”

The three-mile long island, famed for its puffins and its pirate past, relies on rainwater and five boreholes. The biggest rain catchment area is in the south. From there – when it does rain – water tumbles down to a collection tank near the harbour. It is then pumped up to an array of tanks and a purification plant near the old lighthouse.

The island manager, Matt Scantlebury, said a fortnight ago the tanks were at 13% capacity – only enough water to keep the island going for about a week. Tonnes of water was being brought over in 1,000 litre containers on the island boat, the MS Oldenburg, to top up the supply.

The campsite, which is popular with climbers once the cliff-nesting seabirds have gone, was shut. The toilets at the island pub, the Marisco Tavern, were closed. Bath plugs in holiday lets – up to 110 people can stay here – were taken away and people were asked to think twice before flushing toilets.

Happily, on the day the water reached its low point, the island received confirmation that the water in one of its freshwater pools – called Pondsbury – was of a good enough quality to be used.

About 12,000 litres of water has been taken from there every day since and the levels are back up to 22.5%. But now the pond is starting to run dry. “And still no proper rain is forecast,” said Scantlebury. “We know we have to find ways of future proofing ourselves.”

To that end, a new 300,000-litre water tank has been ordered. The idea of a desalination plant – seawater is one thing the island is not short of – has been suggested but Scantlebury said it would be expensive and would probably need more energy than the island was capable of producing.

Tristan Howes, the island’s engineer, said finding ways of conserving the little water Lundy had was crucial. “A dripping tap can lose a lot of water,” he said. A broken pipe would be a disaster.

Staff have got used not only to having a rapid shower but catching the water they use in a bucket and using it to flush the toilet. “It’s about being as efficient as we can.”

Luckily, visitors to Lundy, which is owned by the National Trust and managed by the Landmark Trust, tend to be the sort who don’t mind a little bit of hardship.

after newsletter promotion

Michelle Phillips, an animal lover keen to see the island’s ponies, and her husband, Fred Bullinaria, arrived for a day trip with 1.6 litres of water, four Lucozades and a tube of hydration tablets in their backpacks. “I think that will keep us going,” she said.

Vick and Ed Crane were staying on Lundy for a few days to celebrate their 10th wedding anniversary. They had bought wet wipes to limit their water usage. “We don’t mind roughing it,” said Vick. “That’s part of the Lundy experience. It’s an adventure.”

The residents are positive, always looking for the bright side.

Tara McEvoy-Wilding, assistant warden on the island, said some creatures had done well from the hot summer. “It’s been a good year for butterflies and moths.”

And it has also been a good summer for the Lundy cabbage, a primitive brassica that grows only on the island. “It’s quite a pioneering species and likes dry bare ground where there isn’t much vegetation,” said McEvoy-Wilding. “Hundreds of tiny cabbage plants have started to establish in areas where they wouldn’t normally. So that’s positive, at least.”

McEvoy-Wilding said residents had become accustomed to using less water. “You’re more mindful – you only have a short shower and you don’t always flush the toilet. In a way it’s not a bad thing. It makes you think about how much water you could be saving every day by just making very small changes.”

But that doesn’t mean that McEvoy-Wilding is not hoping for rain. “It’s amazing how little rain we’ve had. We had one day in August when it rained for an hour. Absolutely torrential. I was caught in it and got drenched but the ground was so dry it just poured off the island.

“I’ve got an allotment and it’s been hard to keep my vegetables alive. The pumpkins aren’t anywhere near as big as normal. Some nice, steady rain would be perfect.”

Dining across the divide: ‘He says net zero is a waste of money as we’ll hit 3C anyway. I think that’s nihilistic’

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 11:00:25 GMT

An English teacher and a personal trainer disagreed on emissions targets, but how did they fare on public spending and defence?

Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how

Occupation English teacher at a secondary school

Voting record Edward flips between Labour and Green

Amuse bouche He runs spoken word poetry nights in Bristol

Occupation Personal trainer

Voting record Mostly Conservative, but voted for Tony Blair

Amuse bouche He used to be a stressed-out, unfit lobbyist, and decided to make drastic changes. He started running 10Ks, then ultra-marathons, and when he was 50 he ran round a 400m track for 24 hours, “because I’m an idiot”

Martin I was slightly apprehensive, wondering if it would descend into an argument. But he’s a really nice guy.

Edward We got on really well. It was a delightful evening.

Martin I had the squid to start, then crab pasta with pistachio and chilli – it was lovely. Also, a Sicilian lemonade and my favourite dessert, affogato.

Edward I had a very tasty tuna tartare to start, then for main a beef ragu and a glass of red wine, and finished with an affogato.

Martin My view on net zero is that we already know it’s basically impossible, and if you give people an impossible target, they give up. Carbon capture is fundamental to the UK’s ability to hit net zero, and nobody has yet proved that it’s scalable beyond test sites.

Edward If you don’t have a target at all, then nobody works towards anything. But I do think there needs to be more oversight, ensuring we’re putting the money into things that are most likely to have the biggest effects, and not just box-checking.

Martin The temperature limit was supposed to be 1.5C, but it could be as bad as three. If we’re going to miss it by that much, it’s pointless.

Edward He was saying we’ll probably hit 3C anyway, so what’s the point in spending the money? I think that’s slightly nihilistic.

Martin The civil service employs more than 550,000 people. I think that’s too many. The former head of No 10 comms under Boris Johnson found there were 4,000 more communications staff than they realised. I think we could fix a lot of our issues with tech, rather than throwing more bodies at them.

Edward Given the scale of the issues they’ve got to address and the size of the population, I don’t think that’s a crazily large number of employees. What we need is better management of it. We don’t need ministers with no experience in these areas coming in and making massive changes because they want it to look good on their CV.

Martin I think we need to increase defence spending, not on soldiers but cyberwarfare and drone technology. I thought Edward had a really interesting take: that some of the costs of defence are probably going to be triggered by the climate crisis. Because if we continue where we’re going, there will be conflicts over resources and mass migration from certain countries as they become unliveable.

Edward We agreed future attacks are unlikely to be bombs or people invading the UK, but attacks on banking systems or possibly drone attacks. For me, defence means if something gets cut off from the outside, you’re able to exist on your own and support yourself. If you are vulnerable as a nation to oil prices, then you are vulnerable to conflicts. I think one of the strongest lines of defence against foreign bad actors is being energy independent – which we could be with proper investment. We’ve got sea around us, we’ve got sun, we’ve got wind, we’ve got nuclear.

Martin I assumed that Edward would have the view that nuclear power was abhorrent. But he didn’t. So my takeaway is realising that not everybody who’s involved or invested in the environmental movement thinks the same way. I don’t know if he changed my mind, but he definitely made me think.

Edward It was really lovely to meet somebody I probably wouldn’t normally come across. I thought he was going to be much more extreme than he was. I think we’re not so different in what we want, we just have different ways of getting there.

Additional reporting: Kitty Drake

Edward and Martin ate at Citro, London, N6.

‘I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a cannibal’: Rachael Stirling on eating her mother Diana Rigg’s ashes

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 11:00:25 GMT

When the actor confessed to ingesting a few flakes of her mother’s ashes on opening nights, reactions ranged from recognition to disgust. But, she says, grief makes animals of us all

There have been headlines of late that make me out to be an ash-guzzling savage nightly devouring her mother’s charred remains. “Rachael Stirling eats mother Diana Rigg’s ashes before going on stage” declared a dozen news outlets last month, while others referred to the “strange habit only she really understands” and “Dame Diana’s daughter admits eating her ashes in bizarre tribute”. I’ve written a book about our relationship, All About My Mother, in which I do confess to nibbling a grain or two, but I didn’t expect to be portrayed as a matricidal cannibal by the press.

My mother was Diana Rigg, an iconic actor with a 60-year career. Young ’uns will know her as the Queen of Thorns from Game of Thrones, be-wimpled spouter of the best verbal roasts on television: “I’ve known a great number of clever men. I’ve outlived them all. You know how? I ignored them.” Old ’uns, meanwhile, go dewy-eyed at the memory of her leather-catsuited telly triumph as Emma Peel in The Avengers from the 60s, the first woman to perform kung fu on western television. She was also the only woman ever to marry James Bond. She appeared in The Great Muppet Caper because I was profoundly in love with Miss Piggy, and her child-murdering Medea was the toast of Broadway. She won an Emmy and a Tony, and had countless honours bestowed upon her for her many stage performances. She was a complete original and very witty to boot.

I missed her so intensely, I wrote the book to bring her back to life. Mum never wanted a biography in her lifetime, having been put off by a couple of limp jobs that managed to make her seem a bit dull or, worst of all crimes, earnest. My mother was not earnest. She was honest, sometimes eye-bleedingly so.

I was her only child, and followed her into the acting profession. She strongly disapproved of my career choice, and this caused some rumpuses, I can tell you. We ran the gamut of emotions from A to Z and eventually we made our way back to the love we’d had in the early years. In the end, the love bits between us did conquer all the awful bits, though there are some joyful and some jaw-dropping stories to share.

Which brings us neatly back to the subject of ashes and my ingesting of them.

Groucho Marx wished to be cremated, with one tenth of his ashes to be “given to my agent, as written in my contract”. Dying in the Covid lockdown, my mother wished to be cremated, too, but with no ceremony, and scattered in places she loved. Pragmatic to the last, she even made sure we’d paid for the cremation on her bank card before she died. However, we never thought to decide what receptacle her remains would be returned in, so it wasn’t until after her death that I found myself browsing the selection of “scatter tubes” on offer.

Scatter tubes are cardboard containers of varying sizes. Some are plain, others have images printed on them. These are pretty unoriginal, pictures of doves and sunsets – or was it a sunrise – and images that felt to me a bit sur le nez. It turns out most things are quite on the nose when it comes to death. There isn’t much of a market for irony. Not many skull and crossbones, or red stilettos, or tubes with “I told you I was ill” written on them. In the end I settled for a variety of receptacles in a variety of sizes, with the least offensive floral decorations on them. I needed quantity, as my mother had many places to go. She was to be scattered from the air across the green fields of England from a biplane by her aviator friend Tracey Curtis-Taylor; she was to be scattered in her garden in France and mine in London; and on the site of the actors’ church in Covent Garden.

I did not expect human ashes to be so heavy. But they are very heavy. I discovered this when my mother’s mortal remains were returned to me one bright September morning. The cremation company had told me, when organising delivery, that taking receipt of the ashes could be an emotional event. Certainly, the carbonised corpse of my beloved Ma was the strangest delivery I’d ever expected, and not one to be left on the porch or with a neighbour. So I sat waiting, like an obedient dog awaiting her mistress by the front door.

My mother was delivered to me by the gentlest of gentlemen from the cremation firm in Yorkshire, where my mother was born. He pulled her out of the boot in a box wrapped in plain cloth. With kind eyes searching my face, presumably to see if I was going to start bawling and drop her, he handed her to me with the tenderness with which one might hand over a newborn babe.

While cremation frees the family to celebrate the life of a loved one in the great outdoors and away from the stuffy formality of funerals, things don’t always go to plan. Everyone has seen a movie where the ashes are scattered and the wind picks up and blows them into the faces of the grieving party. The best story of an ashes mishap took place at a scattering of my father-in-law, Donald Garvey, Dad to seven glorious children, the sixth of whom is my husband, Guy Garvey. There we were to celebrate the greatly missed Don with his huge family at the Great Orme in Llandudno, the site of many a Garvey family holiday. Don had stated he wanted the day to emulate a painting by Jack Vettriano where a woman in a red dress dances with her partner in tails on a stormy day at the beach. Words were spoken on the clifftop, and an intrepid few descended to the shore. Granddaughter Lucie, in a scarlet off-the-shoulder dress, hoicked up her skirts and waded into the unusually clear and calm blue sea to scatter her beloved grandad, as per his specific wishes, in the Welsh tide. Job done, as Lucie solemnly made her way back to her family on shore, she piped up with the now immortal line, “I think I’ve got some of Grandad in mi’ knickers.”

The tiniest tube containing my mother was about three inches tall. I’d like to point out that I think scatter tubes are really badly designed. They open exactly the opposite way to the direction they look like they should, so you can easily scatter a loved one’s ashes by mistake. The contents of this tube had – mostly – gone where they were supposed to go, though it still contained the odd grain or 20 of my mother, so I couldn’t possibly throw it away. Plus it was conveniently pocket-size, so I took to carrying what was left of her with me everywhere I went. So far, so normal.

The next play I did was at the same theatre I had last performed at pre-Covid. It was the last show my mother ever saw, Love, Love, Love at the Lyric in Hammersmith. The new show, Scandaltown, was by the same writer, Mike Bartlett, and also at the Lyric. Everything felt eerily similar, yet between the two plays Ma had died and the whole world had turned on its arse. Now, here I was going to rehearsals in the same room, with some of the same people, but without Ma to chat to about how the play was going at the end of the day. Strange new world.

As I placed her tube in my rucksack on the first day working on the show, I remember thinking how thrilled she’d be, back in a rehearsal room once more. Nearer opening night, I decided she’d enjoy a permanent stint in my dressing room. My mother had used this same dressing room in 1985, when she was performing in Little Eyolf, a grim Nordic drama from 1894 by Henrik Ibsen. It is the “Number One” dressing room, the room nearest the stage, and here she was once again, sitting in front of a Hollywood mirror with its necklace of blazing bulbs, although this time in a tube. The only thing she missed out on was actually going on stage with me. That was her happiest place, after all, but I could not hide the tube anywhere in my tight-fitting gold lamé suit without having a very peculiar lump in my costume. So there she stayed, in her dressing room, waiting for the call to the stage that never came.

Actors are an emotional tribe at the best of times and come opening night I was a wreck. My maiden first night with no mother in the crowd made me sad, but this was a high-energy Restoration-style comedy so I had to pull myself together quick-smart. I looked at the small tube containing mama residue, and I don’t know what I was thinking, but I found myself opening it. The wrong way round. A few grains fell on to my dressing table and as I panicked and tried to put them back one by one with varying degrees of success, the PA system blared, “Miss Stirling, this is your call to stage.” It was time to make my entrance. The adrenaline started kicking in and now my heart was pounding. It was time to go.

In a panic, like a cocaine addict from a movie who can’t bear to waste a grain of the good stuff, I licked my finger, picked up the few spilt cinders, and popped her on my tongue. Grainy, in case you were wondering, but it didn’t feel wrong, it felt completely right. I laughed out loud at myself and the ludicrous situation. And then, just like that, my nerves disappeared.

I know this sounds batshit, but it made complete sense to me. After all, quite a lot of people think they are eating the body of Christ on a weekly basis, and at least this way I really could say I took her with me on stage that night, back on the boards where she belonged.

When I told a widow at the party afterwards what I had done, her eyes widened in recognition and she whispered urgently, “I do that, too!”

The difference is, she didn’t talk about it. No one talks about it. It’s secret animal behaviour and, let’s face it, most people do a lot worse in private. It’s just they keep shtumm. But it felt much more important to tell the truth – and I love feeling that some of her is on stage with me. She had refused to retire, after all, and this was my way of enabling her to keep on trucking.

I have done the same on every first night since then. As the five-minute call hits the PA before every press night, I open the tube – which I have become adept at – stick my finger in and whatever is collected goes in my gob. Some people listen to music before going on; some do press-ups. I eat the last vestiges of my mother. She was on stage with me on the opening night of Noël Coward’s Private Lives in 2023. Just knowing she was there gave me the confidence to play the part that night, to be joyful, to “Go Fly My Girl”, as she used to write in my first-night cards.

She’d have adored going on to the Hampstead theatre stage with me when I played Sarah Siddons in The Divine Mrs S, a play about the 18th-century actor whose revolutionary realism in performance caused her audiences to scream and faint. Ma used to quote Siddons to me. She’d say, “If it can be found in nature, I know it can be played” so of course she’d want to be with me under the spotlights as I said those exact words. Before the opening night of Giant at the Royal Court in 2024, the smash hit show about Roald Dahl’s antisemitism in which I played his wife, Felicity Crosland, to John Lithgow’s Roald, once more I nibbled on a crumb. I can’t not do it these days, even though there is hardly anything left; it’s the thought that counts.

She’s even been back to Broadway, baby. When Giant transferred to New York in March this year, my mother came with me. Oh, there’s no business like show business, and there was one terrible night when I returned to my dressing room post-show to find there had been a huge leak in the roof above my chair and everything was sopping wet. My first thought was, Oh no, Mother’s gone mushy! But in fact the outside of the tube was only a little damp and inside was bone dry.

Love is animal, and grief is certainly so. Dogs sniff bums by way of greeting; my mum bit mine on a regular basis and said as much on national television. “I sink my teeth into her flesh! I bury my nose in her stomach!” she declared to a bemused Michael Parkinson. Isn’t that sort of the same thing, and is it really so strange of me to put my mother, whence I came, back in the same mouth she formed in utero? It is my own act of faith. “Ashes to ashes, funk to funky,” as Bowie wrote. “I’ve loved all I’ve needed, love. Sordid details following … ”

Love made cannibals of us both. Despite a widow seeing the sense in my actions, judging by the looks on the faces of most people I tell, few others are in agreement. Reactions vary from sour lemon-sucking grimaces to downright disgust. Despite this, I will not be persuaded to give up the habit. I will die on the hill of my ash-eating, and to any who question my sanity, I reply, “It is natural! I’m sure it is, really! I promise I’m not going mad. It’s what she would have wanted!”

All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling is published by John Murray at £25. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.
