‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil war

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 11:00:24 GMT

John Mitani spent years studying a huge community of chimpanzees in Uganda. But then things took a dark turn – and his findings stunned the scientific world

John Mitani can still remember the first time he set foot in Uganda’s Kibale national park. The old-growth east African rainforest enveloped him, its canopy stretching to heights of 40 metres. Fruit trees bowed under the weight of African star apples and bountiful Ficus mucuso figs. And then there were the chimpanzees. Furry black blobs darted through the jungle, their raucous calls often deafening.

It was the summer of 1995, and Mitani, a primatologist from northern California, had just come from working with the chimps living in the Mahale mountains of Tanzania. At the time, Mahale was home to the largest known population of chimps, with about 100 individuals. But there were rumours that this section of Kibale – only accessible via a 12-hour drive from the capital, Kampala – might host an even more unusual abundance of apes.

“It only took a few days to realise that something weird was going on at this place,” Mitani, now 72, recalls. “There were chimps everywhere.”

He was then a professor at the University of Michigan, and with his colleagues would eventually count nearly 200 chimpanzees living together peacefully in the forests of Ngogo, a research area in the central section of Kibale first established in the 1970s for the study of red colobus monkeys. Such a large chimp troop was then unheard of in primatology.

Later that year, Mitani co-founded the Ngogo Chimpanzee Project with the Yale university primatologist David Watts, using a $500,000 (£380,000) award from the US National Science Foundation. Three decades on, the project is one of just 12 long-term studies worldwide of chimpanzees in their natural environment, and has transformed what we know about one of our closest relatives.

It took years to build trust with the population, Mitani says. The chimps were not accustomed to human presence and were quick to run away whenever researchers approached. Days were spent chasing them over hills and down valleys. “It was fun, exciting and exhilarating. It was also a challenge.”

The first ape to break the ice was a 25-year-old male with an easily identifiable cleft palate that Mitani would later name Hare. During his second year at Ngogo, Mitani was observing chimpanzees in a massive fig tree when Hare descended. Mitani assumed he would run away as he had done in the past. Instead, the chimp walked slowly toward the next fruit tree, permitting Mitani to follow.

“When I realised what was happening, I almost started to cry. After working so hard for so long, it was tremendously gratifying to have gained Hare’s trust,” Mitani wrote in the 2022 anthology Chimpanzee Memoirs.

Mitani estimates he has spent 85 months of his life hiking the forests of Ngogo, or approximately seven years. What began as a few basic structures and tents has grown into a large – albeit rustic – research camp that has housed the nearly 90 researchers who have worked with the Ngogo project over three decades.

The findings that have emerged from Ngogo over the years have stunned the scientific world, similar to the discoveries first made at Gombe in Tanzania by Jane Goodall in the 1960s and 1970s. Mitani and his colleagues documented the lowest mortality ever recorded for a wild chimp population, suggesting that good habitat conditions could lengthen life expectancy to close to that of human hunter-gatherers.

They found that unrelated males could form strong alliances and cooperate, moving beyond the accepted paradigm that only close kin would work together. Hunting and meat-eating (particularly munching on the red colobus monkeys) were found to be important for male social bonding, not just nutrition.

But the most notable – and disturbing – finding of Ngogo began on a June day in 2015. Mitani and his fellow researchers were observing a cluster of the group when the chimps began to display nervous behaviour and scattered at the sounds of approaching group members. “All of a sudden, the individuals I was following just ran down the hill for no apparent reason,” Mitani says. “Chaos erupted. They started to run around and chase each other.”

That moment, in retrospect, was the first sign of what would become a years-long bloody conflict – chronicled in the 2023 Netflix series Chimp Empire – between a once close-knit group of chimps. In a study published this April in the journal Science, Mitani and his colleagues describe what may be the first “civil war” among wild chimps.

By 2018, two distinct chimp groups had formed in Ngogo. Nine males and 19 infants have been killed during the conflict. Scientists later found that the unexpected result of this lethal aggression was that female fertility doubled and offspring survival increased substantially at Ngogo.

But for Mitani, who has spent much of his life among the Ngogo chimps, witnessing the split was far more personal. “I was in denial. I was still in this mindset that they were doing so well together as a big group,” he recalls.

“It’s been hard to watch. In the first 20 years, going back to see the chimps was fun. I always looked forward to these visits. But it’s gotten to be increasingly difficult to go back and see this, to see these killings continue.”

So much so, he adds, that it took him more than a decade to write the paper on the dark events they had borne witness to in the forests of Ngogo. “I think I was dragging my heels because maybe I didn’t really want to write about this.”

Still, Mitani pushes back against the takeaway that the civil war says anything about humans’ evolutionary propensity for violence and in-fighting. This behaviour, he adds, has not been witnessed among bonobos, with whom we also share a common ancestor dating back approximately 8m years.

“Many of us who study chimps emphasise the similarities, and for good reason,” Mitani says. “But when it comes to the behavioural similarities, sometimes I think my colleagues stretch things a bit too much. If there is one thing I’ve learned from studying chimps all these years, it is that they are not us.”

Though the greatest threat the Ngogo chimps now face is, in a way, themselves, Mitani says the presence of researchers on the ground over many decades has helped to conserve these populations. Researchers work with the wildlife authority to remove snares for other wild game that occasionally trap a chimp by mistake, for example.

But Mitani, who now lives between Michigan and Arizona, worries for the future of research at Ngogo. The project has received the bulk of its funding from the US National Science Foundation’s behavioural and cognitive sciences division. Under the Trump administration’s proposed 2027 budget, that funding is due to be eliminated.

“The chimps there have many more important stories to tell us,” Mitani says. “This is one of the reasons I am so concerned about the war on science and truth in this country.”

He will return again to Ngogo this month – and for as long as he is able. “The funny thing is that the hills at Ngogo get increasingly steeper every year. And the distance between the trails seems to get longer. But I feel blessed that I still can do it.”

If there is any legacy to his life’s work, he hopes that being able to impart some knowledge of the complex lives of these animals will give people a better appreciation of the chimpanzees. That maybe that will inspire people to ensure we continue living on a planet alongside them. “That would be the grand, big hope.”

‘Some aren’t going to make it’: how pressure on farmers threatens UK food security

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 11:00:24 GMT

Food producers are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability of British supply chains

“There are so many decent, capable, productive, efficient arable farmers out there, asking how they are supposed to finance the crop they are meant to be putting in the ground,” Jamie Burrows says.

Sitting in his tractor at his arable farm in Norfolk, Burrows is listing the multiple challenges facing him and other food producers.

Crop growers such as Burrows are ploughing and cultivating their fields, preparing the ground – hardened and dried out during the long, hot summer – for their next crop.

But machinery requires fuel, and the cost of red diesel – used for agricultural vehicles and machinery that is taxed at a lower rate than standard diesel – has almost doubled since the conflict in Iran began in late February. The cost of most fertilisers used to grow crops and feed for animals has also soared by about 20% over the same period.

“Some of these businesses aren’t going to make it,” concludes Burrows, who is also the chair of the crops board at the National Farmers’ Union (NFU). “It is very, very difficult.”

These are among the latest worries for Britain’s food producers, who also faced a succession of heatwaves and drought conditions during the UK’s hottest summer on record, which resulted in England’s worst recorded cereals harvest, according to official production estimates.

Farmers, the first link in the food production chain, are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability and precarity of the UK’s food supply.

Food experts, academics, businesses and the public spending watchdog, the National Audit Office (NAO), have in recent weeks called on the government to work on making the UK’s food system more resilient.

The climate crisis, this year’s huge El Niño weather pattern, geopolitical shocks, energy outages and cyber-attacks are all considered threats to food chain security.

Amid calls for ministers to treat food as a national security issue, parliament’s influential public accounts committee is to begin a series of hearings on Monday as part of its inquiry into the resilience of the UK’s food supply.

MPs on the committee will look at the NAO’s findings on the shortcomings of the last catastrophe planning exercise by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which largely excluded food supply chain businesses.

Britain produces about 60% of the food it needs to feed itself, but is more dependent on imports than many European peers. The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future emergencies than several European neighbours.

Some in the food industry believe there are signs Andy Burnham’s government is beginning to take the threats to Britain’s food system more seriously.

The Cabinet Office will launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for possible future emergencies. The government’s Prepare website outlines steps it says people should take, which include storing items at home, including bottles of water and nonperishable food, such as tinned meat, fruit and vegetables that do not require cooking.

Despite this, a recent warning from more than 150 food experts and academics accused ministers of being “complacent” about food security and not having a plan to feed people in an emergency.

“Historically we have done pretty well coping with specific events such as Covid and we’ve managed to ride through them, but we’re moving into a period where we’re having multiple crises impact at the same time,” says Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who signed the letter.

These include the worsening climate crisis and increased water scarcity in regions that now provide some of the fresh produce UK households rely on, including the Mediterranean and north Africa.

Meanwhile, Behrens and other experts, including Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, have been warning for some time that the UK’s food distribution network is concentrated, leaving it exposed to potential disruption or targeting by bad actors.

Lang has previously stated that the UK’s supermarket network is supplied by just 131 distribution hubs – serving 12,300 stores – while the industry body the Cold Chain Federation has warned that most of Britain’s food imports enter the country through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway.

The UK government wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s. Behrens says other nations, particularly Scandinavian countries, now have “far greater national preparedness”.

He says: “They’re looking at community responses and how much households can have on hand. They’re looking at their own local production and some countries have strategic stores of grain.”

Mother of one Ana, 42, is one of a small but growing number of citizens who have been preparing for possible future emergencies for some time. Now living in south Wales, she is originally from eastern Europe and grew up in a family that grew food and preserved it for the colder months. She now shares tips on her YouTube channel, advising other households on resilience and how to build an emergency stockpile.

“It’s just a normal way of life, basically safeguarding yourself and your family,” she says. Ana describes herself as a “prepper”, but wants to move away from its negative connotations, such as panic buying or being a survivalist.

“The stereotype was … that preparedness is American, really weird, all camo and blokes in the bushes, hunting and eating squirrels and mushrooms,” she says. Instead she wants to help other citizens learn how they could cope for a few hours, days or even weeks without power, water or being able to get to the shops.

“If the stereotype had been dispersed originally by the government, then people would look at preparedness as an everyday thing,” she says.

Rob Haward, the chief executive of organic vegetable box delivery company Riverford, believes the UK’s food supply chain needs a “very complicated rethink and a different vision for future security”.

Devon-based Riverford distributes about 65,000 boxes a week to customers and about 70% of the produce it sells is grown in the UK, although it also has long-term relationships with growers in Spain and Italy.

While the UK is always going to import fruit such as bananas, which cannot be grown in large volumes domestically, Haward believes consumers can also play a role by returning to eating more seasonally.

Haward says longer-term contracts can help farmers, giving them confidence to invest in their land and what they grow. He adds: “There are different ways we can try to create a food and farming sector different to now and much more resilient to the future world,” such as working to restore soils to better withstand the changing climate. He also wants government to “pull levers” such as offering lower business rates to greengrocers.

Labour has got the message – it’s developing nations suffering most from bond market turmoil

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 10:11:19 GMT

Just as Brown and Blair did in 2005, Andy Burnham aims to champion debt relief to help developing countries

Developing nations face triple shock, UN warns

From Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless.

Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere.

Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank may be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans.

That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency.

Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed 45% of government revenues in the global south, and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future.

There have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including from African Union heads of state, and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa.

The G20 – the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis.

However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran.

Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, and Labour has made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing.

The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.”

He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond, securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries.

As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support.

“There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference.

Yet she and other ministers have made clear they are open to proposals – and ready to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind making progress on this formidable challenge.

One ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues.

Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives.

The “hope initiative” also envisages potential relief for another six small island developing states that do not meet the threshold on the basis of their debt burden but are regularly battered by natural disasters. These could be offered a five-year “holiday” from the moment of the next extreme weather event they face, at the cost of a further $700m a year.

An even more expansive version would embrace another five countries, including Pakistan and Angola.

Crucially, because the international financial institutions – including the IMF and the World Bank – tend to be preferred creditors, only chipping in when other help is exhausted, the costs to them would be relatively low.

Echoing Andy Burnham’s slogan – so far confined to the domestic sphere – Matthew Martin, DFI’s executive director and the author of the plan, says: “Let’s bring hope back to the poorest countries in the world, through an ambitious but financially and politically feasible initiative, which will free up $13bn for them to spend on their climate and development goals.”

It remains to be seen how bold the government is prepared to be in setting its G20 agenda, but the groundwork is being done.

Labour trashed its reputation as a champion for international development when Keir Starmer took the axe to aid spending to pay for defence. Perhaps 2027 could be the year Burnham starts to rebuild it.

Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:00:22 GMT

This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day

Humankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.

Donald Trump’s blanket denials of the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some as the latest harbinger of apocalypse, could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.

While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity – existential AI threats remain, as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating, global proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima, how much longer can our luck hold?

Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putin recently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal, comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time, Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacks deep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.

Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US is upgrading its nuclear arsenal of 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing a lucrative deal with Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.

Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’s status as a nuclear weapons state. South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim, whom he bizarrely terms a friend. “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit, is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow – which, at this rate, there may not be.

Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “the most dangerous nuclear moment” since 1989. Global military spending reached nearly $3tn last year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paper published by the non-partisan Arms Control Association (ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.

The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too, is the fast-developing contest for control of space, notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and others advances rapidly. Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.

If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.

After RAF Fairford incident, how big a threat to the UK is Iran?

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:00:21 GMT

Although there is scepticism about Tehran’s capabilities, it has become clear it wants Britain to feel it poses a risk

Britain may have been only peripherally involved in the bombing of Iran that Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu started, but in the past fortnight it has become clear that Tehran wants to pose a threat inside the UK in response.

In the aftermath of the confused incident near RAF Fairford, western officials are weighing up whether to warn publicly that Iran now has US military targets in Europe on its mind, such as the air force base in Gloucestershire.

That could come even though there remains British scepticism about Iran’s capability to pull off a drone raid on a secure facility far from Tehran.

What is already accepted by MI5 is that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has sought to coordinate and promote the targeting of the Jewish community in the UK and Europe, starting from March with a string of arson attacks directed at synagogues and similar sites.

That is itself a significant step up from the regime’s longstanding campaign of assassination plots and threats against critics overseas, tasks the IRGC has traditionally hired criminal gangs to carry out.

Exactly what happened at RAF Fairford remains unclear, though Iran may have gained something from it for very little. A week later, last Sunday, a worried US decided to withdraw the 12 B-1 bombers it had stationed there, with leaks to US media suggesting there was a fear of a Ukraine-style drone attack.

What is known is that five men from London drove up in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, one of whom called 999 as they did so. All five were arrested in Whelford, a village next to the airbase, only to be released on police bail a day later when no explosives were found or discernible plot discovered.

Two more men have been arrested on suspicion of terror offences, and released on police bail. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has said there were “strong indications” Iran played a part, and on Thursday the Met police chief, Mark Rowley, said “you will see more progress on this investigation”.

RAF Fairford is an exposed site, with plane spotters easily able to get up close enough to photograph and track the forward-deployed US B-1 and B-52 bombers, which with permission from the former prime minister Keir Starmer were taking off to make attack runs into Iran in the spring and early summer.

“Iran has a track record of planning and carrying out attacks especially on opponents of the regime in the UK. Given the use of Fairford by US bombers, it’s only prudent to assume that they would see an interest in attacking a wider range of targets, whatever their involvement in the Fairford incident,” said Lord Ricketts, a former UK national security adviser.

Dr Antonio Giustozzi, a terrorism specialist with the Royal United Services Institute, suggests the drive to the village was “a feint” where individuals, who may have been unwitting, were sent “to hint at what could happen”. But he is sceptical that Iran could pose a real military threat to Fairford or elsewhere.

As for attacking Fairford, piloting first-person view drones of the type used in Ukraine is a skill requiring several days if not weeks of training, while an operation on an airbase would probably take months to prepare. “I doubt that Iran could bring in military-grade explosive to the UK; the last people to do so were the IRA,” Giustozzi said.

A genuine attack on RAF Fairford or similar would almost certainly be a one-way mission ending in capture or even death, which it would be it hard to recruit for. But despite the low risks, the US chose to withdraw the B-1 bombers, which cost $300m (£225m) each, as a precautionary move. It was “an operational decision to reduce the risk”, Rich Knighton, the head of the UK armed forces, said on Thursday.

This week, a US congressional research report counted that 81 US military planes, helicopters or drones had been destroyed or damaged in the Iran war, including several struck on the ground at bases in Saudi Arabia and Jordan, a reminder that Iran fought back more effectively than the US acknowledged. The value of lost aircraft and air defence systems is estimated at $1.9bn and $3.3bn respectively.

Meanwhile, Trump, desperate to lower oil prices, has set back any future attack on Iran until after the US midterm elections in early November. But regardless of other justifications for the US withdrawal from RAF Fairford, and the police investigation – which has yet to lead to any charges – the wider Iran threat in the UK is now elevated.

A week ago, two Iranian nationals, Salam Ahmadyan from Liverpool and Rahman Salehi from Salford, were charged with terror offences, accused of trying to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade chlorine powder bomb.

Prosecutors told a magistrates court on Saturday the pair were in contact with a third party, believed to be in Iran, who directed them and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”. A trial at the Old Bailey has been scheduled.

Early in May, the US indicted Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, 32, an Iranian-Iraqi dual national, accusing him of promoting and coordinating 18 arson and other low-level terror attacks against Jewish and US sites in the UK and Europe during March and April 2026. He was, the US authorities said, a commander with Kata’ib Hezbollah, an Iraqi group long backed by the IRGC.

The following month, in a Manhattan courtroom, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty and said he was “a prisoner of war”. He faces a terrorism trial, accused in one instance of participating in an arson attack on a synagogue in London via a FaceTime video call. Though nobody was killed in the campaign, al-Saadi is accused of telling an associate that he was engaged in “psychological warfare”.

The group al-Saadi is accused of running, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia (HAYI), also claimed credit for the firebombing of four Jewish community ambulances in north London in postings on social media. Four people pleaded guilty to arson in the case in August, in an attack that caused an estimated £1m of damage. Sentencing and a full airing of the facts in court are not due until next year.

Jonathan Hackett, a former US marine and intelligence specialist, says the threat in the UK and Europe will endure because Tehran believes it serves a purpose, though it will alter depending on who becomes responsible after al-Saadi. “The psychological effects alone are certainly important; the goal is to create a wedge between the US and its allies,” he added.

The hill I will die on: Pumpkin-spiced latte is a con. It’s time to put an end to Big Autumn

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 07:00:19 GMT

The aesthetic of crisp mornings and roaring fireplaces has created a personality driven by social media. Let’s just admit the reality: mud, drizzle and shorter days

It’s getting earlier every year, that first meme about golden leaves and pumpkin-spiced lattes. This year, I swear, I spotted one in early August, while we were still sweltering under our fourth heatwave of the summer.

Because, of course, for those that like crisp mornings, Halloween and glasses of red wine in front of roaring fires, the arrival of autumn brings with it something else: the incessant need to tell everyone just how much they love this perfectly pleasant, if perpetually damp, season.

I call it Big Autumn. The idea that liking autumn is enough to sustain an entire personality. I don’t know when it first happened but my instinct is that it’s been driven by an almost entirely brown-and-orange aesthetic pushed out via Pinterest and Instagram, and not by the often grim realities: grey drizzle, shorter days, the sense of impending Christmas.

It’s not that I have an issue with the season itself. Sure, my partner and I refer to it as “mud season” because we have a spaniel and two young children, and our house won’t feel truly clean again until the end of March. But I’m partial to a roast dinner and a fairy light, I like oversized jumpers and, although I avoid Halloween, I find Bonfire Night quite magical, even if I do always over-layer and end up sweaty and overstimulated.

No, it’s not the season I take issue with but rather our need to define ourselves by our preferences. It’s a trend that has been perpetuated by social media. See also: being a cat person or a boy mum. It smacks of Christian Girl Autumn, a viral meme from 2019 that emerged as an antidote – one in knee-high leather boots and an oversized scarf – to Hot Girl Summer.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

To me, it merely highlights our modern-day compulsion to construct and curate personalities rather than simply inhabit them. It’s as though the internet has encouraged – nay, forced – us to paint ourselves with broad brush strokes rather than with the nuance and intricacy that a human life calls for. It demonstrates a terminal lack of imagination, although perhaps lives spent juggling always-on jobs, constantly popping WhatsApp groups and the astronomical cost of literally living have left us so burned out we haven’t the time or the energy to add more detail.

I suspect my irritation lies in the fact that liking autumn has not only become a personality, but – because spending and social media go hand in hand – a way of getting us to part with money we don’t have. A pumpkin-spiced chai latte doesn’t come for free and, go on, you definitely need that new-season chocolate-brown knit. Autumn has become a lifestyle, a commodity, not just the passing of the baton from one season to the next.

Maybe my frustration with the people for whom a love of this meteorological phenomenon becomes their defining characteristic is that I fear they are unknowingly playing into the hands of Big Autumn. Or maybe I really do just hate drizzle.

Chloë Hamilton is freelance journalist

Capital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future?

The Guardian Sun, 11 Oct 2026 05:00:16 GMT

Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions, but an avalanche of mishaps has put the system’s flaws in the spotlight

It took more than an hour to establish the two intravenous lines through which Christa Pike would be injected with a giant and normally lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital, and in that time she did everything she could to assist those who were attempting to kill her.

“Please try here,” she said over and over again to Tennessee’s execution team, pointing to specific parts of her body where she thought they might find a vein as they repeatedly stabbed her with needles. “Please try here, I think it will be OK. Please try up on my shoulder, higher.”

When the team finally achieved what they thought would be a working line, allowing her execution to proceed, Pike, 50, made a point of thanking them. “Miss Pike was kind, and she was cooperative,” her lawyer Randy Spivey, a witness in the death chamber, said.

The world knows what happened next. For reasons as yet not fully understood, the drug did not enter her bloodstream, probably spilling into her arm tissue.

Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder when she was 18 of her classmate Colleen Slemmer, remained alive. She is the only person ever to survive a full “lethal” injection execution.

On Tuesday she remarkably regained consciousness. She is now able to talk and walk around the room, her lawyers have said.

In comments to reporters, Spivey said that he was haunted by the harrowing failed execution. “What I saw is not something that should ever happen again. It was done in all of our names.”

The events of the past 10 days – starting with Pike amicably assisting her executioners and ending with her waking up shackled to a Nashville hospital bed, her arms grotesquely swollen, facing a long and uncertain road to recovery – has thrown America into a frenzy. If this is the outcome of a punishment carried out in “all our names”, then what are we doing about it?

“This is a very big moment,” said Laura Porter, executive director at the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, an alliance of 60 abolitionist groups. “When you see something as horrific as this, the impact is enormous, as it throws attention on the death penalty’s flaws.”

Porter has been closely involved in America’s struggle with capital punishment for almost a quarter century, since she became a leader of New Yorkers Against the Death Penalty in 2003. At that time death row prisoners were still being killed at a rate of more than one a week.

There were 71 executions that year in the US (down from the 1999 pinnacle of 98). Since then, Porter has watched and agitated as the number has steadily declined for almost two decades, reaching a low of just 11 judicial killings in 2021.

“I believe that the death penalty will die by a thousand cuts,” she said. “Every time there’s a botched execution like Christa’s, or a wrongful conviction, or the execution of an intellectually disabled person, public understanding of the system’s flaws grows.”

How great a difference a few years can make. Six years ago, there was such confidence in the historic fading away of the practice that the authoritative Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) began its yearly report with the words: “Capital punishment continued to wither across the US in 2019”.

But as Mark Twain might have put it, reports of the death penalty’s own death turned out to be an exaggeration. Fast forward to last year, and DPI was recording that the 47 executions carried out in 2025 marked the highest incidence in 16 years.

No awards for guessing the key individual behind the resurgence. Less than a year after DPI’s “withering” pronouncement, Donald Trump embarked on one of the most concentrated bursts of US state killing of its own citizens in modern times.

Toward the end of his first presidency, the Trump administration executed 13 federal death row prisoners. They included Lisa Montgomery, a woman with such a shocking history of childhood sexual abuse it bears comparison to Pike’s own.

Since his return to the White House last year, Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions. On his first day back he issued an executive order on “restoring the death penalty” in which he said it was “an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes”.

The statement was a classic Trump fabrication. The US justice department itself has concluded that there is no proof that the punishment deters criminals. Many prisoners on death row cannot be described as the most heinous, not least the 4% who by conservative estimations are innocent.

At federal level, Trump has been hampered by Joe Biden, who before he left office commuted the death penalties of all but three prisoners on federal death row. Using his power as commander-in-chef, Trump still managed this week to order the military execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooter.

On Thursday the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, breathlessly announced that Hasan would face a firing squad of soldiers at Fort Hood on 3 December in the first public execution to be staged in the US since 1936. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

The Pentagon’s plan to livestream Hasan’s execution prompted a second wave of desbelief that ricocheted around the globe , threatening to drown out even the consternation over Pike’s treatment. US politicians denounced the idea as “disgusting”, while the UN issued the US government with the same stern warning it has given Afghanistan and Iran that the move would be tantamount to torture.

When not presiding over an administration that seems determined to turn the clock back 100 years, Trump has also used his squawk box to exhort death penalty states, where most capital punishment activity occurs, to hit the gas. Many have obliged.

First among them has been Florida. The outgoing governor, Ron DeSantis, appears to have been so inspired by Trump’s 2020-21 killing spree that he greenlit a record 19 executions last year.

DeSantis will come close to matching that shattering number in 2026. Florida has already put to death 16 prisoners this year, with two more executions pending, though the governor cancelled a lethal injection procedure on Friday without giving an explanation.

Nationwide, the US is set to kill up to 38 people this year – the most recent just on Wednesday when Texas executed convicted murderer Jamaal Howard. That tally would be down from last year’s high, but still represent a larger display of state killing than in any year since 2013.

In cheerleading the revival of executions, Trump has been backed by a supporting cast of Christian nationalists. These Bible thumpers have injected their eye-for-an-eye brand of retributive justice into the wider Maga movement.

Brooklyn Walker, an assistant professor at the University of Tennessee Knoxville, has studied Christian nationalist views on justice. She has found them to be far more embracing of retribution, including the death sentence, than other US religious groups.

Christian nationalist leaders frequently invoke Old Testament notions of punitive justice “as part of the idea of creating a social order, and then requiring people to fit within it,” Walker said.

Doug Wilson, an Idaho pastor who wants to turn America into a theocracy and has close ties to Hegseth, has pushed for legal appeals to be streamlined. That way death row prisoners could be dispatched more quickly.

Joel Webbon, another leading Christian nationalist pastor from Texas, has argued for the death penalty to be expanded to include women who make false sexual assault accusations. The day after Pike’s failed execution he posted to his 120,000 followers on X that “you cannot be pro life without being pro death penalty”.

The energy blown into capital punishment from such far-right religious pundits is affecting the furious debate that has now erupted in Tennessee over what should happen to Pike. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for Tennessee governor, wants to plug back in the electric chair.

Blackburn’s call for the return of “Old Sparky” speaks volumes about the state of capital punishment. The horrifying scenes at Pike’s attempted execution were part of a wider unravelling of lethal injections, the protocol that has been dominant in the US for almost 50 years.

By DPI’s calculations, there have been 12 botched executions in the past five years alone. Five of the condemned prisoners involved, including Pike herself, survived the procedure meaning that they were rendered immobile while a team of masked strangers failed to kill them for up to several hours.

Amid such unconscionable suffering, the claim made on behalf of lethal injections that they are a medicalised and humane form of ending a life has come unstuck. Who would dare to classify what Pike endured as humane?

Proponents of the ultimate punishment have been forced to seek alternatives that might avoid some of the pitfalls of lethal injections. But the moment they have introduced such often archaic methods they have run into a whole new set of headaches.

Two of the prisoners who survived recent lethal injections, Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith, were executed by Alabama a year later under the experimental technique, nitrogen gas. The method is regarded by veterinarians as too cruel for the euthanisia of cats and dogs, and it has now been blocked for human use by a federal court.

Other states have tried the firing squad. But when South Carolina took this path last year with Mikal Mahdi, a convicted murderer, the marksmen missed the target of the prisoner’s heart, causing him a prolonged and likely agonising death.

Such an avalanche of mishaps, spanning botched executions, experimentation, and even dark insinuations of deliberate miss-targeting, is what Porter means by her “death by a thousand cuts”. It gives her and her army of abolitionists the material they need to sustain a long campaign.

As a seasoned abolitionist, Porter knows that she is facing tough adversaries in Trump and the Christian nationalists. But she draws sustenance from the 23 states that have scrapped the death penalty which, if you add the four states that have put the practice on hold, pushes them into the majority.

Then there is the growing number of young Americans who no longer support the punishment. In the most recent Gallup poll that asked the question, from 2024, only 42% of 18 to 34 year olds approved. (In last year’s poll the overall extent of support had fallen from a 1995 high of 80% to 52%).

She also takes heart from the burgeoning ranks of Republican state lawmakers willing to raise objections. And by the increasing unwillingness of juries to mete out new death sentences.

Most of all, she’s buoyed up by the powerful accord she has found from an unlikely source: families of capital murder victims. Amid their grief, some families have had the strength and conviction to join the fight to spare the lives of those who killed their loved ones.

“In every campaign I’ve been part of where we’ve ended the death penalty – in Connecticut, Maryland, Virginia, and many more – victims’ families have been among the lead voices,” Porter said.

To those voices we may perhaps, in time, be able to add one more. It would be the most unlikely voice of all – that of a woman whom the modern state, with all its paraphernalia, could not silence: Christa Pike.

Her lawyers tell us that she is angry and confused, her mind foggy. But she is also able to inquire after the well-being of others, including, poignantly, the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer.

She is not out of the woods: on Saturday she was released from hospital and returned to the women’s prison in Nashville, where she will still receive medical care. But coming from a state of unconsciousness so profound that even her own legal team feared she might be brain-dead, her reemergence has been nothing short of astonishing.

It all leaves so many questions, her lawyer Spivey said ruefully on Wednesday. “We have to ask, ‘How much suffering is enough?’”

Spivey directed the question at Tennessee. He might just as well have been addressing America.

In three years, Israel’s war on Gaza hasn’t just changed the Middle East, it’s changed the world

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 12:00:56 GMT

A whirlpool of violence has engulfed everywhere from Lebanon to Yemen. Meanwhile, the west has destroyed any political authority it once had

There was a world before 7 October, 2023, and now there is a world after. For Gaza, for Israel, for the wider Middle East, and for everyone else too. Not all hinge points in history are obvious at the time. Three years on from the day it began, and precisely one year since a supposed ceasefire was agreed, this one is now impossible to ignore.

The before-and-after pictures tell part of the story. An update to Google Maps, released last week, underscores just what three years of relentless Israeli military onslaught has done to Gaza. Satellite images show how entire towns have been reduced to rubble. Mosques and hospitals, visible three years ago, have now disappeared. Meanwhile the once-empty shoreline is now crammed with tents. This is what it looks like when an attempt has been made to destroy a people.

For Israel, too, there has been a before and after. Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu had cultivated a sense of security, even of impregnability. The ease with which Hamas carried out its terrorist attack, killing 1,200 Israelis, including hundreds of young people at a music festival, destroyed that belief for ever.

Three years on from 7 October, both Israel and Gaza have changed beyond recognition. But the consequences of Hamas’s attack and Israel’s brutal response, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, have spread far wider.

Under the pretext of protecting its own borders, Israel has launched wars and military offensives across the region, sending troops into Syria; effectively annexing parts of southern Lebanon, deploying the same tactics there that it used in Gaza; and starting, with the US, an unwinnable war with Iran that has spiralled into a regional conflict affecting all six Gulf states.

The Iran war has sparked a new conflict between the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, which this week triggered a mutual defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey, dragging two other countries into the maelstrom. Across the Red Sea, some of the same combatants are involved in the war in Sudan and a fresh conflict inside Ethiopia.

More than a dozen countries across two continents are now entangled in a rising number of wars, with overlapping participants and numerous competing interests.

But there is something else, more insidious, that has changed. The rule of international law, tenuous as it was, has been openly replaced by military might. In 2022, western leaders – building a coalition rightly opposed to Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – made moral appeals based on the violation of international law. In Gaza, they encouraged and supported Israel, even when it was clear that the rules were being broken. That hypocrisy has not gone unnoticed, not just in the global south but among many millions of citizens in the west.

We have watched this happen in real time. Despite the ban on international journalists, anyone with a phone knew what was happening in Gaza from the early days of Israel’s response. Hundreds of Palestinian journalists have reported on the bombing of hospitals and schools, the bombing of cafes and wells, the killings at food distribution points, the deaths of children and babies. War crimes have never before been broadcast in real time, relentlessly, every hour of every day, around the world.

Gaza has also changed how wars are fought. Israel has pioneered the use of AI to select targets, accelerating our descent into a future for which we are unprepared.

All of this was allowed to take place in a time when the west could still argue that the “international rules-based order” existed. It may have been destroyed by Donald Trump, but we cannot forget that the dismantling began under Joe Biden. It was Biden who ensured the flow of weapons to Israel continued uninterrupted, Biden who insisted that every United Nations security council resolution calling for a ceasefire was vetoed, and Biden who attacked the international criminal court when it sought to indict Netanyahu for war crimes.

US support for Israel has always been strong and, on the whole, unquestioned. But even Republican presidents have understood they have influence over Israel’s actions and have been prepared to use it.

Ronald Reagan suspended an arms deal in 1981 after Israel annexed the Golan Heights. A year later, his administration stopped supplying cluster weapons to Israel after Menachem Begin’s government used them in populated areas during its invasion of Lebanon. In 2002, the killing of 15 Palestinians in Gaza was enough for Colin Powell, the then secretary of state, to announce a review of Israel’s use of American arms.

Israel was also given a free pass by every other member of the G7, including those run by centrists or centre-left politicians. French president Emmanuel Macron, German chancellor Olaf Scholz, Justin Trudeau in Canada and Australia’s Anthony Albanese all initially gave Israel their backing.

Only António Guterres, the much-maligned UN secretary general, emerges with a modicum of credit. Less than three weeks after 7 October, he called Israel’s response “collective punishment of the Palestinian people” and demanded an immediate ceasefire.

The one ray of hope for the future is that our shared understanding of what has happened over the past three years means that in many countries the political winds have shifted.

Before Andy Burnham even entered Number 10, he apologised for how Labour had handled the early days of the conflict. The UK now has a prime minister who was one of the few western politicians to call for a ceasefire just weeks after 7 October. Ed Miliband’s willingness to accurately describe Israel’s actions in the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” indicate a change in attitude that could lead to more concerted international action against Israel.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

In the US, support for Israel has fallen through the floor. For a Democrat who wants to be president in 2028 there is no credible path to the White House that doesn’t involve support for the Palestinian cause. And yet, we cannot simply close our eyes and hope that a change in America will magically restore the world to how it was on 6 October 2023.

Nor should we pretend that the previous era was one we should wish to return to. Did we enter a new world on 7 October, or did we just notice where we were? In the three years before the Hamas attack, the wars in Tigray and Sudan saw many of the same trends play out.

In Tigray, the northernmost part of Ethiopia, a war between the central government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front killed 600,000 people. There were brutal massacres, forced starvation, widespread use of drones – and absolutely no accountability. In Sudan, too, hospitals have been hit by drones, women have been raped, children have been shot dead. Again, we could see it happen. Again, there were no consequences.

Gaza, though, has undoubtedly accelerated the trend, normalising the immoral. The wars that have begun, that have spiralled out of control and pulled more countries and more actors into their orbit, cannot easily be stopped. There is a momentum to this conflict, a hardening of positions, as each new outrage leads to a response. When there is impunity, when there is no price that those responsible will ever pay, there are terrifyingly few levers to pull. If war crimes go unpunished, they only escalate.

And so a family in Addis Ababa fears the sound of a drone crashing into their home. A village in Lebanon is evacuated, destroyed and the land made uninhabitable. A mundane job at Riyadh airport becomes a daily deadly gamble. A crew of badly paid seafarers pray to their gods as they cross through the strait of Hormuz. The dreams of millions of children shrink from university, fame or fortune, to the brute reality of survival.

And in Gaza, crammed into tents, deprived of enough food and water, two million Palestinians are still living under the brutal rule of Hamas and the daily threat of death from a military force that fears no consequences.

This is our world now. We need to recognise that, if anything is going to change.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

From The Social Reckoning to Harriet Kemsley: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:49 GMT

Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s sequel to The Social Network, and the Last One Laughing star reckons with divorce in her new standup tour

The Social ReckoningOut nowThe David Fincher-directed The Social Network has only come to seem more canny over time, with the site co-founded by Mark Zuckerberg being held responsible for all manner of social ills. In this sequel from Aaron Sorkin (this time directing and writing) based on the incidents around the 2021 leak of internal Facebook memos, Zuck is embodied not by Jesse Eisenberg but Jeremy Strong.

The UprisingOut nowPaul Greengrass (United 93) tackles the 1381 peasants’ revolt, a fracas caused partly by the decision to introduce a new tax of four pence per person, regardless of whether you were in the greedy elite or a worker who might make about £2 in a whole year. Heading up the rebels with a cause are Andrew Garfield and Cosmo Jarvis.

The Lost Children of TuamOut nowIn 2017, the New York Times chronicled the efforts of amateur local historian Catherine Corless’s campaign to expose the abuse by Irish nuns that led to almost 800 child and infant deaths in Ireland. This dramatisation of the scandal stars Monica Dolan as Corless and is produced by Liam Neeson.

Other MommyOut nowJessica Chastain stars as both regular mom Ursula and her supernatural doppelganger, creeping around the house interacting with eight-year-old Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark) in this Blumhouse horror directed by Rob Savage (Dashcam). An adaptation of Josh Malerman’s creepy 2024 novel, Incidents Around the House. Catherine Bray

Arab Strap12 to 17 October, tour starts EdinburghThe Scottish duo returned last month with their ninth album Half-Told Tales. A 14-song collection of strangely danceable odes to ageing (You You You), angry warnings about masturbation (I Get Noise), and an overarching sense of black humour, it should make for a fun night out. Michael Cragg

ManifestWembley Arena, London, 16 OctoberLike their girl group contemporaries Katseye, this Turkish sextet were created via a TV singing competition. They also share some of their musical DNA, with Manifest’s brightly hued songs bubbling like a sugary soft drink. Support on this debut arena show comes from UK girl band newcomers XO. MC

606 Club 50th anniversary festival606 Club, London, 12 to 25 OctoberWest London’s much-loved 606 Club celebrates its 50th anniversary over a fortnight, with star guests including Jamie Cullum (13 Oct), Gwilym Simcock (15 Oct), and many trailblazers of UK jazz. Founded and run by saxophonist Steve Rubie, “The Six” is as devoted to good music as it’s ever been. John Fordham

Oxford international song festivalVarious venues, 10 to 24 OctoberAn ambitious local event turned major international fixture, this festival celebrates 25 seasons with big-name performances on the theme of love. Highlights include baritone Matthias Goerne and pianist Tamara Stefanovich in Schubert’s Winterreise (10 Oct), and songs by György Kurtág from baritone Benjamin Appl and pianist James Baillieu (Mon). Flora Willson

Light and Magic: The Birth of Art PhotographyTate Modern, London, 14 October to 21 FebruaryThe Tate’s big autumn show takes a global look at the more conceptual, artier side of photography, with 200 prints by 80 artists from across the world, including Madame Yevonde, who saw the camera as more than a documentary tool.

Prem Sahib, Gordon Matta-ClarkDe La Warr Pavilion, Bexhill-on-Sea, 10 October to 4 January Prem Sahib has been making some of the most interesting art in the UK over the past few years, all about queer intimacy and clubbing, and he is getting some well-deserved institutional attention here alongside the brilliant late American conceptualist Gordon Matta-Clark.

Julia IsídrezNottingham Contemporary, to 10 JanuaryUK museums’ fascination with indigenous art continues unabated with this show of ceramics by Paraguayan Guaraní artist Julia Isídrez, filled with mythical creatures and multi-headed amphibians.

Frieze art fairRegent’s Park, London, 14 to 19 OctoberEvery autumn, Frieze shows up in a massive tent in Regent’s Park and plays host to the best art galleries in the world. It is a cultural phenomenon, and well worth visiting if you can stomach the price of entry. Eddy Frankel

Harriet KemsleyBrighton, 11 October; Hull, 14 October; Leeds, 15 October; touring to 26 FebruaryOn stage, the Last One Laughing star comes across as a giggly, chaotic oversharer – but you don’t become a successful standup without serious finesse and focus. Kemsley’s current show Floozy sees the 39-year-old relate her experiences of post-divorce dating in deceptively daffy style. Rachel Aroesti

The Cherry OrchardHarold Pinter theatre, London, to 9 JanuaryAutumn is the season when all the stage stars come to play in the West End – and there are none bigger than Kristin Scott Thomas, who stars alongside Stephen Mangan in Chekhov’s richly rewarding final play. Miriam Gillinson

Middlemarch Parts 1 & 2Swan theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, to 16 JanuaryNina Raine has adapted George Eliot’s exquisite novel into a play in two parts, directed by Jeremy Herrin – who is so good at injecting ambitious shows with shape and purpose. Nia Towle plays Dorothea Brooke alongside Amanda Root, playing both George Eliot and matchmaker Mrs Cadwallader. MG

English National BalletLiverpool Empire, 15 to 17 October; touring to 25 OctoberThere are two ways to watch the ENB this week: see them live in Rudolf Nureyev’s staging of Romeo & Juliet, with one of the best ballet scores ever written. Or settle down with some popcorn for their sumptuous production of Sleeping Beauty, recorded at the Royal Albert Hall in cinemas (13 to 18 October). Lyndsey Winship

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

Treasure IslandParamount+, 12 OctoberRobert Louis Stevenson’s 1883 novel – responsible for creating the pirate caricature of the popular imagination – was first adapted for television 75 years ago. This new version stars David Oyelowo, Jack Huston, and Hayley Atwell as Bess Hawkins, who helps her son Jim in his hunt for fabled riches.

VisionQuestDisney+, 14 OctoberIt can be juvenile, but Marvel lore has also powered some of the cleverest TV of recent times. This mind-boggling spin-off of 2021’s WandaVision rejoins Paul Bettany’s ex-Avenger Vision as he tries to understand what it means to be an android. James Spader co-stars as his maker, the villainous AI Ultron.

TimeiPlayer & BBC One, 11 October, 9pmThe bracing, brutal prison drama returns for series three, this time shifting focus to disturbed teens locked up in a young offenders institute. Siobhan Finneran reprises her role as a disenchanted chaplain, while David Tennant joins the cast as a custodial manager at the end of his tether.

Killing AnnaChannel 4, 12 October, 11pmAn expat Syrian academic sees a video of a civilian massacre in Damascus and uses social media to track down the chief perpetrator; she then poses as Anna, a regime sympathiser, to encourage him to reveal details about his work in this remarkable documentary about vigilantism in the digital age. RA

Planet Zoo 2PC, PS5, Xbox; out 14 OctoberThe popular zoo management sim returns, letting players build their animal kingdoms from a vast toolset of detailed habitats. The addition of aquariums and bird sanctuaries bring in new animals to observe and care for.

Valor Mortis PC, PS5, Xbox; out 14 OctoberA dead soldier of Napoleon’s army finds himself reanimated in an alternate 19th century filled with plague-ridden monsters. An epic fantasy adventure crammed with gutsy combat and supernatural peril are his certain fate. Keith Stuart

Remi Wolf – MudOut nowThe Californian genre alchemist returns with her third album of sideways pop. Less eccentric and neon-splattered than her previous outings, here Wolf contemplates heartbreak on the contemplative Bottle, while the stuttering Twiggy spins through memories via an earworm melody. MC

Dawn Richard – Creole Culture Out now After two albums with avant-garde multi-instrumentalist Spencer Zahn, girlband member turned experimental art-pop practitioner Dawn Richard returns to more solo endeavours with this seventh album. Influenced by her heritage as a Black and Native American woman, songs such as the single Chuuuuurch are relentlessly thrilling.

Troye Sivan – She’s the BestOut nowAfter the commercial highs of 2023’s Something to Give Each Other, there is a palpable sense of confidence on Australian banger merchant Sivan’s follow-up. Its title track is an experimental melange of spoken word and 90s trip-hop, while sugar rush banger Party contorts Madonna’s Music into new shapes.

Jamie T – Ghosts (100 Days of Morning)Out nowFour years after scoring his first No 1 album, south Londoner Jamie T is back with this sixth record featuring a collaboration with Damon Albarn. As the title suggests, its lyrical focus is on various spectres of his past, with the nostalgia motherlode being the galloping lead single 3310.

13 MinutesPodcastThe BBC’s space podcast returns with a new series on the Hubble telescope touching on its delayed and over-budget launch and the discovery of a fatal flaw in the build. We hear how scientists salvaged the operation.

@DictionarycomInstagramManaging to make the mundane functionality of the dictionary more interesting, dictionary. com’s Insta account posts unusual “word of the day” picks, as well as analysis on the linguistic choices of artists such as Taylor Swift.

The Last First: Winter K2Apple TV, out nowThis vertigo-inducing film follows the extreme climbers who in 2021 attempted to be the first to summit the Pakistani‑Chinese K2 mountain in winter. During the gruelling expedition they exposed how dangerously commercialised modern climbing has become. Ammar Kalia

Five Great Reads: unmarked graves, Happy Mondays, and a childhood without sugar

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 04:24:22 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

This selection of reads from across the Guardian has chronicles of evolution, investigations and interviews which ask us to think about how we remember our loved ones when they are gone, and – of course – stories that leave you with a little something sweet.

Enjoy.

Peter Giesel was buried in an unmarked communal grave. The state government laid Giesel to rest in a cemetery on the outskirts of Sydney in a single plot with three others. This week, a Guardian Australia investigation found there are more than 100 cases like his across New South Wales. The Guardian revealed Vietnam veterans, rough sleepers and other impoverished Australians are being buried in graves often holding four or more people, a practice relatives such as Giesel’s sister, Nicole, have described as “unspeakable” and “a disgrace”.

Persons without means: This is the designation the state gives to those who are unable to afford their own funerals. Over the course of the investigation, the Guardian discovered at least 18 individuals known to homelessness services in Sydney who have been placed in unmarked graves in the last 10 years.

Notable quote: “How could such a heartless thing happen to someone who gave so much of his heart to others,” asks Giesel’s friend Elaine Grady (pictured).

An immediate response: When asked about the revelations, NSW Health delivered an apology to the dead and their loved ones, acknowledging they had not always been treated with the dignity and respect they deserved.

How long will it take to read: Less than seven minutes.

Further reading: Shared graves and stories such as Jayne and Barbara’s, have brought this issue to national attention.

Young people around the world are lonelier than ever, and examples of this are not hard to find. In online forums, users ask: “How do you deal with touch starvation?” Another asks: “The loneliness is unbearable, is anyone else experiencing this?” The answer to the latter question is yes. From Germany to Australia to the UK, studies show teenagers and young adults are finding social connections harder to form.

Why? The list is long. In her new book, the loneliness researcher and clinical psychologist Dr Michelle Lim examines why young people have turned toward solitude. She cites a long list of overlapping factors, including hyper-competitive education culture, social media, shifting family dynamics, the cost-of-living crisis, the grief many are still feeling from the Covid pandemic, and the rise of automation, “which means a trip to the supermarket can be conducted entirely without speaking to another human”. Young adults are simply not being offered the opportunities to form meaningful connections, Lim says.

“People are getting used to being alone”: Lim’s biggest fear is what she calls “social atrophy”. Young people, she writes, can fall into what she calls the “loneliness loop”. When you experience loneliness, it can cause you to run away from further social interaction out of fear, making connections harder to come by.

How long will it take to read: Five minutes of solitude.

Further reading: Community-maxxing, and making new friends and connections as adults.

Taking drugs, drinking heavily and dancing to the tunes of the Happy Mondays on stage made Bez famous. The story goes, as the Manchester music scene was exploding, band member Shaun Ryder urged Bez (whose real name is Mark Berry) to jump on stage with the band when they were supporting New Order. His “wild-eyed dancing” is now synonymous with the music itself, and as the band celebrate the 35th anniversary of their landmark album Pills ‘n’ Thrills and Bellyaches, Bez is back at it as the Happy Mondays go on a global tour.

A change for the good: After decades of partying, one might expect Bez to show signs of wear from his life on the road with a rock band. But when interviewer Emine Saner showed up at “his lovely cottage, down a rural track in Herefordshire”, Bez appeared unscathed by the years of drugs and drinking. Having given up cocaine and sugar, the former 24 hour party person now “juices every day, eats only organic food, drinks filtered water and works out with weights in his garden”.

Notable quote: “There’s sheep everywhere now,” Bez told Saner. At first, Saner took it as “a reference to our zombified society”, but he meant “actual sheep in the field” they just entered.

How long will it take to read: Just over five minutes, giving you enough time to Step On.

Further reading: Which is the best Happy Mondays song?

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Denise Brown’s sister Nicole was murdered by OJ Simpson. On the last night the two sisters spent together, Nicole looked out the window to see Simpson driving by. “He’s constantly following me,” she told Brown. After her sister’s murder and the evidence of long-term abuse that emerged during the trial, Brown became a campaigner against domestic violence. She sat down with the Guardian to discuss what she wishes she had known before her sister’s death, and how she hopes her new book can save lives.

It’s rarely simple to leave: Brown says she told her sister all the wrong things. “You’ve got to leave him. You’ve got to get out of this situation. What are you doing?” she told Nicole. Brown now realises she was being unsupportive at the time, and has learned it is often not easy for a victim to leave. “Batterers usually threaten to take children away, threaten family members. When you are in a cycle like Nicole – like a lot of victims of domestic violence – was in, you are the only one who realises how dangerous that situation can be.”

The car chase: The day after Nicole’s funeral, Simpson was scheduled to turn himself in to the police, but elected to go on the run. While millions watched on TV, Brown says she joined in the chase. “We were out of our minds. We got on the road, but he was so far ahead of us. I mean, come on, really?” She laughs at herself, but says: “It was a time of our lives that was insane.”

How long will it take to read: Five minutes.

Further reading: More stories of survival.

In Australia, domestic and family violence counselling is available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). Other international helplines may be found via www. befrienders. org

In the dark days after the second world war in Britain, many foods, including sugar, remained rationed. Adults had just 3 tbsp (40g) a day to stretch between cups of tea and desserts. Children were offered even less, with the very young expected to have no sugar at all. But then the brakes came off, and sugar consumption in the UK almost doubled. Now scientists are looking back on this era to study the impact of sugar on our health.

Notable quote: “History created an experiment that we could never deliberately run over a human lifetime,” says Dr Jiazhen Zheng at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

What have they learned? Using data from the UK Biobank to compare the health of people born shortly before and after sugar rationing ended in the UK, scientists from the University of Southern California found that the longer people had spent under rationing, the lower their risk of developing type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure in mid- to later life. Another study, this one led by Zheng in Hong Kong, found reduced sugar exposure was associated with a lower risk of a growing list of health conditions. “In our work,” Zheng says, “we have seen associations with cardiovascular disease, liver disease, respiratory health, dementia and, more recently, broader measures of ageing.”

How long will it take to read: A sweet three-and-a-half minutes.

Further reading: Everything you need to know about sugar.
