Singapore GP, tasty Tests and the Premier League’s return – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:06:15 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

New Zealand’s proud record at Eden Park – a 53-match unbeaten streak against all comers – is under threat as the hosts face in-form Australia at their Auckland fortress. Still shaken by a 3-1 series loss to South Africa, the battered and bruised All Blacks will strive to rebound in the opening Bledisloe Cup Test against a Wallabies side unbeaten in six matches and brimming with energy after a spellbinding victory over the Springboks. Les Kiss has made an impression since succeeding Joe Schmidt in July, racking up four wins and a draw. A 42-38 upset of the world champions in Perth two weeks ago showcased a measured Wallabies gameplan, built on a solid set-piece, careful game management from scrum-half Ryan Lonergan and successful contesting of high kicks. Follow the action with our live blog.

After an interminable three-week international break, the Premier League returns with a tremble in its hitherto cocky stride as fallout from the Manchester City scandal continues to spread its toxicity among the elite. Enzo Maresca’s side face the music at Anfield on Sunday but before then there’s plenty of tasty clashes to keep blog host David Tindall on his toes. Manchester United and Tottenham badly need a win when they meet at Old Trafford, while Arsenal aim to bounce back at home to Leeds after a rare defeat. There’s also Aston Villa v Brentford, Chelsea v Bournemouth, Ipswich v Fulham and Sunderland v Brighton brushing off the dust on Saturday. For updates and good vibes, join the conversation by sending your thoughts to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

Australia began a daunting 12-month stretch with a three-Test series against South Africa at Kingsmead on ⁠Friday, before tours of India and England next year and the defence of their ODI World Cup title. Having not won a Test ⁠series in England since 2001, India since 2004 and South Africa since 2014, the ​Baggy Greens face one of their toughest ‌assignments in recent years. Join us for our live blog, with Geoff Lemon reporting on the second day in Durban.

George Russell needs to throw everything he can at stopping – or just delaying – Kimi Antonelli’s title charge. That won’t be easy from the back of the grid. The Briton was third, with Mercedes teammate Antonelli ahead of him in second, when his power unit packed in during the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, leaving him with a penalty this week for an engine change. He made a good start on Friday by setting the fastest time in practice and must hope to make an impact in the final sprint race of the season as well as qualifying. Russell and his rivals will have an unusual daylight race on the streets of the city state, before the typical night race on Sunday. Philip Cornwall steers the live blog, with Giles Richards reporting.

Greg Wood is under starter’s orders to live blog the second day of Newmarket’s big autumn meeting. Top of the bill is the Darley Dewhurst Stakes (3pm), with Godolphin’s Desert Castle pitted against Coolmore’s Darkness Falls. The Charlie Appleby-trained mount made his debut at Newmarket in August when the word was clearly out as he was an odds-on winner. Aidan O’Brien’s Darkness Falls represents a stiffer rival, but his best furlong was his last over a mile-and-one at Leopardstown and Desert Castle should have too much speed. Also the Ian Williams-trained Beylerbeyi is aiming to be the first back-to-back winner of the Cesarewitch Handicap (3.40pm) over two and a quarter miles. Earlier, Boiling Point will seek a second victory of the season for Karl Burke in the Darley Stakes (1.15pm). A Listed winner at Goodwood in May, he should dominate in a small field.

Arsenal are aiming to strike back when Leeds visit the Emirates in Saturday’s early kick-off. A perfect start to the campaign for the defending champions ended dramatically with a 3-0 defeat at Brighton in their last outing. The visitors, fifth in the table, can gauge their progress under Daniel Farke following heavy 5-0 and 4-0 defeats by the Gunners last season. The Yorkshire club sit three points behind Mikel Arteta’s hosts and are one of only five unbeaten clubs after five games. Barry Glendenning helms the blog with Paul MacInnes reporting.

Sarah Rendell keeps the updates flowing from the four mid-afternoon kick-offs, with Chelsea v Bournemouth front and centre of the live blog. Marco Rose’s winless side head to Stamford Bridge lying 17th, with three draws and two defeats from their first five matches. To add to his burden, the Cherries will be missing Alex Scott. Their star midfielder faces up to two months out with a thigh injury he suffered on England duty. Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea, who stand 10th and with the Premier League’s highest goals against total of 12, are looking to end their three-match winless run in all competitions against a side whom they remain unbeaten in their past nine top-flight meetings.

Spurs have had a lamentable start to the season; United not much better. Tottenham sit rock bottom of the table, with just two points. A team assembled for the princely sum of £300m are playing like paupers. Surely the only way is up for Roberto De Zerbi and his torpid team? After keeping clean sheets against Nottingham Forest and Everton, Aston Villa ripped their defence apart last time out. United, meanwhile, have five points from their opening five games – their joint fewest at this stage of a Premier League season and hardly the start expected under Michael Carrick after their barnstorming finish last season. United are without a win in their past three Premier League games. Scott Murray brings the noise, with Jamie Jackson and John Brewin reporting from Old Trafford.

Tom Bassam expects to be kept busy on Sunday morning, providing all the build up to a day of weighty action. Yes, the 4.30pm Premier League kick-off at Anfield tops the bill, but there’s plenty of intrigue on offer elsewhere as Crystal Palace meet Nottingham Forest and Hull face Everton. There’s a tantalising local match-up in the Championship with the midday Southcoastico as Southampton host Hampshire neighbours Portsmouth. In the Scottish Premiership, Celtic travel to Motherwell’s Fir Park. The Steelmen lost their three matches before the international break against Dundee, Aberdeen and Rangers, while the visitors matched them by losing back-to-back matches against Rangers on either side of a defeat to Ferencvaros in the Europa League. Martin O’Neill’s side are desperately looking over their shoulders with Rangers closing the gap to two points at the top of the table. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your views.

Rob Smyth and James Wallace pick up the live blog baton for day three of the first Test.

Max Verstappen’s victory from pole, with fastest lap, at last weekend’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia came 16 races into F1’s new rules era ⁠and exceeded expectations for those who doubted ⁠the British-based team could match Mercedes and Ferrari by building one of the most complex power units in motorsport history from scratch. Sepang was also the first pole of 2026 achieved by a car not powered by a Mercedes engine. Mercedes have won 11 of the 16 races, Ferrari and McLaren two each. Audi and returning Honda are still far off the pace. There is hope then for the Red Bulls that the corner has been turned after months of frustration. Daniel Harris tracks the action, lap by lap, with Giles Richards reporting.

What kind of reception awaits Oliver Glasner on his return to Sellhurst Park – hostile or huggy? The Austrian flounced out of Crystal Palace at the end of last season, only to turn up at a club with a revolving door of managers in Nottingham Forest. After winning the FA Cup, the Community Shield and the Conference League while at the helm in south London, there was bemusement among Eagles fans when his next stop turned out to be the City Ground. After Steve Cooper’s exit in December 2023, Forest churned through four managers before Glasner’s arrival. The hosts have lost both of their Premier League games at Selhurst Park this season while the visitors have only lost one of their last seven away league games. Also on John Brewin’s blog radar is Hull against Everton, an enticing clash of eighth versus seventh, with the visitors unbeaten in their past five games.

Batten down the hatches: City’s first game back after an international window dominated by the guilty verdict in the club’s long-running case with the Premier League arrives. It just had to be at Anfield. City have long considered a trip to Liverpool the most fearsome away game of the season. It just got even tougher, with Erling Haaland, Rayan Cherki and the rest likely entering a cauldron of fury and indignation. Liverpool might consider themselves the team who suffered most from the slew of City’s financial misdemeanours between 2009 and 2018. Under Jürgen Klopp, Liverpool won the Premier League in 2020 but also finished second to Pep Guardiola’s City by one point in both 2019 and 2022. So expect indignant Liverpool fans to be seething inside and outside of Anfield. Rob Smyth helms the blog with David Hytner, Andy Hunter and Will Unwin our reporting team.

Gridiron fanatics are rapidly latching on to Graham Searles’ weekly live blog covering the best of Sunday evening’s NFL action. In addition to the five 6pm kick-offs, he’ll be covering the San Francisco 49ers v Seattle Seahawks later. Games between the Hawks and Niners are typically intense, as the two rivals often compete for NFC West supremacy. The Seahawks came out on top last season, winning a week-18 showdown for the division title and a blowout in the divisional round against the 49ers before winning the Super Bowl on San Francisco’s home field with a raucous celebration in their rival’s locker room. The teams will meet for the first time in the 2026 season when unbeaten San Francisco (4-0) visit Seattle (3-1).

The Supreme Court Justice and the Columbus Statue

The New York Times October 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Peter S. Canellos

Mr. Canellos is the author of “Revenge for the Sixties: Sam Alito and the Triumph of the Conservative Legal Movement.”

The Chambersburg neighborhood of Trenton, N. J., was once a thriving Italian American community, a Little Italy of square brick tenements and bungalows in the shadow of the giant smoke-belching Roebling steel plant.

Today, it’s still an immigrant enclave, although the recent arrivals are mostly from Central America. The plant shut down, and what remains of its 20th-century heyday is the Italian Peoples Bakery (“goes back to 1936”) and a curious stump of a platform where a statue once stood. A close inspection reveals that the stump is in the shape of a boat.

On a Sunday in October 1959, the whole neighborhood, including the future Supreme Court justice Samuel Alito and his family, stood alongside church leaders and diplomats to erect an image of their hero, Christopher Columbus, peering from the prow of a ship as he approaches the New World.

For the Alitos, this was a moment of pride. Trenton’s vibrant Italian American community was asserting its place in America. As Justice Alito would later put it in interviews, Italian immigrants who arrived in the United States in the early 20th century, including his relatives, were derided as foreigners. They embraced Columbus, who was born in Genoa and whose ships reached the New World more than a century before the Mayflower, because they were his countrymen. His story proved that they belonged.

The statue remained in Columbus Park for more than 60 years until Trenton’s mayor, Reed Gusciora, decided in 2020, after repeated acts of vandalism left the statue doused in red paint, to remove it, and the park was renamed Unity Square Park.

Most Italians had left Chambersburg by 2020. Many of the town’s residents, chiefly Black and Central American, decried Columbus as a symbol of slavery and genocide. “What we know about Columbus simply makes his image a poor fit for a city that is as diverse as Trenton,” the mayor said at the time.

But what the statue symbolized has not been forgotten. As it lay in pieces in a warehouse, a six-year saga ensued in which local Italian Americans, supported by a valuable ally — Justice Alito himself — feuded with the city to restore it. After years of patient advocacy, Italian Americans in Trenton have agreed to compromise. They are negotiating to acquire the statue and re-erect it outside a Knights of Columbus hall in neighboring Hamilton.

But despite optimism surrounding this year’s Columbus Day, the city has yet to approve the transfer.

Justice Alito was 9 years old when he attended the ceremony unveiling the statue. His father and his grandparents on both sides of his family had immigrated from southern Italy and settled in Chambersburg. In New Jersey, his parents struggled with poverty and discrimination while they worked their way through college and graduate school, his mother becoming a school principal and his father the longtime head of the New Jersey Office of Legislative Services. Their American journey has long been celebrated in speeches and interviews by Justice Alito, who felt personally affronted when he heard about the challenges to the statue.

Gilda Rorro, a longtime leader in the New Jersey Italian community, began lobbying to reinstate the statue in Chambersburg after discussing the matter with an upset Justice Alito in 2020. She said she read aloud a statement written by the justice to the Trenton City Council arguing that the statue does not symbolize Columbus’s deeds but rather the immigrants themselves.

“Poor Italian peasants made a long and difficult journey leaving everything they knew behind. And while many people in this country did not accept them, they wanted to claim that they had a rightful place here,” Dr. Rorro said, quoting Justice Alito’s message to the City Council in 2020. “That is what the statue symbolizes, and removing it is an insult to the Italian American community, tantamount to saying that their experience, all that they endured and contributed, accounts for nothing.”

A sitting Supreme Court justice lending his credibility to one side in a local dispute with painful racial and ethnic dimensions might raise a few eyebrows, but Justice Alito has a history of nudging the boundaries of judicial rectitude. That same year, he delivered a speech to the Federalist Society that denounced Covid-era restrictions that might have come before the court. Four years later, he declined to recuse himself from cases involving President Trump after his wife flew what appeared to be pro-Trump flags over their houses.

But his advocacy for the Columbus statue reflects something else: a personal project that reveals his views on immigration.

In the term that ended in June, Justice Alito was the author of opinions that drew sharp criticism from immigrant groups, marking him as the court’s most prolific defender of Mr. Trump’s crackdown on immigration. At the same time, as the Columbus dispute demonstrates, he has been an effusive defender of the immigrant experience of his fellow Italian Americans.

Justice Alito has never stinted in expressing his Italian pride. His undergraduate thesis at Princeton University was about Italy’s Constitution. He visits the country frequently in the summer. He paid tribute to the heroic Italian prosecutor Giovanni Falcone at the Supreme Court, and decried in a university talk the TV hit “The Sopranos” for furthering offensive stereotypes of Italians.

On the court, however, he seems to be notably unmoved by tales of hardship and sacrifice by other groups of immigrants. In 2018, he joined a 5-to-4 majority that rejected challenges to Mr. Trump’s so-called Muslim ban, finding that the president’s proclamation was based on nonreligious factors. In the 2024-25 term, Justice Alito showed deference to the second Trump administration when, for instance, he wrote a fiery dissent to an emergency order backed by seven of his colleagues that blocked Mr. Trump from deporting Venezuelans without a hearing.

In the last court term, Justice Alito’s immigration opinions stood out even further. He wrote for a 6-to-3 majority in overturning a lower-court order prohibiting U. S. border guards from intercepting migrants with potentially lawful claims to refugee status before they cross into the country. “A running back does not arrive in the end zone when he reaches the one-yard line,” Justice Alito argued, in ruling that the refugee statute doesn’t apply if an applicant is forcibly deterred even a few feet from the border.

Justice Alito wrote for the same majority in rejecting challenges to Mr. Trump’s removal of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians. Despite Mr. Trump’s having once called Haiti and Somalia “shithole countries” (and suggesting the United States should seek more immigrants from Norway and Sweden), Justice Alito rejected a bias claim based on the Constitution’s equal protection clause. Mr. Trump’s comments, he wrote, were not “overtly racial.”

Then, in the June 30 decision rejecting Mr. Trump’s order to deny birthright citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants, Justice Alito dissented. While the court’s majority, including two conservatives, cited the plain meaning of the 14th Amendment in granting citizenship to anyone born in the United States, Justice Alito insisted that the framers had not anticipated “birth tourists.” The court’s granting legal status to children of undocumented parents, he argued, would “degrade” American citizenship.

Earlier generations of Trentonians used similar terms in attacking Italian immigrants. News stories expressed concern over everything from “Many Foreign Names on Business Signs,” as a 1904 Trenton Sunday Advertiser headline put it, to excessive drinking and violence. A local newspaper, The Daily True American, put it bluntly in 1903: “Little Italy Must Keep Place Clean.”

Jeffrey Laurenti, a Chambersburg resident who knew the justice during their high school years and shares the goal of reinstating the Columbus statue, interpreted Justice Alito’s legal opinions as reflecting his “larger view of executive power” more than animus toward the immigrant plaintiffs.

But Justice Alito doesn’t always defend assertions of presidential power. In 2023, he alone supported the right of states to challenge President Joe Biden’s immigration priorities. And he has sometimes gone beyond legal theory to express the need for justice for individuals like a grieving father who was subjected to protesters at his son’s funeral and religious Christians who oppose same-sex marriage and thus risk being labeled “bigots.”

Justice Alito hasn’t expressed similar empathy for today’s Chambersburg residents. Susan Ryan, who produced a film on Chambersburg called “From the ’Burg to the Barrio,” has noted that the Central Americans whose foreign-sounding names are on the same storefronts where Italian names once appeared have much in common. The two generations of immigrants, she said, have similarities “in terms of their interests in family, food and work, and religion.”

The way Justice Alito talks about Italian immigrants often involves overcoming obstacles, not efforts to change their status before the law. In his telling, Italians seized on Columbus for practical reasons, since the great explorer was already celebrated by non-Italians.

“When Italian immigrants arrived here, they were often scorned,” Justice Alito told We the Italians, an online magazine. “Many thought they were hopelessly backward and could never fit in. Looking for a way to say that they did belong, Italian Americans, exercising a bit of furbezza, simply latched onto the Columbus symbol that the general population already knew and valued.”

That is the symbol that stood tall and proud over Chambersburg for 61 years, and the Italian Americans who wish to restore it have every right to invest their pride in its restoration.

“Furbezza,” more often spelled as “furbizia,” has a very useful meaning. According to the Cambridge Italian-English dictionary, it translates to “cunning, craftiness, shrewdness.” It is a vehicle for exercising your smarts.

It is a good way of taking care of yourself and your own.

Peter S. Canellos is a former editorial page editor of The Boston Globe and a former executive editor of Politico.

Four Hours and Three Minutes at Cornell

The New York Times October 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

David French

By David French

Opinion Columnist

Four hours and three minutes.

That’s the total time that elapsed between 1:42 a. m. — the apparent moment when a Cornell student put the words “free pussy” in a group Snapchat message that could be seen by dozens of members of the Cornell chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity — and 5:45 a. m. on Oct. 20, 2024, roughly the time when Jane Doe says she lost consciousness, bringing her ordeal to an end.

What happened during that time period? Multiple men came into the room and — according to a lawsuit filed by Jane Doe last month and various documents disclosed in the case — at least some of the men snorted drugs off her body and had oral and vaginal sex with her, all when she was unquestionably very drunk and very high.

As dreadful as all that is, I’m also interested in what didn’t happen. No one, apparently, acted to end the encounter. Instead — as the group message indicates — men celebrated. “I fucking love chi phi,” one brother wrote. “Like you can walk in and whip it out,” he said later. “Shop still open?” asked another.

I want to be careful here and not draw a straight line from our porn-saturated culture to this dreadful incident. Sexual depravity existed long before pornography was ubiquitous, but this encounter was almost a textbook example of what porn teaches men about sex. It’s not about intimacy. It’s not a manifestation of love, much less care. Instead, sex is an entirely self-regarding and inherently exploitative act.

I’m not writing this column to adjudicate legal guilt. The facts are complicated, and it is almost always difficult to know precisely what happened when copious amounts of drugs and alcohol are involved.

Hovering over the entire case is a New York legal standard that draws a sharp distinction between voluntary and involuntary intoxication. Put simply, if you’re voluntarily intoxicated but not “physically helpless” (passed out, for example), proving incapacitation becomes extremely difficult. But if you’re involuntarily intoxicated, you are considered incapacitated — even when your level of intoxication is the same as that of the voluntarily intoxicated person.

Think of it like this: If the Cornell men forced Jane Doe to drink shots or snort ketamine, then, in the state’s eyes, she’d be incapacitated. But if she voluntarily drank and consumed ketamine to the same level of intoxication, she would not be considered incapacitated.

This makes little sense. Calling intoxication voluntary doesn’t render intoxicated people more aware or capable of making informed decisions. They’re just as vulnerable to predation as they would be if, say, they were unknowingly served spiked fruit punch.

Any man of decency should recognize that the legal distinction (assuming he is aware of it) isn’t a grant of moral permission. And any man with any degree of moral fiber who saw that message should have immediately acted to end the encounter, even if it cost him the “brotherhood” he loves.

Last week, Christine Emba wrote a beautiful and compelling guest essay in our pages about the inadequacy of consent as the primary moral basis for sexual intimacy. It’s the legal base line, not a moral threshold. But what is the moral threshold?

Conservative Christians like me often respond with a pat answer: marriage. But even that’s inadequate and incomplete. Marital sex can be every bit as abusive and exploitative as an encounter in a frat house. Instead of consent, I’d suggest a different standard, one that applies not just to sex in marriage — and not just to sex alone — but to all of our human interactions.

Let’s talk about care.

In other words, we should constantly ask ourselves, “If I cared for this person, what would I do?” Even if an obviously drunk or high person is asking you for sex (though whether that happened in this case is disputed, especially as events unfolded later in the evening) — and even if you’re powerfully attracted to that person — if you truly cared for the person would you initiate or engage in an encounter that any sentient person knows might be deeply regretted the next morning, the next day or the next week?

Is an orgasm so sacred to you that you can’t wait until sobriety to have sex?

And if you see a message like the Snapchat message at Cornell, imagine what you’d do if you actually cared for the person they’re talking about. Would you not put STOP in all caps in the chat and race to that room? Or do we delegate any concern or regard for people like Jane Doe to someone who might have a closer relationship to her?

It can take an immense amount of courage to actually care enough about another human being to intervene — especially if a person you don’t know needs protection from people you do know. Earlier this month, just as new details about the Cornell case seemed to be hitting the news every day, we covered the My Lai massacre during the Vietnam War in the Law of War class I teach at Lipscomb University in Nashville.

For those who don’t remember, the My Lai massacre was one of the worst episodes in American military history. American soldiers in Vietnam went on a killing spree, murdering hundreds of innocent civilians.

Obviously, the massacre was far more extreme than anything that happened at the Chi Phi house, but I bring it up for a simple reason — to introduce you to a man named Hugh Thompson.

Thompson is an American hero. He was the Army helicopter pilot who saw the massacre from the air, immediately radioed an alarm and landed his aircraft, placing it between his own brothers-in-arms and a small group of innocent civilians they were pursuing. He even ordered his crew to open fire on American soldiers if they tried to kill the people he was protecting.

He cared for innocent people he did not know, and probably would never know, and he cared for them enough to risk his life and the rejection and scorn of his own brotherhood to save their lives. In the process, he also showed care for his brothers-in-arms — he stopped them from continuing to commit the most heinous of crimes.

Think about how much less courage it would have taken to act that night at Cornell. Then consider again that no one intervened. To them, “Free pussy” wasn’t an alarm bell; it was an invitation.

Details of the Cornell case emerged just as we learned more about the criminal case against Andrew Tate, one of the most celebrated influencers in the manosphere. He made his fortune (such as it is) in part through pornography, by reportedly coercing women into becoming cam girls online.

Now he’s facing charges in the United Kingdom, including rape, human trafficking and possessing extreme pornography (including images of bestiality). This man was celebrated in parts of right-wing America.

In fact, as ProPublica reported in 2025, Paul Ingrassia, a White House official (and a former lawyer for Tate and his brother) asked Department of Homeland Security officials to return Tate’s electronic devices to him when they were seized upon his entry to the country.

Chi Phi at Cornell, which was shut down in 2024 and remains barred from campus, represents the culture that Andrew Tate — and countless others like him — have built. We do not have to declare what happened that terrible night illegal to know that it was depraved.

Thompson and Tate sit at opposite ends of the moral spectrum. They represent the angel and devil on the shoulders of young men. One offers aggression without virtue, sex without love and money without meaning. The other laid down his life for people he did not know.

But to put things in language that many young men will understand: Hugh Thompson was strong. Andrew Tate is weak. He’s a slave to his desires and all his aggression is directed at those who are more vulnerable than he is.

“Courage,” C. S. Lewis wrote in one of my favorite quotes, “is not simply one of the virtues but the form of every virtue at the testing point, which means, at the point of highest reality.”

How do we know what courage is? When we see a man risk himself to care for another person, that’s courage. The legal judgment may be uncertain, but the moral verdict is already in. On the most traumatic night in a young woman’s life, a good man could not be found.

Saudi Arabia Has Few Options as Houthis Aim at Heart of Its Ambitions

The New York Times October 11, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

News analysis

Three deadly attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen on an airport in the Saudi capital underscored the asymmetrical nature of their conflict with the kingdom.

By Vivian Nereim and Lisa Friedman

Reporting from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

After the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman faces growing pressure to find a way to stop the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen from firing missiles and drones at his country.

Yet the prince, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, has few options as he confronts an asymmetrical conflict with an adversary that has become stronger since he led a disastrous war against it a decade ago, analysts say.

The Houthis have carried out three fatal attacks on an international airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, over the past week. Those included a strike on a passenger terminal on Saturday that killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300, many of them critically, forcing officials to suspend operations at the airport. Saudi officials did not specify the nature of the attack, but a Gulf official and a U. S. official briefed on the strike said that the Houthis hit a terminal at the airport with a cruise missile.

The attacks, which continued on Sunday according to Saudi civil aviation authorities, have brought the kingdom’s faraway war in Yemen home, stripping Saudi Arabia’s civilians of the sense of security that they had largely maintained throughout years of a Saudi-led bombing campaign in neighboring Yemen.

The Houthis say their strikes are retaliatory. They have hit at the heart of Prince Mohammed’s ambitions to transform Saudi Arabia from an insular, oil-dependent nation into a global hub for business and tourism.

There is no easy path forward for the crown prince. Reaching a political resolution with the Houthis has become more difficult as their demands have grown, and attempting to vanquish the group militarily is unlikely to succeed, analysts say. The militia has little to lose and has become increasingly battle-hardened after repeated confrontations with more powerful enemies.

Saudi Arabia is receiving significant military support from the United States to fight the Houthis, including targeting assistance and aerial refueling. President Trump said he would “make a decision” about intervening more directly in the conflict after Saturday’s attack. Mr. Trump, however, carried out a bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, and declared a swift victory after the United States burned through weapons and munitions at a rate of about $1 billion in the first month alone.

“The only realistic solution for the Saudis is an end to the Iranian-American war, in which the U. S. gets the Iranians to commit the Houthis to an end of hostilities as part of the overall deal,” said F. Gregory Gause, a Saudi specialist at the Middle East Institute, a Washington-based research group. “Unfortunately for the Saudis, it is not clear how much President Trump listens to them on this.”

The Saudi government will probably try to weaken the group before negotiating a deal to end the conflict, said Yasmine Farouk, the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula project director at the International Crisis Group, a research firm.

From Saudi Arabia’s perspective, it is too early to enter talks while the Houthis still “retain the capacity to launch” such attacks, Ms. Farouk said.

In recent days, the Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, has issued repeated warnings to airlines and travelers against using Saudi airports, declaring them a “theater of operations for our forces.”

The attacks on the airport came ahead of several large political and business events in Saudi Arabia, including Prince Mohammed’s flagship annual investment summit, during which world leaders, billionaires and executives typically descend upon Riyadh. It is unclear whether high-profile guests will feel safe enough to attend now.

“The problem for the Saudis is that they experience more damage from Houthi strikes on their infrastructure than the other way around,” Mr. Gause said. “A strike on Riyadh Airport could lead someone thinking about investing in the country to reconsider.”

In contrast, much of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, which the Houthis control, has already been destroyed.

The attack on Saturday was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since a suicide bombing at a mosque in 2015, and the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran in February.

The Houthis rose to power in 2014, when they took over Sanaa, routing Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

Soon after, Prince Mohammed, in one of his first acts as Saudi Arabia’s 29-year-old minister of defense, pledged to restore the Yemeni government by declaring war against the Houthis, at the time a ragtag group of rebels.

The prince has since consolidated his power inside Saudi Arabia and beyond. Yet the Houthis have also become stronger and more self-sufficient, and they pose one of the most intractable challenges to his plans. The militia, which rules over its impoverished territory with an iron fist, appears to be calculating that it can inflict more pain on Saudi Arabia than the kingdom can inflict on it, analysts say.

The Saudi-led bombing campaign a decade ago precipitated one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and contributed to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people in Yemen from violence, hunger and disease. Rights groups said the campaign disproportionately targeted civilians. In one of the most notorious strikes, which spurred international condemnation, a Saudi fighter jet bombed a school bus in 2018, killing 44 children and 10 adults.

Yet the Houthis survived, cementing their power over northern Yemen.

A truce in 2022 brought a fragile peace to the country, until the United States and Israel attacked Iran more than seven months ago, sparking a regional war.

Tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began to escalate in July, when an airstrike hit the international airport in Sanaa. The militia accused Saudi Arabia of launching the attack. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government claimed responsibility and said it had been acting to prevent an unauthorized Iranian plane from landing. Analysts, however, say it is unlikely that the Yemeni government, which depends heavily on Saudi Arabia for financial and military support, acted on its own.

After that attack, the Houthis, who have long bristled at restrictions on their airspace that are enforced by Saudi Arabia, announced that they intended to enforce a “blockade for blockade” policy. They declared an embargo on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, which has become an important alternative route for Saudi oil exports after the Iran war disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Yemen’s civil war reignited, with fierce clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces allied with the Yemeni government. That culminated last week, when the Yemeni government announced a new offensive against the Houthis, promising to push them out of the territory they had seized over the past 12 years. Saudi Arabia announced a new bombing campaign to support the government.

Despite the escalating conflict, Saudi officials have sought to maintain a sense of normalcy. The authorities kept Riyadh airport open after two deadly attacks, and closed it only after the mass casualty event on Saturday.

“The Saudis have been claiming that they are the great kingdom and that ragtag militia cannot possibly threaten their security,” said Abdulghani Al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sana’a Center, a Yemeni research organization. “They’re still keeping the facade despite the fact that it’s been totally ripped to shreds.”

On Sunday, while foreign diplomats in Riyadh received warnings of a potential missile bound for the capital, advising them to shelter in place, a meeting of energy ministers in the city went forward as planned. The only announcement from organizers asked attendees to take their seats as they awaited the arrival of Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, the Saudi energy minister.

“It is sad not to have all of our friends, but understandably they have their own precautionary measures which did not enable them to be with us,” Prince Abdulaziz told the crowd.

Bob McNally, the president of Rapidan Energy Group, a Washington-based research group, said he arrived “safely and soundly” on Saturday. But about 30 minutes after he left Riyadh airport, it was struck.

Still, Mr. McNally said he was not surprised that the Saudi government was moving forward with the events.

“Saudi has a lot invested in this, literally and figuratively, and they’re determined to go ahead,” he said.

Kate Kelly and Jonathan Swan contributed reporting from Washington.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Lisa Friedman is a business correspondent covering energy for The New York Times.

Saudi and Yemeni Airports Hit in New Round of Strikes

The New York Times October 11, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, was struck a day after suffering a devastating attack. The Houthis said Saudi aircraft hit the Yemeni capital’s airport.

By Euan Ward and Vivian Nereim

Reporting from Beirut, Lebanon and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

The Saudi and Yemeni capitals were rocked by new strikes on Sunday, a day after the Iran-backed Houthi militia carried out a devastating attack on the Saudi capital's airport, the kingdom’s deadliest attack in over a decade.

Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen, said on social media that an “unidentified projectile” had struck the airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, causing a fire on Sunday. The Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement that the latest strike at the airport, King Khalid International, which suspended operations on Saturday, had caused injuries and that damage assessments were underway.

In Yemen, Houthi-run media reported on Sunday that Saudi aircraft had struck the international airport in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa. The Houthi-run health ministry said that a child had also been killed in a strike on a residential building in the capital. Saudi airstrikes have killed 91 people since Sept. 3, mostly women and children, according to Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the ministry.

The Houthi attack on the airport in Riyadh followed a spate of increasingly brazen and deadly strikes by the militia on vital Saudi infrastructure in recent days, which have rattled the kingdom and frayed nerves in its capital.

On Saturday, those attacks culminated with a strike by the Houthis on a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh, the deadliest attack in a Gulf Arab country since the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February. That strike killed at least 12 people and injured hundreds, the Saudi authorities said. On Sunday, the Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said an Indian national injured in the attack had also died.

Saudi officials did not specify the nature of the attack on Saturday, but a Gulf official and a U. S. official briefed on the strike said that the Houthis had struck the airport with a cruise missile.

The latest escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began in July, when the militia accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa airport while an Iranian plane was trying to land. Fighting intensified last month with the Houthis seizing Yemen’s Red Sea coast from the Saudi-supported government. Backed by Saudi warplanes, Yemeni government forces launched a counteroffensive last week, plunging the country back into a full-blown war.

The metastasizing conflict, which has imperiled Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to become a global business and tourism hub, has eroded the sense of security that Saudis had largely maintained through years of war in neighboring Yemen. On Sunday, schools across Riyadh notified parents that in-person lessons would be canceled for the week. Many workplaces also told employees they could work from home.

Racked by years of conflict, the Houthis have little to lose by comparison and have become battle-hardened after repeated confrontations with more powerful, wealthier enemies.

With financial and military support from Iran, the Houthis have invested heavily in weapons manufacturing in recent years, allowing them to mount increasingly sophisticated cross-border strikes, analysts say.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.

Euan Ward is a Times reporter covering Lebanon and Syria. He is based in Beirut.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

How the White House Manufactured a Narrative About a Trump Aide’s Call Logs

The New York Times October 11, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A release of selected records from the classified documents inquiry is a case study in how omitting context can create political ammunition.

By Charlie Savage

Charlie Savage writes about national security and legal policy. He reported from Washington.

On the afternoon of Friday, Oct. 2, the White House invited a mix of mainstream and right-wing reporters to an online briefing about “weaponization.” A briefer previewed records the White House planned to release from the investigation of Donald J. Trump’s retention of classified documents while out of office, and his obstruction of their retrieval.

The files reflected scattered topics. Among them: an internal debate over probable cause to search Mr. Trump’s social club and residence, Mar-a-Lago; plans to execute any search warrant while Mr. Trump and his family were away; and the collection of phone logs of Mr. Trump’s top aide, Susie Wiles.

Most facts were already known or minutiae, and mainstream reporters ignored the files when the White House posted them on Monday. But Trump allies pushed an alarmist and decontextualized interpretation through the conservative information ecosystem. By Wednesday, a reporter from Trump ally and MyPillow founder Mike Lindell’s website asked Mr. Trump about it in the Oval Office. The president thanked her for the question, denouncing the inquiry as “weaponization.”

“They did things to people that were associated with us that nobody should have been able to do, and it all came out just recently in the files,” Mr. Trump said.

The episode shows how the Trump administration and its allies selectively disclose government files, omitting context to discredit investigations that led to Mr. Trump’s federal indictment and that anger his supporters. As the midterm elections approach, it also shows how a grievance narrative can be manufactured and inserted into national political discourse.

The Oct. 2 briefing was led by John Solomon, a former mainstream journalist who is now employed by the White House as a so-called special government employee. He has been active for years in presenting pro-Trump narratives, including during the 2019 events related to Ukraine that led to Mr. Trump’s first impeachment. In 2022, Mr. Trump named him his representative to the National Archives so he could gain access to records related to the investigation into the 2016 Trump campaign’s ties to Russia.

Mr. Solomon chairs a White House “transparency” task force that has released batches of government documents on more than half a dozen occasions since July. The documents appear to have been selected to bolster narratives Mr. Trump has promoted, including those that cast doubt on the integrity of U. S. elections and seek to discredit investigations into his conduct.

In an interview, Mr. Solomon acknowledged conducting the briefings. He said that he is unpaid and has no security clearance, but that about half-dozen task force officials do. He said he suggests categories to search, and task force officials sift through “millions of pages” for responsive documents. The White House counsel then declassifies them.

Mr. Solomon said he is briefed in advance on the files’ contents, but sees them only shortly before briefing other journalists. He described himself as a “pool reporter” — the term for a reporter chosen to share information with a larger group of news organizations when there is not enough room for all to fit — seeking more information for the public. He said he always encourages journalists to do their own reporting.

“It isn’t an effort at subterfuge,” he said. “It isn’t an effort at not giving you something in context. It’s giving you what the government made available and then giving you a chance to go find the rest of the story.”

Mainstream reporters have only occasionally found news in Mr. Solomon’s presentations. But once he completes his role as White House briefer, he writes articles based on the same material for his website, JustTheNews. com. In this case, his article — like his briefing — presented known information as revelations and omitted key context about new details. Its narrative entered a right-wing media echo chamber.

Mr. Solomon highlighted a paragraph from an F. B. I. Washington field office email from July 2022 saying that the office, unlike Justice Department counterespionage prosecutors, “does not believe” the available evidence established probable cause that Mr. Trump was still illegally keeping more classified documents at Mar-a-Lago. At issue was whether there was sufficient evidence to justify a search warrant.

On a podcast the following Monday with the right-wing commentator Benny Johnson, Mr. Solomon said the first of “three major revelations in the documents” was that before the Mar-a-Lago raid, “very senior F. B. I. officials, including an assistant director, raised concerns that the F. B. I. had not met the probable cause standard for authorizing a raid,” but “were overruled.”

That paragraph was not a revelation. It has been public since last December, when the F. B. I. gave Senator Charles E. Grassley, Republican of Iowa, files containing it verbatim. Mr. Grassley and conservative news outlets had highlighted it then just as Mr. Solomon did in his briefing and Monday reporting.

Mr. Solomon’s presentation, both times, also omitted key context: The field office’s legal doubts came before Mar-a-Lago surveillance footage emerged that showed a Trump aide moving boxes from a storage area before a lawyer came to search it for subpoenaed classified files. The additional evidence resolved legal concerns about probable cause.

The Washington field office’s assistant director, Steven D’Antuono, has testified that he and his team continued to urge officials to try again to obtain Mr. Trump’s voluntary compliance with the subpoena before escalating to a search — but for prudential, not legal, reasons. (The eventual search recovered more than 100 classified documents that Mr. Trump had not turned over when purporting to comply with the subpoena.)

A more complicated example involves Ms. Wiles’s phone logs. She ran Mr. Trump’s political action committee while he was out of office, then his 2024 campaign. She is now the White House chief of staff.

The files showed that in early to mid-2023, investigators — operating under Jack Smith, the special counsel appointed to oversee the federal inquiries into Mr. Trump — logged Ms. Wiles’s calls using a device known as a pen register, which creates a record of who called whom and when, but does not collect conversation content. The F. B. I. can get a court order to use one if a judge agrees that a low legal standard — mere “relevance” to an investigation — is met.

The collection of her call logs was already known. Court filings in 2024 showed that her phone records since January 2021 had been subpoenaed from a phone company. (The material identified her as “Person 49,” but accompanying excerpts from her April 7, 2023, investigative interview pointed to her identity.) Kash Patel, the F. B. I. director, told Reuters in February that the agency had subpoenaed Ms. Wiles’s phone logs in 2022 and 2023.

The actual news, then, was subtle: Investigators had used a pen register in addition to subpoenas, meaning they had logged her calls in real time in addition to collecting logs of her past calls. By omitting that context, right-wing news accounts created the sensational impression that the scrutiny of her call activity itself was a revelation.

The White House did not release case-file material explaining why officials and a judge might have deemed Ms. Wiles’s call logs relevant to the investigation, leaving that to imagination or insinuation. But two reasons for investigators’ interest in her are known.

She was a witness. According to the indictment, Mr. Trump showed her a classified map, evidence he knew he possessed such records. More broadly, she oversaw his political action committee’s hiring and payment of lawyers provided to his employees who were also witnesses.

Investigators suspected that this could have been a scheme to monitor and shape testimony by the employee-witnesses about Mr. Trump, although they did not find sufficient evidence to charge any such conspiracy.

The indictment, for example, said a decision to pay for the defense of a Mar-a-Lago property manager — eventually Mr. Trump’s co-defendant, charged with conspiring to cover up the box movements — followed confirmation in a Signal chat with Ms. Wiles that the worker remained “loyal” to Mr. Trump and would do nothing to affect their relationship.

The “Person 49” material released in 2024 included Ms. Wiles’s call logs with Stanley Woodward Jr., now a senior Justice Department official. Mr. Trump’s political action committee hired him to represent both the Trump aide who moved the boxes — who also became a co-defendant — and a computer worker at Mar-a-Lago.

But the computer worker later replaced Mr. Woodward with his own lawyer, then told investigators for the first time that Mr. Trump, via the property manager, had pushed him to delete surveillance footage of the box movements, according to the indictment.

The court files released in 2024 also show that in her April 7, 2023, interview, a prosecutor pressed Ms. Wiles on whether free lawyers were contingent on employees not divulging damaging things about Mr. Trump. She “unequivocally” denied it.

The newly released material included F. B. I. reports flagging Ms. Wiles’s “contacts of interests”: about 20 lawyers, half a dozen journalists, political advisers and Mr. Trump. There were bursts of such calls around key moments, like her April 7 interview.

The names of lawyers are redacted. Mr. Solomon described investigators as having “tracked Trump defense lawyers’ calls.” That framing is misleading; they were tracking Ms. Wiles’s calls, not logging the lawyers’ calls with other people. It is not clear from the files, moreover, who each lawyer’s client was. Some might have been representing employee-witnesses.

Ms. Wiles’s six reporter contacts included Mr. Solomon, who left his name unredacted; names of reporters at ABC News, CNN, The New York Times, Politico and The Washington Post were blacked out. In promoting the files, Mr. Solomon expressed incredulity at how that could be of legitimate interest to investigators.

The missing context: As news reports recounted nonpublic investigative developments like grand jury subpoenas and sealed court rulings, Mr. Trump, his campaign spokesman and sympathetic commentators kept blaming Mr. Smith’s team for the leaks, accusing them of prosecutorial misconduct. (Unlike prosecutors, subpoena recipients may discuss grand jury matters.)

After publishing his account Monday morning, Mr. Solomon appeared on right-wing podcasts, including Stephen K. Bannon’s and Mr. Johnson’s, repeating his decontextualized account and suggesting the activity was unconstitutional.

By afternoon, other right-wing outlets emphasized another released file. It showed that when searching Mar-a-Lago was first proposed in May 2022, an F. B. I. official’s to-do list included determining travel plans for Mr. Trump, his wife Melania and their 16-year-old son Barron, all of whom lived there part of the year.

In context, officials wanted to do any search while the entire family was away, to keep it low key. Out of context, this was presented in sinister terms as the F. B. I. “tracking” Melania and a child. Around 4 p. m., for example, a Newsmax host opened an interview by asking the defense lawyer Alan Dershowitz if he objected to Mr. Smith and the F. B. I. having “tracked” Melania and Barron Trump. He called it “terrible.”

Late that afternoon, the National News Desk of Sinclair, a conservative owner of many local stations, distributed a similar segment for the evening newscasts of its stations. Fox News posted a similar article, but included the context for checking the Trumps’ travel plans.

The New York Post went further, inaccurately reporting: “Biden F. B. I. tracked Melania and Barron Trump’s travel — and even tapped Susie Wiles phone, documents show.”

The tapping claim was unambiguously false. The documents did not describe wiretapping, which means eavesdropping on private conversations. The legal difference is significant: Fourth Amendment privacy rights cover call content but not call logs, the Supreme Court has said.

Mr. Trump’s top policy aide, Stephen Miller, shared the New York Post headline and declared, “This was a seditious conspiracy against the Republic waged from within the Department of Justice and at the highest levels of government.” Representative Randy Fine, Republican of Florida, reposted it, too, declaring, “This is 1000 times worse than Watergate.”

That Tuesday evening, Mr. Trump’s social media account fanned the narrative, posting another right-wing site’s story: “Jack Smith Spied on Trump Staffer’s Communications and 20+ Lawyers: Report.” Then came Wednesday’s Oval Office question from Mr. Lindell’s reporter.

On Thursday morning, Fox News ran another article covering essentially the same ground as Monday’s.

And on Friday, the White House press office again invited selected reporters to another late afternoon briefing on “weaponization.” Another document release was coming.

Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

Charlie Savage writes about national security and legal policy for The Times.

In Unlikely Turn, Law and Order Heats Up L. A. Mayor’s Race

The New York Times October 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Two Democratic candidates choose opposite tacks on public safety and policing, seeking to corral undecided voters.

By Shawn Hubler

Like most big cities, Los Angeles has steep challenges: homelessness. Extreme weather. Housing affordability. Budget shortfalls. Law and order has for years been a relative bright spot. Not since the 1960s has the city experienced such a low homicide rate.

In an unlikely turn, however, public safety has emerged as an abrupt flashpoint in the city’s fierce mayoral contest. Last Tuesday, Nithya Raman, the challenger, vowed to replace the police chief if elected. Two days later, Mayor Karen Bass stood next to the chief as they applauded a sweeping crackdown on drug dealing on Skid Row.

Points of contention between the two Democrats have included 911 wait times, who would best handle security for the 2028 Olympics and who did or did not use the words “fascist liar” to describe the police chief.

The traditional Republican argument that Democrats are soft on crime has been losing steam this election cycle as crime rates drop across the country. G. O. P. candidates are neverthelessi making a go of it in places like Michigan, where they are going after Abdul El-Sayed in the Senate race, and North Carolina, where Roy Cooper has been under attack in another Senate contest.

In liberal Los Angeles, though, politics are more blue-on-blue, and the usual dividing lines on law and order have been scrambled this year as a Democrat and a democratic socialist take different tacks on the police force as they vie for the city’s top elected post.

In a year of resounding success for democratic socialists around the country, the election in the nation’s second-largest city is also poised to test whether that organization has shed its image of demonizing the police that lingers from the days of protests over George Floyd’s death.

Ms. Raman, 45, is a Harvard-educated policy expert backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, an organization that has argued that law enforcement receives too large a share of public funding. Ms. Bass, 73, has made her career as a progressive leader, but has been criticized for being too aligned with the police, whose union has endorsed her and spent significantly to back her re-election.

And as the two women, formerly allies, enter the homestretch, the city’s conventional political wisdom has been upended by a Trump-like Republican influencer who in June placed third in the mayoral primary, failing to make the runoff.

That influencer, Spencer Pratt, whose house burned in the Palisades fire, railed at City Hall and charged that Democrats had let the city degenerate into a wasteland of identity politics and homeless “zombies.” Brash and far-reaching, Mr. Pratt’s argument was also heavy on law and order, and he repeatedly pointed to the squalid streets of Skid Row in downtown Los Angeles as evidence that the city was being failed by liberals like Ms. Bass and Ms. Raman.

As they compete for his supporters, at stake is the 25.53 percent of the primary vote he won, a potentially pivotal bloc in a contest in which polls show roughly one voter in three is undecided.

“Spencer Pratt was a conservative outsider — he was tough on crime, and he wanted to shake up the system,” said Dan Schnur, a former Republican political consultant who now teaches political communications at several universities in California. And as polls show Ms. Raman starting to pull ahead, Mr. Schnur said, the two remaining candidates are each now vying for “exactly one half of Pratt’s persona.”

So Ms. Bass is now highlighting her record on crime as proof that she’s more centrist than Ms. Raman, Mr. Schnur said. And Ms. Raman, a relative unknown despite six years on the City Council, is seeking to show “that she’s more of an outsider than Bass.”

Those dynamics were on display last week as Ms. Raman’s campaign ramped up its social media to capitalize on her momentum, while Ms. Bass stood side by side with the Los Angeles police chief, Jim McDonnell, whom Ms. Raman has criticized for the department’s response last year during raucous immigration protests.

First Ms. Raman was filmed with a progressive online provocateur, Ed Choi, who asserted in the video that Los Angeles had become “extremely fascist” since Ms. Bass appointed Mr. McDonnell to lead the Police Department. Ms. Raman, who in 2024 had voted for Mr. McDonnell’s appointment, said the chief had not “met this moment,” noting the use of tear gas last year in quelling protests. Then she repeated a vow that if she is elected, she would hire “new leadership within the department.”

At the influencer’s behest, according to Ms. Raman’s campaign, she then joined him in reciting his tagline: “Only you can stop fascist liars!” As they spoke, an image of Ms. Bass appeared onscreen.

The video, which was posted by Ms. Raman’s campaign and then disavowed by her and removed when it drew backlash, was swiftly condemned by the mayor.

Ms. Bass charged that Ms. Raman did not “hold our police officers in high regard” and was “crossing the line” in “labeling them fascists.”

“It’s dangerous and extreme rhetoric, and it has no place in this city — let alone from someone trying to become mayor,” Ms. Bass said.

Ms. Raman’s campaign said she had been referring to federal immigration agents. Ms. Bass retorted that her challenger was “not ready for prime time.”

To suggest a search for a new police chief with the 2028 Olympics looming was “naïve,” Ms. Bass repeated in interviews and appearances with donors.

In an ironic twist, the Trump administration’s top prosecutor in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli — who is often at odds with city Democrats over arrests and detention of immigrants — praised Ms. Bass for her “leadership” in supporting a sweep of about two dozen suspected midlevel drug peddlers. He warned against Ms. Raman’s D. S. A. supporters, some of whom advocate defunding or disarming the police.

Ms. Raman’s campaign points out that she has not called for the police to be disarmed or defunded. Rather, she wants civilian mental health and homelessness professionals to handle more calls that do not require an armed response. But Mr. Schnur noted that in Los Angeles, the debate among voters is less about ideology or policy than livability.

“When Los Angeles voters think about crime, they tend to do so not in the context of danger but rather disorder,” he said. “Crime and homelessness and even traffic and potholes add to the impression of whether a city is working or not.”

In a statement, Ms. Raman’s campaign pointed out that “911 wait times have gone up under Mayor Bass” and that “we have 1,500 fewer officers than we did several years ago, even though we’re paying half a billion dollars more each year.”

“That,” she added, “is a failure of public safety management.”

In an interview, the mayor, whose approval ratings dropped precipitously last year after it emerged that she had been out of the country when the Palisades fire erupted, did not deny that she hoped voters would look at the tens of thousands of homeless people who have been moved indoors on her watch and the historic lows in the city’s crime rates. She asserted that safety and livability have been enhanced in Los Angeles since 2022, when she was elected amid the pandemic wreckage.

“I’m certainly hoping that they’ll look at both of us,” she said, referring to voters, and added, “And then say, is this what I really want?”

Shawn Hubler is The Times’s Los Angeles bureau chief, reporting on the news, trends and personalities of Southern California.

Trump Told Ukrainians to ‘Get a New President.’ Ukraine Shrugged.

The New York Times October 11, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump lashed out at President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries. Mr. Zelensky said he’ll stop — if Russia does too.

By Maria VarenikovaDzvinka Pinchuk and Ivan Nechepurenko

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

Ukraine on Sunday shrugged off President Trump’s suggestion that it ditch Volodymyr Zelensky as its president because it has continued to strike Russian oil refineries.

Mr. Trump has called out Mr. Zelensky for the strikes, blaming them for rising global energy prices. Ukraine needs “a new president,” he said on Saturday.

Mr. Zelensky shot back on Sunday that Ukraine was ready to stop striking Russian refineries, but only if Russia stopped striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. “Any de-escalation steps must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees,” he wrote on X.

On Saturday, after Mr. Trump made his comments, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said that Mr. Zelensky “has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide.”

“Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well,” he added.

Mr. Zelensky has previously said he would hold elections if Russia agreed to a cease-fire. In an interview with ABC News on Sunday, he said to hold a vote safely, there would have to be a cease-fire lasting 60 days.

Ukrainians have grown accustomed to Mr. Trump’s off-the-cuff foreign policy.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump announced in a social media post that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy cease-fire.” Neither Kyiv nor Moscow has confirmed that there is such a deal.

Mr. Zelensky said that he had discussed Mr. Trump’s announcement in a call with international allies, and that they were “awaiting details from the American side.”

“Ukraine supports the cease-fire, and it is important that Russia supports it as well,” he wrote on social media.

But shortly after Mr. Trump’s announcement, Russia struck a power plant in Kharkiv, in eastern Ukraine, according to Mr. Zelensky’s office — an attack that offered a stark indication of Moscow’s position on a possible cease-fire.

On Friday the Trump administration lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales, saying the move would lower prices.

But some question whether Russian diesel will indeed ease the pinch. And lifting sanctions on Russian diesel will undermine U. S. energy sanctions. Some European countries, including Germany, said they would stand by sanctions despite the U. S.-Russia diesel deal.

“Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war,” wrote Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, on X. “This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t.”

Online, some Ukrainians bristled at the suggestion that Washington or Moscow should dictate who leads their country, but largely dismissed Mr. Trump’s remark as domestic politicking before the midterm elections in the United States.

“Trump is trying to save his own skin ahead of the elections,” Iryna Tsariuk, an activist from Odesa, wrote in a social media post on Facebook. “He doesn’t care at all about Ukraine or the fact that Russia killed more than 70 people on Wednesday and Thursday,” she added.

Russian missile and drone strikes continued overnight Saturday to Sunday, wounding eight people in Kyiv, the capital, and killing an 11-year-old boy in Dnipro, a city in central Ukraine, according to local authorities. After Russian strikes on energy and water infrastructure, Kyiv authorities urged residents to stock up on water.

“Russia is leveling Ukrainian cities, starving people in Oleshky, killing entire families in one attack, but for some reason you won’t find Tweets that Putin has gone too far,” wrote Yarema Dukh, a political analyst and communications expert, referring to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

Even Ukrainians who oppose Mr. Zelensky have objected to Mr. Trump’s most recent remarks, arguing that decisions about Ukraine’s leadership must be made by Ukrainians.

Mr. Zelensky has faced widespread criticism in Ukraine over corruption allegations involving people in his inner circle and over his personnel decisions, including the dismissal of his popular defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov.

The share of Ukrainians who trust Mr. Zelensky has fallen from 65 percent last year to 58 percent, according to the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology.

But if anything, the rebuke from the U. S. president has the potential to unite Ukrainians. Mr. Zelensky saw a bump in support at home after Mr. Trump criticized him in a White House meeting in 2025.

"There is nothing in the world that could boost Zelensky’s approval rating today more than Trump’s childish outbursts at him, screaming that he needs to be replaced,” Mykhailo Lavrovskyi, a Ukrainian serviceman, said on X.

In Russia on Sunday, Ukrainian drones hit another major data center operated by the Russian technology giant Yandex. The center, in the Vladimir region east of Moscow, was the company’s third to be attacked in Russia over the past four days, prompting widespread internet disruptions across the country.

Web services were also knocked offline for Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg and Vkusno I Tochka, the fast-food chain that replaced McDonald’s in Russia.

In a statement on Friday, Yandex called its data centers its “iron heart” and said restoring services was a “top priority,” though “unfortunately, it is a complex challenge.”

Maria Varenikova covers Ukraine and its war with Russia.

Ivan Nechepurenko covers Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, the countries of the Caucasus and Central Asia. He divides his reporting time between Moscow and Tbilisi, Georgia.
