America’s Elected Officials Are Living in Fear

The New York Times October 11, 2026

A Times investigation has found that violent threats have become a new normal among public officials, reshaped private lives, cost millions in security and pushed people out of office.

By The New York Times

A Times investigation has found that violent threats have become a new normal among public officials, reshaped private lives, cost millions in security and pushed people out of office.

Supported by

Times Investigation

A Times investigation has found that violent threats have become a new normal among public officials, reshaped private lives, cost millions in security and pushed people out of office.

By Nick Corasaniti

Photographs by Haiyun Jiang

In January, a caller began leaving threats in the voice mail inboxes of members of Congress: “I want to see their throat cut from ear to ear.”

Another caller left a blunt threat for a U. S. senator: “I’m going to murder you, and I’m going to start with your children.”

A state attorney general received this three-word missive: “Bang, bang, bang.”

Serving in public office in the United States is dangerous. From state and local government to Congress, an unending river of violent threats is washing through the mailboxes, offices, voice mail and texts of those who govern the nation. Thousands of public servants are living, working and, in the final weeks of election season, campaigning in a state of fear.

And it’s getting worse, officeholders said in dozens of interviews.

An investigation by The New York Times examining hundreds of records obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, court documents and law enforcement logs has found that, over a two-year period from 2024 to August of this year, thousands of violent threats inundated the lives of elected officials in unprecedented ways.

Some threats were vague; some were frighteningly specific. They promised torture, stabbing, rape and murder. They aimed at Republicans and Democrats alike, and at a range of officeholders from county clerks to United States senators. They targeted spouses, parents, siblings and children.

At least 44 governors, as well as their staff and families, have been subjected to violent threats over the past two years, The Times’s investigation found. That’s also true of at least 70 of the nation’s 100 senators, and at least 185 members of the House of Representatives — nearly half the body. More than half of the country’s secretaries of state, most of whom serve as their states’ chief election officers, have received threats of violence.

Actual violence also spiked during that period: assassination attempts against Donald Trump, the killing of Charlie Kirk, the assassination of the legislative leader Melissa Hortman and her husband in Minnesota, the firebombing of Gov. Josh Shapiro’s home in Pennsylvania. For many elected officials, the escalation is a grim testament to the toxicity of violent rhetoric and how it can shake the country’s democratic institutions.

The threats have also reshaped private lives. Dozens of officials have fortified their homes, installed cameras and hired private security guards, often at their own expense. They’ve changed their daily routines, moved their children to new schools, grocery-shopped only at certain times and places. They’ve scrubbed the internet to remove personal information about themselves and their loved ones.

Some of them have altered what they say in public and, in rare cases, how they govern. Some, including members of Congress, have quit. Both parties have struggled to recruit candidates, especially women.

And policing violent threats against officials is a difficult task. The Times’s review of federal court data from the past two years found only 53 cases in which individuals were charged with threatening public officials, excluding the president.

Vague state and federal laws and free speech protections can make prosecution challenging. Anonymous letters and screen names can be hard to track. The sheer volume of threats can make hunting down those responsible virtually impossible.

This new normal can also be measured in dollars spent. In the 2017-2018 election cycle, candidates for federal office spent roughly $6 million on security-related items, according to campaign finance records. In the current midterm cycle, candidates had already spent at least $25 million by Aug. 1, with the final general election sprint still to come. That excludes what many officials are spending from their own pockets.

Overall, the threats tallied by The Times are likely undercounts; state laws and communication policies bar many offices from disclosing security issues. Many members of Congress said privately that it’s hard to imagine any remaining offices on Capitol Hill that have not experienced a violent threat this decade.

The rhetoric is abetted by the anonymity of the internet, a polarized political landscape and the entrenched public opinion that politicians are not improving American lives. Those receiving threats include divisive figures who have juiced the increasingly belligerent tone of political rhetoric, as well as others who avoid inflammatory talk but are targeted for their policies, ideology or party affiliation.

Representative Derrick Van Orden, a Republican from Wisconsin seeking re-election next month, attended the “Stop the Steal” rally on Jan. 6, 2021, in support of President Trump’s false claim that he had won the 2020 election. Mr. Van Orden was outside the U. S. Capitol that day when a mob attacked it, though he has denied entering the building. He was elected to Congress in 2022.

That’s when the threats began.

“I was a Navy SEAL for over 22 years,” Mr. Van Orden said in an interview with The Times. “I hunted terrorists around the world a lot and was very successful at that. Never had a single threat to my family. Ever.”

Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

Representative Derrick Van Orden Republican, Wisconsin

Now, Mr. Van Orden travels with armed security personnel. His family, he said, is “protected 24 hours a day.”

For much of her political career, Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former Republican House member from Georgia, injected herself into the most pitched political battles. Her liberal foes said she courted controversy to raise her profile. But her rapid rise also came at a cost.

What started out as a flood of threats primarily from the left evolved into menace from the right, too, after Ms. Greene’s break with President Trump last fall.

Former Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene Republican, Georgia

Ms. Greene’s dispute with the president centered largely on Jeffrey Epstein, the sexual predator who eventually killed himself in jail. Like many on the far right, Ms. Greene had agitated for the release of government files pertaining to Mr. Epstein. Then she began agitating directly against the president she had once fawned over, when his government refused to do so.

Her disillusionment expanded after Mr. Trump took the country to war against Iran. She believed his tariff policies and curtailment of health subsidies were hurting her constituents in rural northwest Georgia, she said, and flouting his promise to put “America First.”

Her breaking point came after the president called her a “traitor.” Of the torrent of threats that followed, one stood out. It was aimed at her son.

“That’s the one that bothers me on a visceral level,” she said.

Ms. Greene reached out to Mr. Trump, hoping for compassion from a president she had stood by for years. She forwarded copies of the threats to him, hoping that seeing the threats against her family would be enough to tone down the attacks.

She got a five-word reply from the president: “Your fault, you deserve it.”

Weeks later, Ms. Greene announced her retirement from Congress.

“I looked at what are the risks and what is the reward,” she said. “And for me, it was, I’m not going to be treated that way, and I’m not going to have my children’s lives threatened.”

A White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, did not deny the contents of Mr. Trump’s text, but he said the president condemned political violence.

“Having survived multiple assassination attempts — and having seen his dear friend Charlie be assassinated last year — no one understands the dangers of political violence more than President Trump,” he said, referring to Mr. Kirk.

Women are often more aggressively targeted than men, and harder to recruit, said Greta Neubauer, the Democratic minority leader in the Wisconsin State Assembly. Mothers are more apt to avoid the risk to themselves and their families, she said.

If potential recruits don’t bring up fears of violence on their own, Ms. Neubauer does. “There is an amount of risk that you and your family are going to need to accept if you choose to do this,” she regularly says to potential candidates. “And we want to make sure that you are fully aware of that in advance.”

Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat from Minnesota, nearly walked away, too.

He was inundated with violent threats after Kamala Harris, then the vice president, selected him as her running mate in 2024. But it was the assassination of two close friends, the former Minnesota House speaker, Melissa Hortman, and her husband, Mark, in June 2025 that led Mr. Walz to question his resolve to keep going.

Gov. Tim Walz Democrat, Minnesota

The tragedy also altered Mr. Walz’s daily life. His security team was on increased alert. He felt helpless to protect state lawmakers who felt exposed and unsafe after losing one of their own.

“We’re a part-time legislature,” Mr. Walz said. “These folks go back home and teach school, run their business, they’re dentists, they’re nurses, they do all those things. How do you follow them in the nine months they’re not here?”

A former C. I. A. analyst and Defense Department official, Senator Elissa Slotkin had been trained to deal with a variety of “threat environments.”

Her family had not. So when political foes started targeting her parents, including an ailing father, Ms. Slotkin couldn’t shield them from a toll they had not invited.

Last November, Ms. Slotkin, a Democrat from Michigan, joined five others in a video telling U. S. soldiers that they did not have to follow unlawful orders.

The message infuriated Mr. Trump, who described it as “seditious behavior from traitors” and “punishable by death.” Conservatives labeled the lawmakers the “seditious six.” The threats poured in — especially to Ms. Slotkin, the one who had posted the video on the social-media platform X.

The Capitol Police assigned round-the-clock shifts to protect her. What they couldn’t prevent: her parents’ home being swatted in the middle of the night. Her father, 81 at the time, was dying of cancer when someone called the local police with a false report that a man was killing his wife at the couple’s address.

Senator Elissa Slotkin Democrat, Michigan

The senator’s brothers put security details in front of their homes. Staff members temporarily moved out of theirs. Her father died just a few weeks after the police came to his door.

“I signed up for this, but my family and my staff did not,” Ms. Slotkin said.

Threats to family and staff feel more chilling, several officials said, and the impacts are often more disruptive.

“My daughter just sent me one yesterday,” Mr. Walz told The Times, “where somebody said, ‘Wait what I’ve got in store for you — and then a picture in front of the house.”

Mr. Van Orden moved his family because of violent threats. “I know exactly what these people are trying to do,” he said. “To make me leave the public square through threatening my family, because they know threatening me has no effect at all because of my background.”

Many officials cite a desire to improve their country for their children and grandchildren as motivation for seeking office. The deluge of threats has done the reverse, pushing the civic-minded out of the public square to shield their loved ones from an increasingly toxic world.

Carly Koppes, a Republican county election official in Colorado, saw a new kind of violent threat after her pregnancy became public: messages targeting both her and her unborn child.

Carly Koppes Weld County, Colorado, clerk and recorderRepublican

Rodric Bray, the Republican leader of the Indiana Senate, drew critics, but rarely threats, after he became a well-known power broker in Indianapolis — until his chamber bucked Mr. Trump’s push to eliminate the state’s two remaining Democratic congressional districts.

Amid headline after headline about the intraparty disagreement, threats of violence overwhelmed the staid political atmosphere of the Indiana Statehouse. Mr. Bray became the main target.

Bomb threats were called into his office. Death threats, too. “They were very short,” he said. “Just saying, I’m going to come down there and kill you.” Same with messages about his house. “Just, ‘There’s going to be a bomb mailed to your house,’ or, ‘There’s been a bomb placed at your house.’”

Mr. Bray said he forced himself into a stressful state of high alert. He changed his daily routine. He talked with his family about staying “extra vigilant” around the house and away from home. Friends kept watch. Once, law enforcement noticed something suspicious on his patio, alarming neighbors and keeping family away until it was cleared.

Rodric Bray State senator, IndianaRepublican

Ms. Koppes said she, too, changed her hours and took different routes to work after learning that some threats against her had come from a man living directly across from her office. “Good day War Criminal,” one of them read. “You traitor guilty of treason and sedition; oath breaking piece of trash loser, you should get gang raped.”

Shenna Bellows, the Democratic secretary of state in Maine, and her husband moved out of their home after law enforcement told her it wasn’t safe to stay. Ms. Bellows, Maine’s chief election officer, had been receiving threats at least since 2020, when Mr. Trump and his allies persuaded thousands of his supporters, without evidence, that the election that year had been rigged.

Ms. Bellows was swatted in 2023, a day after she removed Mr. Trump from the state’s presidential primary ballot under the Constitution’s insurrection clause. She later reversed herself after a court ruled against a similar measure in Colorado, but the threats kept coming.

In January, someone posted her cellphone number and other personal information online. Menacing voice mail and text messages poured in. Her social media was inundated. “Shenna bellows I’m coming for you,” one person wrote, adding profanity. “beheaded soon.”

Shenna Bellows Secretary of state, MaineDemocrat

Gina Hinojosa, a Democratic member of the Texas House of Representatives, was out of state when an activist posted a picture of her home online. She urged her family to move in with relatives.

“It was a feeling of being hunted,” she said.

Now the Democratic candidate for governor in Texas, Ms. Hinojosa has installed new fencing and other barriers at home “so that we’re just not as easily accessible, we’re not as easily seen.”

Officials are also buying guns. Jennifer Johnson, a county judge in rural Florida, recently purchased one and enrolled in a firearms course after an animated video of her being murdered circulated online.

Security equipment has become a huge expenditure for officeholders. Much of it has come on Capitol Hill, where, in the wake of the Jan. 6 riot, threats of violence spiked dramatically.

J. Thomas Manger took over as chief of the Capitol Police in 2021. He more than doubled his roster of investigators. Offices were fortified and modernized. Furniture was scrutinized and rearranged. District offices across the country got security assessments.

The House’s sergeant-at-arms, who oversees security in that chamber and helps govern the Capitol Police, spent more than $28 million in 2025, the second most in recent history, according to congressional records.

J. Thomas Manger Former chief, Capitol Police

Among the expenditures: $1.8 million on an alert system, and more than $200,000 on a gunshot detection system.

By the time Mr. Manger retired in May 2025, the volume of threats had gotten worse, he said.

One reason is the difficulty of mounting prosecutions, which reduces the deterrent effect, he said. Fewer than 10 percent of the cases Mr. Manger’s team investigated in 2021 led to criminal charges, he said.

Some of that is due to mitigating circumstances such as a lack of a criminal record or mental health struggles. Some of it results from the use of diversion programs such as counseling.

Making a threat is also a tricky crime to prosecute. Explicit death threats against members of Congress are illegal, but some stop short of that line and are ruled menacing, not explicit.

“One member got a photograph, an actual physical photograph, mailed to them, and it was a photograph of their, I think it was an 8-year-old child walking a dog in their neighborhood,” Mr. Manger said. “All it said on it was ‘cute dog.’”

Some officeholders don’t control government purse strings. State lawmakers, election officials, council members and school board officials are often left to fend for themselves.

Ms. Hinojosa said that almost every fortification she’s undertaken has come at personal expense.

Threats have remade how candidates run for office. Outdoor events are increasingly rare. Sweeping event spaces is a regular part of campaign advance work. Metal detectors and frisks are common. Many candidates have a security official in their inner circle.

Such measures have made candidates feel isolated, yet the public has taken notice.

Gina Hinojosa State representative and candidate for governor, TexasDemocrat

For some, at a certain point, it all becomes too much.

Ms. Greene recalled that her feud with the president came shortly after the assassination of Mr. Kirk. That made the subsequent deluge of threats more personal and more frightening.

“I said, you know what? This is just not worth it for me personally,” she said. “I’m a very happy person without being in Congress. Much happier actually. And probably a lot safer.”

Threats and violence are part of American politics, always have been. Anecdotally it feels like the menace in our political discourse is growing, but could it be quantified? How could we capture the full range of threats public officials are facing today?That was the question Nick brought to me. He had hundreds of FOIAs, correspondence and interviews with public officials, but we needed a way zoom out beyond any individual threat to show how rancor has seeped into every level of American politics. To try to answer that question, a team of journalists analyzed Congressional security spending, totaled up the threats shared with us through FOIAs and interviews with campaign staffers and reviewed hundreds of federal cases where a public official was threatened. The results were staggering.

The Times filed more than 100 open records requests for this project, reviewing thousands of violent threats made in emails, handwritten notes, social media postings, voice mail messages and police reports. The Times conducted more than 30 interviews with current and former elected officials, law enforcement officials, election officials, security experts and political operatives, while reaching out individually to every member of Congress. The Times also used artificial intelligence to compile and filter thousands of pages of court documents. Each case was manually reviewed and confirmed by Times journalists.

Produced by Leo Dominguez, Jeffrey Furticella, Rebecca Halleck, Jacob Meschke and Rumsey Taylor.

Nick Corasaniti is a Times reporter covering national politics, with a focus on voting and elections.

Haiyun Jiang is a Times photojournalist based in Washington.

Threats have altered the lives of State Representative Alma Hernandez, her family, friends and neighbors. They have even transformed her policymaking.

Alma Hernandez, an Arizona state representative, has been a target of numerous violent threats for her political positions and work as a lawmaker. Credit... Adriana Zehbrauskas for The New York Times

Supported by

By Reis Thebault

Alma Hernandez’s home used to feel like her sanctuary. Now it feels like a fortress.

In recent years she has installed cameras, alarms and a lock that opens with her fingerprint. She put iron bars on her windows and a blinding floodlight on her front porch. She cut down two trees in her yard after the police told her they could aid an intruder, and her brother moved in to protect her when the death threats intensified.

Ms. Hernandez, an Arizona state representative since 2019, did not know she was signing up for a dangerous job. But these days, serving in public office increasingly means looking over your shoulder.

“Politicians are no longer treated like we’re human,” she said.

Ms. Hernandez, a fourth-term Democratic lawmaker who is Mexican American and Jewish, has received threats from the far left and the far right. They have come in response to her outspoken support for Israel, her championing of vaccines and her first campaign, which drew attention from David Duke, a former leader of the Ku Klux Klan.

Violent threats have arrived via her social media feed, her email inbox and her office phones. Her home address has been circulated online, and her mother has received menacing calls. Last year, an aide’s car parked outside Ms. Hernandez’s house was struck by gunfire. This year, state police opened an investigation after someone sent her a social media message pledging to “find, torture and brutally murder” her and her friends, along with one of her two Chihuahuas.

So pervasive are the threats that they have altered not only Ms. Hernandez’s life, but also those of her family, friends and neighbors, who now keep a close eye on her home and warn her about suspicious activity. The intimidation has even influenced her approach to policymaking.

“I’ve asked myself, ‘Is it really worth it?’” said Ms. Hernandez, 33, who was the youngest woman ever to be elected to the Arizona Legislature. “I do wonder now, why would any 25-year-old want to do this with their life?”

Across America, threats of violence haunt the daily existence of elected officials, their staff members and their families. A New York Times investigation has found that the nation’s highest-profile politicians — including governors and members of Congress — face consistent violent harassment.

Studies show that violent threats are also rising against lower-level elected leaders, who number more than 500,000 and serve in state legislatures, city councils and school boards.

In a survey conducted this year by Princeton University and CivicPulse, nearly 20 percent of 460 local elected officials across the country reported receiving threats during the first three months of 2026. Just like at the federal level, the perilous climate is pushing some local public servants out of office early and causing others to forgo running altogether, the researchers said.

But unlike national political figures, most state and local officials have few resources to help keep them safe. Faced with violent threats, they are often left to fend for themselves. And after a Minnesota state lawmaker and her husband were assassinated last year, many say they feel more exposed than ever.

City and town officials are even more vulnerable, experts say, and they have been targeted repeatedly in Arizona in recent years. The Bridging Divides Initiative, a research center based in Princeton’s policy school, found 57 confirmed threats against Arizona county and municipal lawmakers since 2022, a figure researchers say is an undercount.

In Maricopa County, home to Phoenix, death threats toward local officials surged after the 2020 election as President Trump’s unfounded claims of voter fraud fueled a torrent of conspiracy theories. One county supervisor was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and decided not to seek re-election, while threats to two other officials resulted in a prison sentence.

At the state level, legislators from both parties have been targeted. In 2022, a former middle school music teacher emailed Senator Wendy Rogers, a Republican, and vowed to shoot her in the head. Last year, Arizona’s secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, a Democrat, allowed candidates for office to use campaign cash to pay for security, citing the dangerous political environment.

That decision helped Analise Ortiz, a Democratic state senator. Last year, her online posts alerting residents that immigration agents were near a school attracted a string of sinister threats, including several that said she would be hanged.

“Walk around with security cause I promise you three months,” one person wrote. Another said Ms. Ortiz’s “car and home and family are easy to find.”

Ms. Ortiz made a list of safe places and lived in undisclosed locations for two weeks as the threats rolled in, she said.

“It’s remarkable that in the United States of America in 2026, as a state senator, I had to fear for my life,” said Ms. Ortiz, whose district is west of Phoenix.

When she returned home, Ms. Ortiz, one of the statehouse’s leading progressives, installed a camera system and petitioned a court to conceal her address.

She also bought a gun and trained to use it.

“It’s horrible we have to think that way,” Ms. Ortiz said. “But ultimately, my home and loved ones need to be protected.”

Ms. Ortiz and Ms. Hernandez represent opposing factions of Arizona’s Democratic Party, but they agree that violent rhetoric has reshaped both of their lives.

“What she experienced and what I experienced are symptoms of the same problem,” Ms. Ortiz said.

Political violence has long shadowed the Hernandez family, three members of which have held elected office. Ms. Hernandez’s brother, Daniel, was an intern for Representative Gabrielle Giffords in 2011 when the Democratic congresswoman was shot outside a Safeway in Tucson.

Mr. Hernandez, then 20 years old, provided first aid to Ms. Giffords as an ambulance raced to the scene. Mr. Hernandez, suddenly in the national spotlight, received his first death threat three days later.

“I’ve seen people at their most unhinged, or I thought I had,” said Mr. Hernandez, who went on to serve as a state representative. “And then it keeps getting worse.”

He said he had been shocked by the amount of hate — especially the antisemitism — directed at Ms. Hernandez and their sister, Consuelo Hernandez, another Democratic state lawmaker. By late 2023, he had become so worried that he insisted on moving into Alma Hernandez’s Tucson house for extra protection. He still lives with her part-time.

Ms. Hernandez first received threats during her first term, when one of her bills so angered vaccine opponents that they flooded her social media and office with ominous messages. The bill, which would have limited vaccine exemptions, went nowhere, but the furor transformed her work: Ms. Hernandez, who has a master’s degree in public health, now says she will never again sponsor pro-vaccine legislation. The cause isn’t worth the harassment, she said.

After Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, Ms. Hernandez said the number of threats increased. She said her vocal support for the Jewish state has drawn more violent messages in the last three years than any other time in her career.

Sam Segal, Ms. Hernandez’s boyfriend, has given her pepper spray and offered to teach her to use his firearms. They’ve also rehearsed chilling scenarios. If she’s attacked by a man, Mr. Segal has told her, “kick right in the middle and run.”

“You don’t know what’s legit and what’s not,” Mr. Segal said of the threats, many of which are anonymous. “There are extremists out there who will go the whole nine yards, and I can’t be with her 24/7.”

The threats have made the couple nervous about having children, they said.

“Would we be OK with bringing a family into this environment?” Ms. Hernandez said. “Quite frankly, the answer right now is no.”

A scary moment unfolded last year, just one day before Minnesota’s former House speaker was killed.

Mr. Hernandez, who was then running for Congress, was meeting with his campaign team at Ms. Hernandez’s house when a bullet shattered the window of his aide’s car, which was parked outside. The police never found the shooter, nor did they determine whether the gunfire was targeted. But the incident deeply rattled the family.

If Ms. Hernandez wins her election in November, she will serve a two-year term in the State Senate.

She said she had not thought much about her political future beyond that. But if she could go back in time, she said, she would choose a quieter, less stressful way to begin her career.

“I would tell Alma almost nine years ago, ‘Girl, wait. Go live your life,’” Ms. Hernandez said. “This has not been an easy time.”

Nick Corasaniti contributed reporting.

Reis Thebault is a Phoenix-based reporter for The Times, covering the American Southwest.

A Russian Spy’s Lone Regret: ‘I Got Caught’

The New York Times October 11, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Though born in Ukraine, Alexsander supports the Russian cause. He wishes he had deleted one photo from his phone.

By Maria Varenikova

Reporting from Prison Colony No. 122 in central Ukraine

He does not claim to be Russia’s brightest spy.

Alexsander had really wanted the job, though. He was born in Ukraine but believed in Russia. And it was hard getting by on his shifts at McDonald’s. So when two Russian operatives approached him with the offer of a piecework spying gig, he jumped.

He was in France at the time, he said. The Russians wanted compromising material on a Western government official. Some of what Alexsander did was real field espionage, like seeing where the official lived. A lot was Google searches. Alexsander didn’t have much need for disguises.

“I had a pair of black sunglasses, but I rarely wore them. Only when the sun was shining,” he said wryly.

Alexsander’s work changed when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. He joined a Facebook group for foreigners enlisting in the Ukrainian Army. He gained other members’ trust. On trips to Ukraine, he reported to Russia the location of Ukrainian forces, their planned assault operations and their personal information. His actions, he said, led to soldiers’ deaths.

Then it all caught up with him.

Driving through northern Ukraine, Alexsander was stopped at a checkpoint. A guard asked to see his phone. He had forgotten to delete a message to his Russian boss.

“I am not saying I am a good spy,” Alexsander told me. “I got caught.”

I met Alexsander on a bright summer day in a meeting room of Prison Colony No. 122 in central Ukraine, where he will remain for the foreseeable future after pleading guilty in a Ukrainian court to the charges against him, including high treason.

It is impossible to corroborate everything he told me, though parts of his story could be confirmed through Ukrainian court documents and interviews with Ukrainian officials.

I had received a call from a shadowy contact saying that Alexsander was open to talking. The Ukrainian government has arranged throughout the war for journalists to talk to Russian prisoners. This, however, would be my first time knowingly meeting a Russian spy.

Alexsander, 42, wore a worn-out gray baseball cap, sweatpants and a tracksuit jacket with white stripes along the sleeves. He looked straight into my eyes with a playful yet penetrating stare. He leaned back leisurely in his chair, oozing self-confidence. Now and again, he smiled at a military officer who was in the room for security reasons.

I wanted to make sure that Alexsander knew what he was doing in deciding to sit down with me. “Do you realize,” I asked, “that what you tell me will be published in an article and that it will not necessarily be a positive portrait of you?”

The last part seemed to surprise him. “Why is that?” he answered.

Alexsander is proud of being a Russian spy. As far as I could tell, he just wanted the world to know his story, though he said he did not want his last name published to protect his family. He kept asking me if I was really from The New York Times. Maybe Russia would remember him, he said, and ask that he be included in a prisoner exchange.

There are 2,570 spies for Russia in Ukrainian prisons, according to Yevhen Pikalov, the deputy justice minister in Ukraine. Ninety-nine percent are Ukrainian citizens. Alexsander, who moved to Israel as a young child, is both Ukrainian and Israeli. He is the only such spy imprisoned in Ukraine, Mr. Pikalov said.

Spies still play an important role even as the war becomes defined by robotic eyes in the sky. Both sides have more weapons than ever. Old-fashioned human spying helps them find targets.

There are a few categories of spies, said Viktor Yahun, a former deputy chairman of Ukraine’s main domestic security agency.

Top-level ones are carefully controlled and rarely uncovered, he said. Catching one every six months counts as success.

Then there are lower-level spies recruited for money. Ukraine captures about 120 of those a year, according to Mr. Yahun.

These spies are a bit like the drones that both countries deploy — inexpensive to develop and produced in bulk. They are often juvenile delinquents, drunks or disgruntled soldiers recruited online for small sums, said Sean Wiswesser, a former C. I. A. station chief who spent much of his career working in the former Soviet Union.

Alexsander appeared to belong to a middle category. He seemed motivated by ideology, a supporter of Russia’s effort to control Ukraine and restore Moscow’s power and influence in Eastern Europe. No more than a dozen such agents are caught each year.

But ultimately, like all but the most valuable spies, they, too, are expendable, Mr. Wiswesser said.

Alexsander said he had served in the Israeli Army and left in 2011. He refused to describe the work he did before the two Russians approached him in France.

The Israeli Embassy in Ukraine and the Israeli defense and foreign affairs ministries in Jerusalem did not answer requests for comment on Alexsander.

The Russians, he said, proceeded slowly with him. The first time they interviewed him, they asked only simple questions, observing his behavior and trying to determine his motivation.

“I told them my ideology,” he said. “First of all, to work on the side of truth. Russia is the truth for me. So, yeah, I count myself, so to say, part of the Russian world.”

Though he was born in Ukraine, most of his family live in Russia. He said he felt alienated while living in Israel and in Western Europe, and wanted to return to his roots. Russian intelligence agencies recruit extensively in the Russian exile community, experts say.

In his early work in Europe, Alexsander was assigned to dig up dirt on a business leader. The man turned out to be squeaky clean. He declared every penny he earned to the tax authorities, never cheated on his wife and was always home for dinner, Alexsander found.

“I’ll tell you, honestly, these people are annoying,” Alexsander said.

Still, the pay was good, he said: about 5,000 euros a month, roughly $5,700.

When Russia started its full-scale war against Ukraine, Alexsander wrote in online chat groups for foreign fighters that he wanted to join the Ukrainian military. He never did, but after befriending the foreigners, he traveled to Ukraine to meet with them. He said he gave them advice, including on how to handle problems with their commanders.

Alexsander sent to Russia whatever he could glean from the soldiers and tried to thwart their efforts. Some of his work could be rather elaborate.

In France, he said, he had baited a couple of French would-be fighters into causing a car accident that got them arrested and foiled their plans to join the Ukrainian Army.

He kept at his assigned tasks for more than two years, until Sept. 10, 2024. On that day, Alexsander loaded his gray Citroën with a box of pistol ammunition and set off toward the Russian border in the northern Ukrainian region of Kharkiv. His goal was to trick foreign fighters into taking part in a sabotage operation that was actually a trap.

Instead he stumbled into a trap himself.

Alexsander never thought that a military guard at a checkpoint would ask him to open his phone. This very thorough guard found a photograph that had been sent to Russia. It showed a passport for a soldier fighting for Ukraine.

“He stuck his nose into something he shouldn’t have,” Alexsander said angrily about the checkpoint officer, breathing out cigarette smoke into an already very smoky room, stripes of sunlight hanging in the haze.

The military officer keeping watch during our interview shrugged as the conversation grew tense. He allowed the guards to bring in more cigarettes.

Alexsander took another puff and peeled off his jacket. On his right arm was a tattoo: “Amat Victoria Curam,” Latin for “Victory loves preparation.”

He said he had just one regret in life.

“If I could go back,” he said, “the only thing I’d change would be to delete that photo.”

Natalia Yermak, Michael Schwirtz and Nataliia Novosolova contributed reporting.

Maria Varenikova covers Ukraine and its war with Russia.

Where Every Tree Hides ‘an Enemy’: How I Watched China’s Paranoia Grow

The New York Times October 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

China Dispatch

Returning to China after decades away, a correspondent finds bullet trains, dazzling skylines — and a surveillance state more paranoid and pervasive than ever.

By Andrew Higgins

Photographs by Gilles Sabrié

Andrew Higgins was based in Shanghai for six months late last year and early this year, an assignment that took him around the country.

It was an enjoyable day of temple and factory visits organized by China Daily, the Communist Party’s English-language mouthpiece, but it ended on an uncomfortable note.

The group I was traveling with in the northern province of Shanxi — mostly foreign influencers hungry for followers and Chinese freebies — was told to line up behind a long banner and be filmed chanting: “Amazing China, Amazing Shanxi.”

I declined to join in, scowling in silence. But, back in my hotel room in the provincial capital of Taiyuan, I felt I had perhaps been too churlish: Getting a bunch of foreigners to chant on cue for the camera about China’s wonders was a transparent but harmless propaganda stunt.

And, to be honest, the 11th century temples we visited — and also the new highway that took us to them — were pretty amazing.

Then I received a message on WeChat, a Chinese messaging app, from an old friend in Beijing, a lawyer whose earnest decency and movie star looks always reminded me of the “good party cadre” characters in propaganda films. I had not seen him for more than 30 years and was planning to visit the following day.

Sadly, his message said, he would not be able to keep our appointment because state security officers, somehow apprised of our plans, had turned up at his door and ordered him to cancel.

China suddenly appeared not so much amazing as alarming.

After decades away from the country where I studied classical Chinese in 1980-81 and then worked as a journalist from 1987 until 1991, I returned in September last year for a six-month assignment. I marveled at how much had changed, sharing the amazement of first-time visitors awe-struck by China’s high-speed trains, dazzling modern cities and gung-ho embrace of the future.

My old friend’s message broke the reverie:

“Every bush and tree seems like an enemy soldier,” he warned, using a Chinese idiom to describe the paranoia of a security apparatus that has also changed dramatically. It has grown bigger, more intrusive and, thanks to high-tech marvels like WeChat and omnipresent surveillance cameras, much more capable of monitoring just about everyone.

China’s economic transformation over the last four decades has been extraordinary, and it infuriates Chinese officials that Western media outlets display what they see as “anti-China bias.” That is shorthand for reporting that dwells on anxiety about the economy, still growing but at a slower pace, and anything else that deviates from China’s undeniable achievements and charms.

Throughout my stay, I struggled to reconcile the reality of a country that has never been richer and seemingly full of promise with a parallel reality of brittle insecurity, in which every bush and tree hides a potential enemy.

Based in Shanghai, I often went on weekends with my wife to a park in the city’s northern Hongkou district, where groups of older Chinese gather to sing songs from their youth. Their favorite numbers are patriotic anthems but the singers, who often included a Uyghur man dressed and made up to look like Charlie Chaplin, were there of their own accord.

Their boisterous camaraderie and national pride seemed entirely genuine.

An official sign nearby, however, clouded the carefree mood: “Opposing Traitors and Guarding Against Spies Starts With Us,” it warned, with a phone number to “report espionage activity.”

The hunt for spies has escalated sharply since Xi Jinping took power in 2012 and began throttling the flow of information in and out of China, building up the Great Firewall to prevent Chinese from viewing many foreign websites.

There are seemingly no limits on what the state can see and hear, and ordinary Chinese have adapted accordingly — most noticeably with regard to the leader himself.

Mr. Xi is everywhere, on television, on billboards and on the front pages of newspapers and websites. But, throughout my stay in China, not one of the hundreds of Chinese I spoke to, mostly in private, ever uttered his name out loud. Even foreigners often avoided it, pointing at the ceiling when they wanted to refer to China’s president.

The Chinese people whom I met on my travels invariably skirted politics, except when I encountered a zealous patriot during a visit to Dazhai, a former Maoist model commune in a remote mountain area of Shanxi. “Which is better, China or America? Tell the truth!” he shouted, in between praise of China’s leadership and ridicule of the United States and Europe.

Nobody voiced open political dissent but many grumbled about the economy, particularly in places like Hainan Island where a runaway property boom has ground to a halt. A retiree from Shandong who had spent all his savings and borrowed money to buy a Hainan apartment that later lost more than a third of its value told me his much younger wife, his second, was threatening to leave him because he had fallen deeply into debt.

About the closest anyone came to openly challenging the authorities was in Shanghai when I met an out-of-town party member and his daughter outside a museum celebrating early revolutionaries.

Pushed and insulted by police officers when he started to video the entrance, which they said was forbidden, he frothed with anger, cursing them as “hooligans in uniform.” When I asked him what was wrong, he replied, using a Mao-era mantra, that the party and its servants “should serve the people but often forget that.”

His daughter, aware of the surveillance cameras planted on the narrow street, told him to shut up.

On the 150-yard walk from my Shanghai apartment in a gleaming new tower overlooking Suzhou Creek to the nearest subway, I counted more than 30 cameras trained on pedestrians. There is also a security check at the station, where guards, unfailingly polite, put all passengers’ bags through a scanner. Behind them was a cabinet stuffed with black batons, helmets and other riot control gear. Next to an ad for high-end dog food, a propaganda poster demanded vigilance against unspecified threats.

Vigilance against supposed spies in China has cursed foreign journalists looking for information, no matter how anodyne, for many decades.

When I worked there as a journalist in the 1980s, communism was crumbling next door in the Soviet Union and restlessness over corruption and one-party rule led to huge protests in Tiananmen Square. The party’s account of events after a bloody crackdown routinely accused foreign journalists of spreading “bourgeois liberalism” and stoking “counterrevolutionary turmoil.” Two American reporters were expelled for “obtaining state secrets through illegal means.”

John Burns, the veteran New York Times foreign correspondent, who died in March, was arrested in China in 1986 and charged with espionage after embarking on long motorcycle trip through the hinterland. The charges were later dropped and he was deported.

I was expelled from China in 1991 after obtaining Communist Party internal documents marked top secret and detailing a crackdown on groups accused of fomenting “splittist” sentiment — party code for cultural self-awareness — among ethnic Mongolians in the Chinese region of Inner Mongolia.

Back then, reporters were followed by furtive men who carried satchels fitted with cameras. The watchers are still there, now equipped with cellphone cameras and smart glasses.

In Dazhai, the former Maoist commune, a photographer and I were followed throughout on foot and by cars crammed with blank-faced men. In Hainan, a man followed us from the street to a sunny beach where we had decided to take a break. Pretending to talk into his cellphone, he kept its camera turned in our direction as we moved around. But the bulk of the surveillance these days is done by A. I.-powered systems that alert security agencies to communication involving people considered potential troublemakers — like foreign journalists.

WeChat and other apps available in China promise privacy, and most Chinese value the convenience they offer. But the apps are required by cybersecurity and other laws to share user data with the Chinese authorities. This facilitates snooping that, at least to many foreign journalists, smacks of digital dystopia.

Quickly realizing that any communication over WeChat risked putting old friends in the cross hairs of the security apparatus, I avoided contacting them. But one friend — the daughter of a former senior official, who was on a business trip back to China after years abroad — got in touch.

When we met for lunch in Shanghai, we reminisced about the 1980s and friends we had in common, nearly all of whom now live outside China. She raved about “Blossoms Shanghai,” a lush, 30-episode television series suffused with nostalgia for China’s roaring ’90s, a period of explosive economic growth and relative openness as the Communist Party relaxed the suffocating grip it imposed after the 1989 Tiananmen massacre.

We entirely avoided the political gossip that used to figure in our conversations. The food was excellent.

When I first went to China as a student, I lived in Jinan, an eastern center for state-owned heavy industry that reeked of coal. The city was still recovering from Mao’s Cultural Revolution, a decade of political turmoil that ended in 1976.

The economy was a wreck. Rice, cloth and even matches were in such short supply they could be bought only with ration coupons. The canteen at Shandong University, where I studied, served only greasy gruel with bits of mystery meat and steamed buns.

Time magazine had just named Deng Xiaoping, the supreme leader at the time, its “man of the year,” hailing his “visions of a new China.”

Deng was clear that the party would remain in control, but his path for China’s future was deliberately tentative. It was called “crossing the river by feeling the stones,” an admission of uncertainty that filled my university with excited debate about how to reach the ultimate goal — a China “rich and strong.”

Mr. Xi has embraced the same goal but has replaced Deng’s invitation to “feel for stones” with dogmatic certainty. The country is exhorted to show “unswerving loyalty” to Xi Jinping Thought, his blueprint for a “new era” with no room for debate.

The campus of Shandong University, open in my student days to the public, is now, like other college grounds in China, sealed off by security guards and studded with surveillance cameras.

One of the few buildings near the campus still standing from when I was a student is a huge, German-built Roman Catholic church, which had been converted into a storeroom and workshop. Lavishly renovated since, the church is now again used for religious services, though these are restricted to Christians willing to register and show their passports or ID cards.

When I first traveled by train to Jinan from Beijing, the journey took all night. It now takes under two hours. Jinan’s main railway station, a grand Art Nouveau building in the center of town built by Germans at the start of the 20th century, has been torn down, replaced by a hyper-modern structure on the outskirts.

I ran into a former classmate whom I remembered as having been something of a maverick. Now a businessman in Shanghai selling private planes, he reminisced about a time when everything was still open to discussion, except the authority of the Communist Party.

Having to constantly bite one’s tongue, he said, was a modest, if regrettable, price to pay for China’s many other changes for the better.

In Jinan, I visited the grave of the man I had often sought out as a student for his intimate knowledge of China’s now muffled past. I knew him as “Lao Wen” but his real name was James Veneris, a former American soldier who, after being taken prisoner by Chinese troops during the 1950-53 Korean War, had opted to stay with his captors and been given a job in Jinan.

Branded an American spy during the Cultural Revolution, he lost his factory job and had been assigned to haul a street cart. His Chinese wife at the time — the second of three — divorced him under duress.

When I got to know him in 1980, he had just been rehabilitated. He had a new wife and a new job teaching English at the university. Eager to avoid getting in trouble again, he plastered his campus apartment with portraits of Mao and Hua Guofeng, the new Communist Party chairman after Mao’s death.

He was alarmed when I told him that Hua’s portraits had suddenly disappeared from my lecture hall, a sure sign that he, too, had been purged.

“It’s all so damn confusing,” he groaned. Lao Wen died in Jinan in 2001.

His marble tombstone, paid for by his son, who moved to America, is in a serene new cemetery on the outskirts of Jinan. A gold inscription in English says he had not died, “just disappeared.” A Chinese inscription on the reverse side remembers him as an “American who loved peace, loved life and loved the people of China.”

His many travails are passed over in silence.

The silence that engulfs so much of China’s past reaches a sinister crescendo in Tiananmen Square, which I had last visited on the night of June 3-4, 1989, when soldiers seized it back from protesting students amid a hail of gunfire.

By the time I left Beijing in 1991, roads around Tiananmen had all been repaved to remove traces of tank tracks. The square had again become a public space filled with people flying kites and playing with their children.

Today, the Chinese capital’s main public square is no longer a place to relax like Red Square in Moscow or Trafalgar Square in London, but a by-appointment-only dead zone. Kites are banned without a permit. All visitors, mostly Chinese from the provinces, are carefully screened.

Before my wife and I could visit in January, we had to apply for permission via WeChat. Once approved, we waited in line for two hours, showing our passports and computer-generated permission notification at three separate checkpoints with airport-style security.

At the final check, a guard pounced on a pen carried by my wife, insisting it contained red ink, which she said was prohibited. She did not say why, but during the 1989 student protests several people hurled red paint at a famous portrait of Mao that faces the square. A security supervisor finally let us through after writing with the pen on a piece of paper and seeing that it was brown, not red.

Now out of China, I often wonder: How can it be that a proud, nuclear-armed world power is scared of red ink?

Andrew Higgins is the East and Central Europe bureau chief for The Times based in Warsaw.

ICE Emails Discuss Using Palantir-Supported Tool to Investigate Voter Fraud

Wired October 08, 2026

As the Trump administration has carried out a nonstop effort to undermine the midterm elections this year, the Department of Homeland Security appears to have looked into whether it could use a Palantir-supported tool to track people it believes have voted illegally.

The revelation is found in a tranche of documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request and published this week by Democracy Forward, a legal advocacy group. As well as revealing that DHS officials have investigated over 150 nonprofit groups in search of evidence they’re helping noncitizens register to vote, the documents show how Immigration and Customs Enforcement is now central to federal voter fraud investigations.

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from Freedom of Information Act requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

More specifically, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)—one of ICE’s two major components—is spearheading the effort to uncover voter fraud, with its Innovation Lab (known internally as iLab) developing tools for agents.

ICE, it seems, wants to build “a system that is going to get good at determining how to find people to investigate and potentially bring action against,” Chinmayi Sharma, an associate professor at Fordham Law School who has closely tracked the Palantir-supported tool called ELITE, tells WIRED.

“You would want to build off of what already exists, what might already have the infrastructure and data sources that you would want,” says Sharma.

“iLab’s processing focuses on DOJ voting rolls and [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] data; criminal histories are currently excluded, with efforts underway to address this,” a worker in HSI’s Countering Transnational Organized Crime unit wrote on May 26 in an email with “Voter Fraud” in the subject line. (Like other workers, their name was redacted in the records released to Democracy Forward.)

“Coordination with iLab continues,” they wrote, “particularly on ingesting processed voter roll data into the ELITE enforcement system to enhance lead management, analytical review, and investigative tracking.”

The existence of ELITE, which stands for Enhanced Leads Identification & Targeting for Enforcement, was first reported in January by 404 Media, which revealed that ICE agents using the tool can create maps featuring potential deportation targets, pull up files on each target, and see a “confidence score” on the person’s current address.

“Voter roll data has never been integrated into ELITE,” a Palantir spokesman tells WIRED.

ELITE was again mentioned in a July 7 email with an attachment named “Fraud WAR”—WAR typically refers to a weekly activity report—from a DHS worker who shared an update on the agency’s “election integrity investigations,” including the news that Connecticut, Georgia, Kentucky, Missouri, Michigan, and New Mexico had “been enriched by the iLab and are pending Palantir entry into ELITE.”

What specifically was enriched and pending Palantir entry is unclear from the records, but in another email in the same chain, a DHS official said that someone from the agency would send the update to the White House.

“ICE does not disclose the existence of investigative methods and techniques,” an agency spokesperson tells WIRED.

“While ICE Homeland Security Investigations is not able to comment on any active investigations, HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED.

The White House did not comment on ICE’s possible use of ELITE to track noncitizen voters in a statement provided to WIRED.

The claim that noncitizens are voting in numbers sufficient to sway the outcomes of US elections has been a central narrative pushed by the Trump administration in the run-up to next month’s midterms. All available evidence shows that noncitizen voting is vanishingly rare.

DHS, under secretary Markwayne Mullin, has led the charge on identifying noncitizen voters but has so far only found a handful of possible cases. Earlier this week, the Justice Department announced it had brought charges in 16 cases involving foreign nationals allegedly committing voting-related crimes. (All were lawful permanent residents.) Last month, a whistleblower alleged that federal employees directed by DHS leadership may have broken the law when they searched state websites for illegally registered voters.

While Mullin and the Trump administration have been vocal with their claims about noncitizen voting and short-term victories ahead of the midterms, in the background, ICE appears to have been working on tools that will work in the long term.

The May 26 email sent under a “Voter Fraud” subject line characterizes a weekly report as emphasizing “a network-based investigative approach, prioritizing organization and facilitation analysis over individual leads, now stated as a strategic direction.”

The language used in the documents related to the agency’s new approach to identifying voter fraud suggests this system was not live or even in pre-deployment at the time, but rather being built for the future, Sharma believes.

“I could be wrong,” says Sharma, “but there's a reason you choose to build voter fraud [investigations] within DHS when it does not intuitively fall within what you would think of as DHS's purview, and I think it's because of the authorities, the infrastructure, the vendor relationships, the contract vehicles, and privileges. There's just a lot of synergies you can take advantage of.”

To refresh everyone's memories a little bit, Musk is the founder and main donor of America PAC, a super PAC that was started in 2024 to help elect President Donald Trump to the White House. They succeeded. Trump is in office. The PAC spent more than $260 million to make that happen. This time around for November's midterms, the PAC has been going about it a little bit differently. WIRED created a live tracker to monitor their donations in real time. You can check it out on the WIRED website. And we learned a lot putting this together. Basically, the PAC is donating to the election's most consequential races. They are not focusing obviously on the presidential race. There is no presidential race this year. But they are all in on the most critical Senate races in the country that are really going to decide the makeup of Congress next year. The PAC is primarily pumping money against Democrats as opposed to for Republicans, which is really interesting. For every dollar that America PAC has spent supporting a Republican candidate, more than two have gone to oppose a Democrat. And that only becomes more extreme in some of these Senate races, right? In Texas where several Musk companies are based, the group has spent tons and tons of money attacking Democrat James Talarico. We're talking like $9 million. Whereas promoting Ken Paxton, around the one million mark. Similar numbers can be found in the Ohio Senate race, in Iowa, really up and down the board. And these races are not random. They represent the path for Democrats to take control of the chamber this November and could open Republicans, Musk included, up to a lot of investigations and regulatory pressure. So this is critical for so many reasons. I'm so excited to talk with you about it. What did you think of the tracker? Did you get a chance to play around with it?

Zoë Schiffer: I did get a chance to play around with it. I was really impressed, not least because you coding something for the internet, an app and web, honestly, groundbreaking.

Leah Feiger: I can take zero, zero coding credit. This all goes to our amazing investigations team who really knocked it out of the park. They did.

Zoë Schiffer: Well, jokes aside. No, I think it's really important. I mean, like you said, the total spending on America PAC's part is less than what they spent previously, but it's much more targeted. They're being really specific. And that's because the stakes are really high. I feel like we should just back up for a second and talk about that. Because there is this chance that Congress flips, that Democrats take control, and it seems like Musk and his associates are taking that very, very seriously.

Leah Feiger: Oh, as they should. Democrats are already telling us, all of our sourcing in Democrats, both on House and Senate side are hungrily talking about all of the investigations and subpoenas that they're going to release the minute that the chamber is theirs. And right now, the polls are looking pretty good for them. This is very much a, if Dems don't mess this up, they have a very good chance of making this happen. I can only imagine that Musk and a similar coterie of fellows are kind of freaking out right now.

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, I am on the record and I'm going to say it again, I think Republicans are going to do just fine. I feel like we've had this conversation before, and I'm sus on the polling. However, you are the politics director, so ultimately I defer to you. That said, I think it is 100 percent true that Musk takes the possibility of investigations and regulations really, really seriously. This was a primary reason why he ultimately decided to go all in on Donald Trump. He said very publicly that if Kamala Harris won the presidential election during the last cycle, the whole country was going to look like California, which was the worst thing that could happen to it, apparently. As someone from California, I disagree, but neither here nor there. It is really hard to build things here. I'll give you that. That said, I find it very hard to imagine a world where really harsh regulations actually do come down on the Elon Musk empire. I think part of the reason for that is SpaceX, and just how dependent the government is on Starlink, on SpaceX technology, on their ability to get stuff into space. SpaceX is the company doing that on behalf of the government now. And so while I do think subpoenas, all of this stuff could happen, will it impact Elon Musk's empire ultimately? I don't know if we have the tools to hold someone like that accountable at this point, frankly.

Leah Feiger: I think that's a really, really good point, honestly. And obviously there's a clear fear that a Lina Khan-esque figure could come in and wreak havoc. But to your point, that havoc will be paperwork. No, I hear you. I hear you.

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, think about it. The one time he was held accountable in a real way was for saying that he had money to take Tesla private. He had funding secured to take Tesla private. What was the outcome of that? He was fined $20 million? How much is Elon Musk worth? Ultimately, even if that number hurts, he doesn't want to pay it, it's kind of a drop in the bucket.

Leah Feiger: No, he's a trillionaire now, again, I guess. And I guess to that point, this is not the first time that super PACs or big money in politics has stirred up a little bit of controversy. We had this big conversation in 2024 about how crazy it was that Elon Musk was just throwing money at the wall, and now he's throwing money again via America PAC, which now feels like a pattern, and it feels like other tech founders and their influence and their PACs are already outsized in this administration. You have PACs from all sorts of groups up and down Silicon Valley that are very involved this election cycle. I'm really interested in what you're hearing about how folks are thinking about this midterm cycle and how they're kind of thinking more future.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I mean, Silicon Valley is not a monolith. You hear a lot from the really loud voices in the room, and a lot of those voices are people who have gone all in on supporting President Trump and the Republican Party. And I think those people kind of align with Elon Musk in some of the fears that you have said, that there will be investigations, that if Democrats take control, it'll slow growth, that they won't be able to lead the race in AI and these other areas. And so they need to go all in and protect that future that they want to see happen. Of course, there are a lot of rank-and-file employees who have more liberal values, and they are staying a little more quiet, but they are contributing to different causes. It's an interesting conversation in the Valley right now because there are a lot of newly minted millionaires, people who worked in AI research and now have a ton of money, and they are having active conversations on what is the best way to deploy, to allocate capital right now? Where do we put the money to have the biggest effect? Is it in philanthropy? Is it in politics? If it's in politics, where should we contribute? There's not one defining take right now, but it is definitely a topic of conversation. Leah, as you and our listeners both know, the debate over AI safety has been everywhere lately. It has escaped containment in a big way. And in that debate, there is one central philosophy that keeps coming up again and again, and it's starting to become kind of the center of attention, effective altruism. Last month, AI researcher Jacob Coxon loudly voiced support for one of effective altruism's central concerns, that advanced AI could destroy humanity. This kicked off a wave of headlines and a pretty intense response from the Trump administration. Senior Pentagon officials labeled effective altruism as a, quote, unquote, "dangerous ideology" and an official Department of Defense social media account implored people to choose, quote, "Americanism, not effective altruism." So we're really seeing these dividing lines. But Leah, just to back up a little bit, when did you become aware, because you're not in Silicon Valley, you're in New York, when did you learn about effective altruism?

Leah Feiger: What's amazing is I can actually pinpoint it to, I would say, maybe 16 months ago, and it was from you. We were on a phone call, and you were like, "Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. And this person is all in on effective altruism." And I was like, "I have no idea what that means. I have never heard of this before. I have never heard of this belief." And you should really describe it to our listeners, but it really, really helped me understand that there was a split in Silicon Valley over AI. I wasn't aware of that before. I just though that people were like, "Yep, we work for these companies. We're ready to go." And you took me through the effective altruists in Anthropic and different side in OpenAI, and it was, I'm sure, like the kindergarten version, but it was really, really helpful. So please take it away.

Zoë Schiffer: So at a very basic level, effective altruism is a belief system built around the idea that people should use their time, money, and resources as efficiently as possible to improve or even save the lives of as many people and animals as they possibly can. At its core, it doesn't fundamentally have anything to do with AI specifically. It really is how can we make as much money as possible and then deploy it in such a way to help as many people as possible or save as many people as possible? This concept or these ideas of effective altruism were popularized by blogs like LessWrong, which is fringe, but in Silicon Valley, it did have a real prominence in the early 2000s. There was researchers at Oxford talking about it. The reason that AI has become a part of this is a lot of the AI researchers came up in this philosophy and they see AI as a true existential risk. And if you're concerned with the welfare of humanity, and then you start to engage a lot with a technology that you think maybe doesn't have a huge risk, but nonetheless a substantial risk of killing everyone, then that becomes the central concern. I think one thing though that I wanted to just lay out, far be it from me to come out swinging for effective altruists, but like any movement, it's a spectrum. You have people who are real fanatics. And when you hear their viewpoints and the trade-offs that they would make to save a maximum number of people, that kind of utilitarian belief system, it sounds totally nutty. But I talk to a ton of people who identify as effective altruists who are completely normal. I was going to say rational, but that feels really loaded in this context. But they're thinking about it really deeply. They don't sound like religious fanatics. They don't seem like people who are members of a cult. And it's not like all these people are getting together and talking. It's a movement, it's widespread. There are different groups.

Leah Feiger: And when you apply it to AI, there is something that I find there's an appealing aspect where you're saying, look, we're just saying that we should be concerned about where this technology is going to go and what it could do to people. That's the baseline, right? Is that a pretty decent summary?

Zoë Schiffer: 100 percent. And if you thought that you were working on a technology that might, 10% chance, kill everyone, the rational thing to do would be to quit and warn everyone about it. So in that sense, what Jacob Coxon did isn't completely shocking. But it has been very interesting to see this go fully mainstream. We have seen AI researchers who are really concerned about AI safety go on Tucker Carlson, Joe Rogan. And again, the Venn diagram of effective altruists and AI safety researchers, it's not a perfect circle, but there is a fair amount of overlap.

Leah Feiger: So OK, Sam Altman, OpenAI, Dario Amodei, Anthropic. Dario has talked about AI being a risk for the world. So would he be in the EA category?

Zoë Schiffer: OK, this is a very, very loaded question. So Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, worked with Dario Amodei for a while. They were both at OpenAI. Then Dario quit, along with a small group of OpenAI researchers and started a new company specifically to try and build AI safely to benefit all of humanity, etc., etc. And they didn't feel like they could do that at OpenAI. So there you get a clear split between, and this is not how they identify, but this is how people categorize them. Sam Altman kind of represents the growth at all costs, capitalist view of artificial intelligence. Dario represents more of the effective altruism, let's do it safely. We have to be the ones to win because only we understand the real risks involved. Dario has said, I believe, in more recent months and years that he doesn't identify as an effective altruist. That said, a lot of the beliefs do overlap. And I think that you do get a sense from talking to Anthropic researchers that a lot more of them appear to fall into the effective altruism philosophy.

Leah Feiger: Are there Slack channels for this? Are there parties? I'm so curious, now that this has escaped into a mainstream lexicon, I'm very interested beyond just the Pentagon being like, be pro-American, say no, how this is going to kind of continue.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I mean, yes, there are group chats. I'm sure there are Slack channels. There's a place in Berkeley called Lighthaven, that's kind of a conference center/group house co-op situation that hosts events. Last time I was there, the possibility of sleeping in one of their bunk beds came up. I was like politely decline forever. No, thank you. But anyway, it's interesting because, as this has gone more mainstream, like you said, the Trump administration has come out and they have really used effective altruism as kind of a overall term to say these people are almost religious fanatics, and they're anti-growth and they're anti-AI progress, and thus they're anti-American. Where of course there is a lot more nuance here. And I think a lot of these people are just trying to take AI safety really seriously. But now you're seeing effective altruism becoming kind of like a slanderous term to say we can't and shouldn't take these people seriously.

Leah Feiger: Why is this controversial? What you're saying doesn't sound that bad. We're just trying to save humanity?

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. Yes. I think one reason is that it's all about trade-offs. And when taken to the extreme, you can see how if your goal is to maximize good or minimize harm, there is a certain amount of harm you would be willing to take, or be a part of, I guess, in order to save a greater number of people. And I think people, somewhat rightly so, get a little freaked out that in an effort to eliminate the possibility that greater harm will be done, effective altruists would be willing to do somewhat harmful things in the present moment because they think they're protecting people from something that could happen later on. And I think the other part, and this is one that I definitely am thinking about, is if you think that you are the only company that's taking AI safety seriously, then you "winning," quote, unquote, the AI race is really important. And what wouldn't you do to win if you think the stakes are humanity level extinction?

Leah Feiger: I kind of think that everyone involved in this conversation sort of needs to enroll at Oberlin for a philosophy 101 class. That's maybe what I'm feeling right now.

Zoë Schiffer: I think Oberlin is what got us into this mess, perhaps. Oberlin philosophy specifically.

Leah Feiger: 102. Philosophy 102. It's the next chapter. Now that you've moved on from Slavoj Žižek, what comes next?

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my gosh. Moving on, it's been a few weeks since Meta released its new AI assistant Muse, and honestly, it's been kind of an unexpected hit for the company. It is still topping the app charts. But the reason that I wanted to talk to you about this is a really interesting situation played out in the Bay Area a few weeks ago. The designer, a freelance designer and lettering artist, Jessica Hische, who was hired by Meta to help design the Muse logo, told her newsletter subscribers like, "Hey, I did this project." In fact, I think the title of the newsletter was “New Work! (Don't be mad at me).” She kind of knew she was going to get some flack from people. But she basically said, "Look, Meta hired me to do this project. Ultimately, I think a big company should be commended for hiring an independent artist instead of just generating a new logo. Here's how the design process went. Hope you like it." That was kind of the message. One of her newsletter subscribers posted it on Threads. You forgot this was a thing. Threads is still very much a thing in the design world.

Leah Feiger: I did forget. I fully forgot.

Zoë Schiffer: And people flipped out. She had people saying they were disgusted with her, disappointed, that they'd followed her since she was in art school and they could never support anything she did again. People were posting photos of her house and speculating about her finances. She felt like the entirety of Threads was like a mob attacking her for three days for having come out and said she was doing this work. Yeah.

Leah Feiger: That's really intense.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, it was a lot. It was really interesting to talk to her because she actually has kind of complicated feelings about AI. She said her husband has worked in this field, and they actually had some disagreements because he was really excited about the technology. It honestly was very AI wife coded, if you read that article. And she was like, "Well, no, this could be really bad for commercial art." Artists who, to support their less highly paid artwork, work for companies occasionally like she does, this could be detrimental. And in fact, that is what Jessica Hische does. She has two shops in Oakland. They're really cute. One is kind of a stationary store. The other one is a space where she hosts kind of kid art workshops and classes and stuff. And she basically fully funds those by taking on corporate work. But she said in the past couple years, her corporate work had really dried up, and that she wasn't getting as many inquiries as she usually does. So when Meta came to her, she was like, "I didn't even feel that conflicted about it. I was like, Oh my gosh, I want to offer one of my employees a health plan. I need to not be so stressed every time Gusto pings me and says I have to run payroll. Yeah, I'll take this." She was paid. Guess how much you're paid if you redesign the Muse logo.

Leah Feiger: I mean, it's Meta. You should be paid half a million dollars in equity.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, you would think. No, she was paid $12,500 more or less.

Leah Feiger: No. No, that's the worst part. That's actually the worst part of this whole story.

Zoë Schiffer: I know. Yeah. She was like, "I thought it was kind of amazing for two days of work." Because it was a sprint. She was just talking about designing the M at first, and then she got a bit more for doing the full typeface of Muse. But yeah, it wasn't even that much. And again, she's using the money to support her small businesses in Oakland. But she said there was a huge contingent of people on Threads who seemed like they were really AI purists, and fundamentally were like, "There is just simply no excuse for working on this technology." And they really saw her decision to work on it as a signal of support.

Leah Feiger: I'm mixed here. I don't know. Go after the company, not the artist is sort of how I feel. But I get that that's not as juicy or exciting as yelling at someone personally on a social media app.

Zoë Schiffer: A social media app that is owned by Meta, to be clear.

Leah Feiger: Really important point there. Yep. Does she regret it?

Zoë Schiffer: It's interesting. I asked her that question and she said ultimately no. She kind of weighed like, "Do I regret talking about it?" But she said ultimately she felt like she was doing a good thing for artists by commending a company that had hired an independent artist. She was like, "These big tech companies are not going to hire artists if they feel like that artist is then going to go slam them on social media. Ultimately, these companies exist and there can be some sort of symbiotic relationship with them," which I'm personally sympathetic to.

Leah Feiger: It's not an Uncanny Valley episode if I'm not at least mentioning or thinking about “Silicon Valley,” the TV show. And I can't not think about the artist in the show who is designing Gavin Belson's box and what that took. And I just remember watching it and being like, why are you putting yourself through this? But also everyone needs a salary. It was painful. Oh, wow. That's a complicated one. That's a little bit tough to hear.
